meta.title: Legal Aspects of Banking
meta.description: 402 questions covering the full syllabus across 9 modules, plus a dedicated Case Studies bank

modules.title: Module 3: Torts, Criminal Law & Special Circumstances
Module 5: Regulation, Customer Types & Company Law
Module 6: Secured Lending Principles & Key Legislation

questionBank.q: Which concept is defined as a body of rules prescribed by controlling authority, having binding legal force and subject to legal sanction?
opts: Morality, as standards of conduct studied under ethics in a society.
Law, as prescribed and enforced by controlling authority with legal sanction.
Religion, as a system of faith and worship linking humanity to a deity.
Convention, as a source courts draw on to fill gaps in contracts.
questionBank.ans: Law, as prescribed and enforced by controlling authority with legal sanction.
questionBank.exp: Manual, 'Introduction to Law': Black's Law Dictionary defines law as a body of rules prescribed by controlling authority and having binding legal force, subject to sanction. Morality, religion, and conventions are distinct concepts from the same section.

questionBank.q: Which concept is concerned with standards and rules of conduct in a society, studied under ethics, rather than enforced by state sanction?
opts: Criminal Law, which punishes individuals for flouting laid-down rules.
Morality, which comprises the standards and rules of conduct studied in ethics.
Religion, which comprises a system of faith and worship linked to a deity.
Civil Law, which regulates private relationships between individuals.
questionBank.ans: Morality, which comprises the standards and rules of conduct studied in ethics.
questionBank.exp: Manual distinguishes morality from law as standards and rules of conduct in a society, studied in ethics. A, C, and D are the other classifications/concepts from the same section, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Which concept involves a system of faith and worship, speaking to a relationship between humanity and a supreme being, distinct from legally binding rules?
opts: Morality, as ethical standards of conduct enforced by social disapproval.
Religion, as a system of faith and worship involving a relationship with a deity.
Civil Law, as a system regulating private relationships between individuals.
Criminal Law, as a system punishing individuals for flouting laid-down rules.
questionBank.ans: Religion, as a system of faith and worship involving a relationship with a deity.
questionBank.exp: Manual distinguishes religion from law as a system of faith and worship involving a relationship between humanity and a deity. A, C, and D are the other distinguished concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A dispute between two private companies over a breached supply contract, with no state prosecution, falls under which classification of law?
opts: Criminal Law, which punishes individuals for crimes against the state.
Civil Law, which regulates private relationships between individuals or entities.
Religion, which governs relationships built on faith and worship.
Morality, which governs ethical standards outside formal legal enforcement.
questionBank.ans: Civil Law, which regulates private relationships between individuals or entities.
questionBank.exp: Manual: civil law regulates private relationships between individuals in a community or society, unlike criminal law which punishes offenders. A, C, and D are unrelated distinguished concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A person is prosecuted by the state and sentenced to imprisonment for an offence. Which classification of law governs this outcome?
opts: Civil Law, which regulates private relationships between individuals.
Criminal Law, which punishes individuals for crimes or flouting laid-down rules.
Morality, which governs ethical standards outside formal legal enforcement.
Religion, which governs relationships built on faith and worship.
questionBank.ans: Criminal Law, which punishes individuals for crimes or flouting laid-down rules.
questionBank.exp: Manual: criminal law punishes individuals for crimes or for flouting laid-down rules, distinct from civil law's private-relationship focus. A, C, and D are unrelated concepts from the same section, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Under the Interpretation Act, a statutory provision drafted using masculine pronouns such as 'he' should ordinarily be read to also include which group?
opts: Only male officers of a company, as strictly construed in banking statutes.
Females, since words importing the masculine gender include females.
Only natural persons, excluding all incorporated bodies referred to elsewhere.
Only the specific individual named in the enactment's preamble.
questionBank.ans: Females, since words importing the masculine gender include females.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.14(a): 'words importing the masculine gender include females.' A, C, and D invent restrictions not found in the material.

questionBank.q: Under the Interpretation Act, an enactment referring to 'director' in the singular should, unless a contrary intention appears, be read to also cover which of the following?
opts: Only the first director named in the company's Memorandum of Association.
'Directors' in the plural, since singular includes the plural.
Only directors appointed after the enactment's commencement date.
Only directors who have personally consented in writing to be bound.
questionBank.ans: 'Directors' in the plural, since singular includes the plural.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.14(b): 'words in the singular include the plural and words in the plural include the singular.' A, C, and D invent restrictions not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: Under the Interpretation Act, which of the following is expressly excluded from the statutory meaning of the term 'land'?
opts: Buildings, which are expressly excluded from the definition of land.
Minerals, which are expressly excluded even though land includes buildings.
Fixtures, which are expressly excluded from the definition of land.
Boundaries, which are expressly excluded from the definition of land.
questionBank.ans: Minerals, which are expressly excluded even though land includes buildings.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.18(1): 'land' includes any building and any other thing attached to the earth, 'but does not include minerals.' A, C, and D reverse or invent exclusions not in the material.

questionBank.q: Under the Interpretation Act, the expression 'to sell' is defined to include which of the following beyond a completed transfer for a price?
opts: To exchange, to barter, and to offer or expose for sale.
To lease, to mortgage, and to grant a right of occupancy.
To donate, to bequeath, and to transfer by way of gift.
To auction, to tender, and to accept a bid in a public sale.
questionBank.ans: To exchange, to barter, and to offer or expose for sale.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.18(1): '"to sell" includes to exchange and to barter and to offer or expose for sale.' B, C, and D invent transactions not listed in the definition.

questionBank.q: Under the Interpretation Act, how does the law treat the 'signature' of a person who is physically unable to write his name?
opts: It is treated as invalid unless a Magistrate countersigns it.
To 'sign', in relation to such a person, means to make his mark.
It is treated as invalid unless two independent witnesses attest to it.
It is treated as valid only if accompanied by a verified thumbprint.
questionBank.ans: To 'sign', in relation to such a person, means to make his mark.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.18(1): 'to "sign" in relation to a person who is unable to write his name, means to make his mark.' A, C, and D invent formalities not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: Under the Interpretation Act, the expression 'writing' is defined to include which of the following modes of representing words?
opts: Only handwritten script, as typed material is expressly excluded.
Printing, lithography, photography, typewriting, and other visible forms.
Only documents bearing an official government seal or stamp.
Only documents drafted in the English language.
questionBank.ans: Printing, lithography, photography, typewriting, and other visible forms.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.18(1): 'writing' and expressions referring to writing include printing, lithography, photography, typewriting and other modes of representing or reproducing words in visible form. A, C, and D invent restrictions not in the material.

questionBank.q: The document a customer signs to open an account, which forms the legal basis of the banker/customer relationship, is best described as which of the following?
opts: A unilateral declaration binding only the bank to its terms.
The Bank Account Opening Forms, the contract document between the parties.
A conditional offer that only becomes valid upon court confirmation.
An implied arrangement requiring no signed documentation.
questionBank.ans: The Bank Account Opening Forms, the contract document between the parties.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'the relationship is contractual, and the contract document is the Bank Account Opening Forms.' A, C, and D misstate the nature of that document.

questionBank.q: Bank Account Opening Forms, where the offeror predetermines terms for the offeree to accept without change, are typical examples of which type of contract?
opts: A collateral contract existing alongside the main banking agreement.
A standard form contract, with predetermined terms for acceptance.
A conditional contract contingent on the offeree's satisfaction.
A quasi-contract arising by operation of law rather than agreement.
questionBank.ans: A standard form contract, with predetermined terms for acceptance.
questionBank.exp: Manual: Bank Account Opening Forms 'typify a contract where the offeror predetermines the terms of the contract which should be accepted by the offeree without any change,' described as a standard form contract. A, C, and D are unrelated contract-law terms.

questionBank.q: Terms of a contract that are specifically agreed between the parties, whether written or oral, and are always unambiguous, are known as which of the following?
opts: Implied terms, intended to be read into the contract by a court.
Express terms, issues specifically agreed between the parties.
Collateral terms, existing outside the main written agreement.
Customary terms, arising from the general practice of the industry.
questionBank.ans: Express terms, issues specifically agreed between the parties.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Express Terms - These are issues between the parties to a contract that are specifically agreed... they are always unambiguous.' A, C, and D are not the concept described.

questionBank.q: Terms that a court will read into a contract only where there are genuine gaps in what the parties have agreed are known as which of the following?
opts: Express terms, as they are specifically agreed upon and unambiguous.
Implied terms, included only where there are gaps in the contract.
Fundamental terms, whose breach strikes at the root of the contract.
Warranties, whose breach is less serious and remediable by damages.
questionBank.ans: Implied terms, included only where there are gaps in the contract.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Implied Terms - Implied terms will be included by the Court only where there are gaps in the contract.' A, C, and D are other real contract-term concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: When a court fills a gap in a banking contract, which of the following sources does the manual identify as one the court may draw upon outside the contract's own terms?
opts: The personal preference of the presiding judge, exercised independently.
The subsequent actions of the parties after the contract was formed.
A newly enacted law that did not exist at the time of formation.
The unilateral instructions issued afterward by only one party.
questionBank.ans: The subsequent actions of the parties after the contract was formed.
questionBank.exp: Manual: courts draw on laws relevant to the contract, conventions, and 'actions of the Parties subsequent to the Contract' to fill gaps. A, C, and D are not among the listed sources.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best captures the meaning of 'legally enforceable' and 'consensus ad idem' as characteristics of a valid contract?
opts: That the agreement creates rights and obligations and reflects a meeting of minds.
That the agreement must be registered with a government agency to take effect.
That the agreement must be witnessed by a Magistrate to be admissible in court.
That the agreement must involve at least one incorporated company as a party.
questionBank.ans: That the agreement creates rights and obligations and reflects a meeting of minds.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a contract is 'legally enforceable (i.e. which creates rights and imposes obligations on the parties)' and 'implies a meeting of the parties' minds (i.e. consensus ad idem).' B, C, and D invent formalities not in the material.

questionBank.q: A contract signed only because one party threatened the other with harm unless they agreed would fail which essential characteristic of a valid contract?
opts: That it creates legally enforceable rights and obligations.
That it is free or voluntary, and not induced by duress or undue influence.
That it reflects consensus ad idem, or a meeting of the minds.
That only parties to the contract may enforce its terms and benefits.
questionBank.ans: That it is free or voluntary, and not induced by duress or undue influence.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a contract 'must be free or voluntary i.e. not induced by duress, undue influence, mistake or misrepresentation.' A, C, and D are other real contract characteristics, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: The principle that generally prevents a person who is not a party to a contract from enforcing its terms or enjoying its benefits is known as which of the following?
opts: Quantum Meruit, for pro-rated payment on part-performance.
Privity of Contract, limiting enforcement to the contracting parties.
Consensus ad idem, requiring a genuine meeting of the parties' minds.
Consideration, being the value given for value received in a contract.
questionBank.ans: Privity of Contract, limiting enforcement to the contracting parties.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Usually, only parties to a contract can enforce the terms of the contract and/or enjoy the benefits that flow from the contract. This principle is known as Privity of Contract.' A, C, and D are other real principles, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A contractor who partially completes a divisible construction contract before termination may still be entitled to pro-rated payment for work done, under which principle?
opts: Privity of Contract, since only parties may enforce the contract.
Quantum Meruit, for part-performance of a valid divisible contract.
Consensus ad idem, requiring a genuine meeting of minds.
Compliance with formality, requiring certain contracts to be in writing.
questionBank.ans: Quantum Meruit, for part-performance of a valid divisible contract.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Quantum Meruit. This principle stipulates that part-performance of a valid divisible contract attracts pro-rated payment thereon.' A, C, and D are other real principles, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A fundamental term of a contract, whose breach strikes at the root of the agreement and usually nullifies the contract, is known as which of the following?
opts: A warranty, a less serious term remediable by damages.
A condition, a fundamental term whose breach nullifies the contract.
An implied term, read into the contract only where gaps exist.
An express term, specifically agreed upon and always unambiguous.
questionBank.ans: A condition, a fundamental term whose breach nullifies the contract.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Conditions - A condition is another name for a fundamental term in a contract. A breach of a fundamental term strikes at the root of a contract...it nullifies the contract.' A, C, and D are other real term-classifications, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A less serious term of a contract, whose breach can usually be remedied through damages rather than nullifying the whole agreement, is known as which of the following?
opts: A condition, a fundamental term whose breach nullifies the contract.
A warranty, a term whose breach is less serious and remediable in damages.
An implied term, included by the court only where gaps exist.
An express term, specifically agreed upon and always unambiguous.
questionBank.ans: A warranty, a term whose breach is less serious and remediable in damages.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Warranties - A warranty is not a fundamental term of a contract. A breach of a warranty is less serious. It can usually be remedied and remedies lie in damages...' A, C, and D are other real term-classifications, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A newspaper advertisement inviting readers to submit applications for a loan product, rather than binding the bank to lend, is best described as which of the following?
opts: An offer, capable of immediate acceptance by any reader.
An invitation to treat, a request for an offer rather than an offer.
A counter offer, responding to a prior proposal with contrary terms.
An acceptance, constituting final and unqualified assent to terms.
questionBank.ans: An invitation to treat, a request for an offer rather than an offer.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Where there is a request for an offer, the appropriate term is an invitation to treat... An advertisement is a good example of an invitation to treat.' A, C, and D are other real offer/acceptance concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank makes a loan proposal to a customer and then, before the customer accepts, withdraws it and communicates that withdrawal. What has the bank done to the offer?
opts: Rejected it, since only the offeree may reject an offer.
Revoked it, by cancelling the offer before acceptance.
Lapsed it, since the offer was necessarily time-bound.
Renounced it, since renunciation refers to acceptance withdrawal.
questionBank.ans: Revoked it, by cancelling the offer before acceptance.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Revocation - This occurs when the offeror after making the offer decides to cancel the offer... such cancellation must be communicated to the offeree... before acceptance.' A, C, and D misapply the other offer-termination concepts listed alongside it.

questionBank.q: A customer who responds to a bank's loan offer by proposing different repayment terms than originally stated has, in contract law terms, made which of the following?
opts: An acceptance, since responding to an offer with any terms constitutes assent.
A counter offer, a response to an offer with contrary terms.
A revocation, since only the offeree may cancel an offer.
A lapse, since the original offer automatically terminated.
questionBank.ans: A counter offer, a response to an offer with contrary terms.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Counter Offer - A counter offer occurs when the offeree responds to an offer with a proposal that is contrary to the terms stipulated by the offeror.' A, C, and D misapply the other listed concepts.

questionBank.q: If a loan offer is expressed to remain open only until the end of the month, and the customer does not respond by then, what happens to the offer under contract law?
opts: It is revoked, since revocation occurs automatically after any time limit.
It lapses, since an offer with a time-bound acceptance expires when time elapses.
It remains open indefinitely, since only express cancellation can terminate it.
It becomes a counter offer, since silence is treated as a contrary proposal.
questionBank.ans: It lapses, since an offer with a time-bound acceptance expires when time elapses.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Lapse of time - Where the acceptance of an offer is time-bound, the offer expires and is terminated when the stated time elapses.' A, C, and D misapply the other listed termination concepts.

questionBank.q: Where the terms of an offer can only be performed personally by the individual who made it, what effect does that individual's death have on the offer before acceptance?
opts: It has no effect, since offers automatically survive the death of either party.
It terminates the offer, where performance can only be by the parties personally.
It merely suspends the offer until the deceased's estate is fully administered.
It converts the offer into a counter offer binding on the deceased's estate.
questionBank.ans: It terminates the offer, where performance can only be by the parties personally.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Death of Parties - The death of parties terminates any offer in existence. This is particularly so where the terms of the offer can only be performed by the parties.' A, C, and D are not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: What must occur for a customer's response to a bank's loan offer to amount to a valid acceptance capable of forming a contract?
opts: It must be made in writing and independently witnessed by a Notary Public.
It must be a final and unqualified assent to the exact terms, communicated to the offeror.
It must be accompanied by part-performance sufficient to attract quantum meruit.
It must expressly reference privity of contract to bind only the named parties.
questionBank.ans: It must be a final and unqualified assent to the exact terms, communicated to the offeror.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Acceptance: This is the final and unqualified assent to the exact terms of an offer. It must be communicated to the offeror. Communication may be in any manner.' A, C, and D invent or misapply requirements not stated for acceptance.

questionBank.q: A customer receiving a bank's loan offer tells the bank outright that he does not want the facility on the terms stated. What has the customer done to the offer?
opts: Revoked it, since only the offeror may cancel an offer.
Rejected it, which occurs when the offeree rejects the offer.
Lapsed it, since an offer expires once a stated time period elapses.
Counter offered it, by proposing terms contrary to those stated.
questionBank.ans: Rejected it, which occurs when the offeree rejects the offer.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Rejection or Renunciation - This occurs when the offeree rejects the offer.' A, C, and D are the other listed offer-termination methods, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A dispute arises over an ambiguous term in a banking contract, and the court resolves it by reference to well-established general custom across the banking industry. Which gap-filling source is the court applying?
opts: The subsequent actions of the parties, prioritizing conduct over custom.
Conventions, a general industry practice courts draw on to fill gaps.
Laws relevant to the contract, since courts prioritize statute over custom.
Quantum Meruit, since part-performance determines implied terms.
questionBank.ans: Conventions, a general industry practice courts draw on to fill gaps.
questionBank.exp: Manual: courts fill gaps by drawing from 'Laws relevant to the contract,' 'Conventions,' and 'Actions of the Parties subsequent to the Contract.' A, C, and D misapply the other listed sources or an unrelated principle.

questionBank.q: A bank lends a customer money purely on a handshake understanding with no signed loan agreement at all. Under the essentials of contract, what is the most likely consequence for a facility that legally requires a written format?
opts: The agreement remains a Simple Contract and is fully enforceable.
The agreement is unenforceable due to failure to comply with the required format.
The agreement automatically converts into an implied term at the court's discretion.
The agreement is enforceable provided consideration was adequate.
questionBank.ans: The agreement is unenforceable due to failure to comply with the required format.
questionBank.exp: Manual, 'Compliance with formality': where a particular format is legally required (Formal/Specialty Contracts), 'failure to comply with the legally required format for a contract renders the agreement unenforceable.' A, C, and D misstate or invent outcomes.

questionBank.q: Unlike a Guarantee or a land transaction contract, which type of contract can generally be made in any form because no particular format is legally required for it?
opts: A Formal Contract, since specialty contracts must always be reduced to writing.
A Simple Contract, since most contracts need no particular format.
A hire purchase contract, since it must always be registered at the CAC.
A land transaction contract, since it always requires the Governor's consent.
questionBank.ans: A Simple Contract, since most contracts need no particular format.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Contracts can generally be made in any form and thus referred to as Simple contracts. Most contracts are Simple Contracts.' A, C, and D misapply the Formal/Specialty Contract category, which is the opposite classification.

questionBank.q: The legal competence or recognition of an entity to undertake obligations and acquire rights under a contract is best described by which term?
opts: Privity of Contract, limiting enforcement to the contracting parties.
Contractual Capacity, the competence to undertake obligations in contract.
Consensus ad idem, requiring a genuine meeting of the parties' minds.
Quantum Meruit, entitling pro-rated payment for part-performance.
questionBank.ans: Contractual Capacity, the competence to undertake obligations in contract.
questionBank.exp: Manual, 'Contractual Capacity/Personality': 'This is the legal competence or legal recognition of an entity or person to undertake obligations and acquire rights in contract...it imports the concept of personality.' A, C, and D are other real principles from the same broader section, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A husband and wife agree informally between themselves that one will handle the household banking. If a dispute later arises, how would a court typically treat the question of intention to create legal relations?
opts: It presumes such intention exists for all agreements regardless of context.
It requires proof of such intention, as it is not presumed in domestic agreements.
It presumes such intention exists, treating domestic and business agreements identically.
It disregards the question entirely, as intention is only relevant to commercial contracts.
questionBank.ans: It requires proof of such intention, as it is not presumed in domestic agreements.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The Courts would generally presume such intention in business agreements but would require proof of such intention in domestic agreements.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: An agreement between a bank and a customer to launder proceeds of crime through a current account would be treated by the courts as which of the following?
opts: Voidable, at the bank's option to enforce or disown.
Null and void, since an agreement based on illegal actions is unenforceable.
A Formal Contract, requiring only that it be reduced to writing.
An implied contract, since courts read consent into any banking relationship.
questionBank.ans: Null and void, since an agreement based on illegal actions is unenforceable.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'An agreement based on illegal actions or terms is unenforceable. The legal term for such an agreement is 'null and void'.' A, C, and D misapply unrelated contract concepts.

questionBank.q: Which of the following persons is, under the manual's discussion of contractual capacity, generally treated as a non-person incapable of contracting except for necessaries and beneficial contracts of service?
opts: A registered partnership, which always has full legal capacity.
A company in liquidation, listed among the examples of non-persons.
A licensed sole proprietor, who has full contractual capacity in all cases.
An incorporated private company, which always has unrestricted capacity.
questionBank.ans: A company in liquidation, listed among the examples of non-persons.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Examples of non-persons, in law, include: Insane Individuals, bankrupts, companies in liquidation and minors...' A, C, and D misstate the capacity of other customer types discussed elsewhere in the manual.

questionBank.q: Among a bank's duties owed to its customers, which concerns the bank's obligation regarding cheques and other negotiable instruments presented by the customer?
opts: To honour commitments made by its authorized officials.
To receive cash directly and accept cheques for clearing.
To keep accurate records and issue periodic statements.
To give reasonable notice prior to closing the account.
questionBank.ans: To receive cash directly and accept cheques for clearing.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Banker's duties: 'To receive cash directly into the customer's account and accept cheques and other negotiable instruments for clearing.' A, C, and D are other real duties from the same list, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank's duty to pay out on a customer's demand during advertised banking hours, at the branch where the account is domiciled or elsewhere by arrangement, is which of the bank's listed duties?
opts: To maintain secrecy on the customer's account and affairs.
To honour drawings on demand during advertised banking hours.
To inform a customer of fraudulent activities detected on his account.
To give reasonable notice prior to closing the customer's account.
questionBank.ans: To honour drawings on demand during advertised banking hours.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'To honour drawings on demand during the advertised banking hours and in a branch where the customer's account is domiciled or any other branch...by arrangement.' A, C, and D are other real duties, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: If a bank detects unusual activity suggesting a customer's account has been compromised, which of its listed duties most directly obliges it to act?
opts: To receive cash directly into the customer's account and accept cheques.
To inform a customer of fraudulent activities on his or her account.
To honour commitments made by its authorized officials.
To keep accurate records and issue periodic statements of account.
questionBank.ans: To inform a customer of fraudulent activities on his or her account.
questionBank.exp: Manual: banker's duties include 'To inform a customer of fraudulent activities on his/her account.' A, C, and D are other real duties, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: When a branch manager approves a transaction within the scope of authority the bank has granted, which duty obliges the bank to stand by that approval even if it later regrets it?
opts: To keep accurate records and issue periodic statements.
To honour commitments made by its authorized officials.
To give reasonable notice prior to account closure.
To maintain secrecy on the customer's account and affairs.
questionBank.ans: To honour commitments made by its authorized officials.
questionBank.exp: Manual: banker's duties include 'To honour commitments made by its authorized officials.' A, C, and D are other real duties, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank decides to close a dormant account without any advance warning to the customer. Which of its listed duties has it most directly failed to observe?
opts: The duty to inform a customer of fraudulent activities on his account.
The duty to give reasonable notice to the customer prior to account closure.
The duty to keep accurate records and issue periodic statements.
The duty to maintain secrecy or confidentiality on the customer's affairs.
questionBank.ans: The duty to give reasonable notice to the customer prior to account closure.
questionBank.exp: Manual: banker's duties include 'To give reasonable notice prior to account closure.' A, C, and D are other real duties, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A customer who has not funded any account with a particular bank writes to that bank asking for details of another person's account balance. Absent any exception, is the bank obliged to respond?
opts: Yes, since a bank is legally obliged to respond to any enquiry about its customers.
No, since a bank is not obliged to respond due to its duty of confidentiality.
Yes, since the duty of confidentiality applies only to government agency enquiries.
No, since banks may only disclose to law enforcement on request.
questionBank.ans: No, since a bank is not obliged to respond due to its duty of confidentiality.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A bank is not legally obliged to respond to enquiries made to it about its customer because the bank owes its customer a duty of confidentiality or secrecy.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: A customer explicitly authorizes, in a manner the bank can verify and consistent with his account mandate, disclosure of his account details to a named third party. Under which recognized exception may the bank now respond?
opts: Bank acting under a public duty, since public interest outweighs confidentiality.
Customer's Consent, where the customer authorizes disclosure in a verifiable manner.
Bank acting in discharge of a statutory obligation, such as anti-money laundering.
Threat to the interest of the bank, which qualifies the duty of confidentiality.
questionBank.ans: Customer's Consent, where the customer authorizes disclosure in a verifiable manner.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Customer's Consent - Banks can respond to any enquiries which the customer consents to,' provided consent is verifiable and in line with the mandate. A, C, and D are the other listed exceptions, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank discloses limited customer information to protect itself from a lawsuit threatening its own financial interest, without the customer's consent. Which exception does this best illustrate?
opts: Bank acting under a public duty, since public interest outweighs confidentiality.
Threat to the interest of the bank, which qualifies the duty of confidentiality.
Customer's Consent, granted in a manner the bank can verify.
Bank acting in discharge of a statutory obligation under anti-money laundering.
questionBank.ans: Threat to the interest of the bank, which qualifies the duty of confidentiality.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Threat to the interest of the bank - A bank's duty of confidentiality is qualified by the bank's need to protect itself from threats to its interest.' A, C, and D are other listed exceptions, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A court orders a bank to disclose a customer's account records in a matter of significant public interest, and the bank complies. Which exception to the duty of confidentiality does this illustrate?
opts: Customer's Consent, granted in a manner the bank can verify.
Bank acting under a public duty, since public interest outweighs confidentiality.
Threat to the interest of the bank, which qualifies the duty of confidentiality.
Bank acting in discharge of a statutory obligation under specific legislation.
questionBank.ans: Bank acting under a public duty, since public interest outweighs confidentiality.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Bank acting under a public duty - Public interest outweighs the bank's duty of confidentiality.' A, C, and D are the other listed exceptions, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank reports suspicious transactions to the authorities purely because anti-money laundering legislation requires it to do so, irrespective of the customer's wishes. Which exception does this illustrate?
opts: Customer's Consent, granted in a manner the bank can verify.
Bank acting in discharge of a statutory obligation, such as anti-money laundering.
Bank acting under a public duty, since public interest outweighs confidentiality.
Threat to the interest of the bank, which qualifies the duty of confidentiality.
questionBank.ans: Bank acting in discharge of a statutory obligation, such as anti-money laundering.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Bank acting in discharge of a statutory obligation - The bank is obliged to disclose customer information by virtue of adherence to certain laws e.g. Anti-Money Laundry legislations.' A, C, and D are other listed exceptions, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Where a bank decides to respond to a third-party enquiry about a customer under a recognized exception, what standard of care must the bank observe in framing its response?
opts: It must give a binding written undertaking as to the customer's future conduct.
It must express only an opinion, exercise discretion, and avoid a negligent misstatement.
It must disclose the customer's complete transaction history to avoid any bias.
It must obtain the customer's renewed written consent before each disclosure.
questionBank.ans: It must express only an opinion, exercise discretion, and avoid a negligent misstatement.
questionBank.exp: Manual: where a bank responds to an enquiry it must exercise great discretion, express only an opinion and not give an undertaking, and avoid a negligent misstatement. A, C, and D invent or reverse these requirements.

questionBank.q: Which of the customer's duties obliges him to ensure his account holds sufficient funds and that any overdraft is repaid once the bank calls for it?
opts: The duty to exercise reasonable care and diligence when drawing cheques.
The duty to deposit cash into his account and repay overdrafts on demand.
The duty to inform the bank of any fraud attempts detected on his account.
The duty to give reasonable notice to the bank prior to closing his account.
questionBank.ans: The duty to deposit cash into his account and repay overdrafts on demand.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Customer's Duties: 'Deposit cash in his account and repay overdrafts on demand.' A, C, and D misapply other customer duties, with D wrongly assigning a banker's duty to the customer.

questionBank.q: Which of the customer's duties obliges him to alert the bank if he becomes aware that someone has attempted to defraud his account?
opts: The duty to deposit cash into his account and repay overdrafts on demand.
The duty to inform the bank of fraud attempts detected on his account.
The duty to honour drawings made on his account during advertised banking hours.
The duty to exercise reasonable care and diligence when drawing cheques.
questionBank.ans: The duty to inform the bank of fraud attempts detected on his account.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Customer's Duties: 'Informing the Bank of fraud attempts on his account.' A, C, and D misapply other customer duties, with C wrongly assigning a banker's duty to the customer.

questionBank.q: A bank charges a customer a standard fee, in line with the banker's tariff administered by the Central Bank of Nigeria, for processing a funds transfer. Which right is the bank exercising?
opts: Right of Set-off, netting a credit balance against an overdrawn account.
Right to Commission, receiving reasonable charge for services rendered.
Right of Lien, retaining a customer's property in the ordinary course of business.
Right of Confidentiality, declining to disclose transaction details to third parties.
questionBank.ans: Right to Commission, receiving reasonable charge for services rendered.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Banker's Rights: 'Right to Commission - The Banker has the right to receive reasonable commission or charge for services rendered...in line with the banker's tariff administered by the Central bank of Nigeria.' A, C, and D are other rights, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A customer who signs and issues a cheque without checking that the account has sufficient funds to cover it may be in breach of which of the customer's listed duties?
opts: The duty to deposit cash in his account and repay overdrafts on demand.
The duty to exercise reasonable care and diligence when drawing cheques.
The duty to inform the bank of fraud attempts detected on his account.
The duty to determine which of his accounts he wishes to withdraw from.
questionBank.ans: The duty to exercise reasonable care and diligence when drawing cheques.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Customer's Duties: 'Exercising reasonable care and diligence when drawing cheques.' A, C, and D are other listed customer duties/rights, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A customer whose properly funded account carries no legal bar on withdrawal instructs the bank, in proper form, to pay him from that account. Which of the customer's rights entitles him to that payment?
opts: The right to be issued with a periodic statement of his account.
The right to be paid on demand, once his instruction is proper and the account funded.
The right to determine which of his accounts he wishes to withdraw from.
The right to informed disclosure of fraud detected on his account.
questionBank.ans: The right to be paid on demand, once his instruction is proper and the account funded.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Customer's Rights: 'To be paid from his account as he may demand provided his instruction is made in proper form, his account is funded and there is no legal bar to his demand.' A, C, and D are other listed customer rights, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: When a bank extends an overdraft facility to a customer whose account subsequently runs into debit, which form does the banker/customer relationship take with respect to that overdrawn balance?
opts: Debtor/Creditor, with the customer as the debtor since the bank is the lender.
Bailor/Bailee, since the bank holds the customer's property in safe custody.
Principal/Agent, since the bank acts on the customer's behalf as directed.
Mortgagor/Mortgagee, since the customer has applied for and obtained a bank mortgage.
questionBank.ans: Debtor/Creditor, with the customer as the debtor since the bank is the lender.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Debtor/Creditor - When the bank acts as the lender, the customer is the debtor.' B, C, and D are other listed relationship forms, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A customer deposits valuables with the bank under a safe-custody arrangement, with no lending involved on either side. Which form does the banker/customer relationship take?
opts: Debtor/Creditor, since the customer's credit balance makes the bank the debtor.
Bailor/Bailee, where the customer is the bailor and the bank is the bailee.
Principal/Agent, where the bank procures foreign exchange on the customer's behalf.
Mortgagor/Mortgagee, where the customer applies for and obtains a bank mortgage.
questionBank.ans: Bailor/Bailee, where the customer is the bailor and the bank is the bailee.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Bailor/Bailee - This exists where there is a safe custody arrangement between the bank and the customer. Customer is the bailor, the bank is Bailee.' A, C, and D are other listed forms, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank procures foreign exchange from the CBN on behalf of a customer, acting on the customer's instructions and binding the customer to the legal consequences. Which form does this relationship take?
opts: Bailor/Bailee, since the bank holds the customer's property in safe custody.
Principal/Agent, with the customer as principal and the bank as agent.
Debtor/Creditor, since the bank is the lender and the customer the debtor.
Mortgagor/Mortgagee, since the customer has applied for and obtained a bank mortgage.
questionBank.ans: Principal/Agent, with the customer as principal and the bank as agent.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Principal/Agent... A typical example is when a bank represents the interest of its customers e.g. procurement of foreign exchange from CBN.' A, C, and D are other listed forms, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A customer applies for and is granted a facility secured by a charge over his property, making the bank the holder of that charge. Which form does the relationship take?
opts: Principal/Agent, with the bank acting on the customer's behalf as directed.
Mortgagor/Mortgagee, with the customer as mortgagor and the bank as mortgagee.
Bailor/Bailee, with the customer's property held by the bank in safe custody.
Debtor/Creditor, with the bank as the debtor since the customer's account is in credit.
questionBank.ans: Mortgagor/Mortgagee, with the customer as mortgagor and the bank as mortgagee.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Mortgagor/Mortgagee - Customer applies and obtains bank mortgage. Customer is the mortgagor while the bank is the mortgagee.' A, C, and D are other listed forms, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank receives formal notice that a long-standing customer has been declared insane by a competent authority. What effect does this have on the customer's existing mandate?
opts: It may suspend or terminate the mandate, as notice of insanity is a recognized ground.
No effect, as notice of insanity is not among the recognized grounds.
It automatically converts the mandate into a trust account for the customer's benefit.
It obliges the bank to immediately close the account without further formality.
questionBank.ans: It may suspend or terminate the mandate, as notice of insanity is a recognized ground.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the banking contract/mandate may be terminated or suspended by, among other grounds, 'Notice of Insanity.' B, C, and D misstate or invent consequences not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: A bank is ordered by a court to freeze and suspend operations on a customer's account. Under which of the manual's listed grounds for termination or suspension does this fall?
opts: Notice of death of customer, as court orders are treated identically to death notices.
Operation of Law, including Court Orders, among the recognized grounds.
Insolvency of an individual or company, as court orders always signal insolvency.
Notice from either party, as a court order is treated as notice given by the bank.
questionBank.ans: Operation of Law, including Court Orders, among the recognized grounds.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists grounds including 'Operation of Law including Court Orders.' A, C, and D misapply the other listed grounds to this scenario.

questionBank.q: A bank fundamentally breaches its contract with a customer, and the customer seeks a court order specifying that the bank must stop a particular ongoing course of conduct. Which remedy is the customer seeking?
opts: Damages, monetary compensation for the breach.
Order of Injunction, specifying actions to do or stop doing.
Rescission, termination of the contract for fundamental breach.
Order of Specific Performance, requiring a party to perform an act.
questionBank.ans: Order of Injunction, specifying actions to do or stop doing.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Remedies for breach of contract: 'Order of Injunction - A Court Order specifying actions which should do or stop doing.' A, C, and D are the other listed remedies, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A customer wishes to bring a fundamentally breached banking contract to an end entirely, rather than merely claim monetary compensation. Which remedy is the customer seeking?
opts: Damages, monetary compensation awarded for a breach.
Rescission, termination usually for a fundamental breach.
Order of Specific Performance, requiring a party to perform an action.
Order of Injunction, specifying actions a party should do or stop doing.
questionBank.ans: Rescission, termination usually for a fundamental breach.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Remedies for breach of contract: 'Rescission - Termination; usually for fundamental breach.' A, C, and D are the other listed remedies, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank teller processes a transaction carelessly, causing loss to a person the teller could reasonably have expected to be affected. Which general principle explains why the teller owed that person a duty in the first place?
opts: A duty of care arises only where a court has expressly recognized the relationship.
Every person owes a duty of care to everyone else who may be affected by their acts.
A duty of care arises only where the two persons are in close geographical proximity.
A duty of care arises only where a direct contractual relationship already exists.
questionBank.ans: Every person owes a duty of care to everyone else who may be affected by their acts.
questionBank.exp: Manual, 'Due Diligence': 'Generally, every person owes a duty of care to everyone else who may be affected by that person's acts.' A, C, and D invent restrictions not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: A bank official takes an action without considering whether a reasonable person could have foreseen that it might injure someone else. If injury results, what does the manual say about liability in that situation?
opts: Liability is excluded, since foreseeability is irrelevant once an act has occurred.
Liability is established, since a reasonable person could have foreseen the injury.
Liability depends solely on whether the official personally intended to cause injury.
Liability depends solely on whether the injured person suffered financial loss.
questionBank.ans: Liability is established, since a reasonable person could have foreseen the injury.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'If injury could have been foreseen by a reasonable man, liability is established.' A, C, and D misstate this foreseeability-based test.

questionBank.q: A banker's obligation to exercise due diligence toward a customer is said to derive from which two possible sources, according to the manual?
opts: Tort only, as contractual duties never arise between a bank and its customer.
The Law of Tort, or a Contract, as in the case of bankers.
Contract only, as tortious duties never apply to regulated financial institutions.
Statute only, as tort and contract can never create a duty of care independently.
questionBank.ans: The Law of Tort, or a Contract, as in the case of bankers.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Due diligence requirement derives from Law of Tort but may arise from a Contract as in the case of bankers.' A, C, and D misstate this dual source.

questionBank.q: In the English case the manual cites as the origin of the modern duty of care, the court formulated a principle defining whose interests a person must have in contemplation when acting. What is that principle called?
opts: The Reasonable Banker Test, formulated specifically for banking disputes.
The Neighbour Principle, formulated in Donoghue vs. Stevenson.
The Vicarious Liability Principle, formulated for employer liability.
The Consensus Ad Idem Principle, formulated for contract validity.
questionBank.ans: The Neighbour Principle, formulated in Donoghue vs. Stevenson.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The scope of the duty of care was articulated in an English case named Donoghue vs. Stevenson wherein the court formulated what is known as the 'Neighbour principle' as basis of liability.' A, C, and D are other real concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Under the Neighbour Principle from Donoghue vs. Stevenson, a 'neighbour' is defined by reference to which of the following?
opts: Persons who live within a defined geographical radius of the actor's address.
Persons closely and directly affected by an act, reasonably in the actor's contemplation.
Persons who have entered into a written contract with the actor prior to the act.
Persons who are formally registered as customers of the actor's business.
questionBank.ans: Persons closely and directly affected by an act, reasonably in the actor's contemplation.
questionBank.exp: Manual quotes the definition as 'persons so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation when directing my mind to the act or omission called in question.' A, C, and D invent restrictions not in the material.

questionBank.q: A civil claim is brought against a bank for a wrong not based on any contractual relationship or geographical proximity. Which body of law most naturally governs such a claim?
opts: Criminal Law, since all civil wrongs are punished as crimes.
Tort, which establishes civil liability not necessarily based on contract or proximity.
Consensus ad idem, a contract-formation concept unrelated to civil wrongs.
Privity of Contract, a doctrine that only applies where a valid contract exists.
questionBank.ans: Tort, which establishes civil liability not necessarily based on contract or proximity.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'It establishes another kind of civil liability as opposed to criminal liability and it is not necessarily based on a contractual relationship or geographical proximity.' A, C, and D misapply unrelated concepts.

questionBank.q: To succeed in a claim under the law of tort, a claimant must prove three specific elements. Which of the following correctly states all three?
opts: A written contract, breach of that contract, and quantifiable financial loss.
A duty imposed by law, breach of that duty, and injury resulting from the breach.
Intention to harm, breach of a statutory provision, and a criminal conviction.
Consideration exchanged, a meeting of minds, and subsequent part-performance.
questionBank.ans: A duty imposed by law, breach of that duty, and injury resulting from the breach.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'To establish a claim in Court under tort, the 3 elements of tort must be proved: Duty imposed by law; Breach of that duty; Injury resulting from the breach.' A, C, and D invent or misapply elements from contract or criminal law.

questionBank.q: A bank employee omits to do something that a reasonable person would have done in the same situation, causing loss to a customer. Which tort does this best describe?
opts: Conversion, an unjustifiable interference with a person's chattel.
Negligence, an omission to do what a reasonable person would do.
Nuisance, injury to a neighbour's enjoyment of his land.
Defamation, a statement injuring a person's reputation.
questionBank.ans: Negligence, an omission to do what a reasonable person would do.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Negligence: Omission to do something which a reasonable man would do or doing something which a reasonable man would not do in a situation.' A, C, and D are other listed torts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank sells a customer's pledged goods to a third party without any right to do so, permanently depriving the true owner of their use. Which tort does this best describe?
opts: Negligence, an omission to do what a reasonable person would do.
Conversion, an unjustifiable interference with a person's chattel.
Occupier's liability, for injury to lawful entrants through use of property.
Nuisance, for injury to a neighbour's enjoyment of his land.
questionBank.ans: Conversion, an unjustifiable interference with a person's chattel.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Conversion: Any unjustifiable interference with any person's chattel (thing) in a manner that deprives him of the use and possession of it.' A, C, and D are other listed torts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank publishes a false statement about a customer that exposes the customer to public ridicule and damages his reputation. Which tort does this best describe?
opts: Nuisance, for injury to a neighbour's enjoyment of his land.
Defamation, a statement injuring reputation and exposing to contempt.
Occupier's liability, for injury to lawful entrants through use of property.
Conversion, an unjustifiable interference with a person's chattel.
questionBank.ans: Defamation, a statement injuring reputation and exposing to contempt.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Defamation: A statement which injures the reputation of the person to whom it refers and which exposes him to hatred, contempt, ridicule, fear, dislike or disesteem.' A, C, and D are other listed torts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A visitor to a bank branch is injured by a hazard on the premises that the bank, as occupier, failed to address. Which tort does this best describe?
opts: Defamation, a statement injuring reputation and exposing to contempt.
Occupier's liability, for injury to lawful entrants through use of property.
Conversion, an unjustifiable interference with a person's chattel.
Nuisance, for injury to a neighbour's enjoyment of his land.
questionBank.ans: Occupier's liability, for injury to lawful entrants through use of property.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Occupier's liability: Liability for injury caused to lawful entrants onto one's property through the use of such property.' A, C, and D are other listed torts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank's construction activity on its own land interferes with a neighbouring landowner's ability to enjoy his property. Which tort does this best describe?
opts: Conversion, an unjustifiable interference with a person's chattel.
Nuisance, injury to a neighbour's possession and enjoyment of his land.
Occupier's liability, for injury to lawful entrants through use of property.
Defamation, a statement injuring reputation and exposing to contempt.
questionBank.ans: Nuisance, injury to a neighbour's possession and enjoyment of his land.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Nuisance: Liability arising from injury done to a neighbor's possession and enjoyment of his land through the use of one's land.' A, C, and D are other listed torts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank employee, while carrying out his duties in an improper way not expressly approved by the bank, commits a tort against a customer. Under which principle can the bank still be held liable for that employee's tort?
opts: Privity of Contract, since only parties to a contract may be liable for a tort.
Vicarious Liability, liability of one person for the tort of another subject to him.
Quantum Meruit, since part-performance attracts pro-rated liability for torts.
Consensus ad idem, since liability requires a meeting of minds.
questionBank.ans: Vicarious Liability, liability of one person for the tort of another subject to him.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Vicarious Liability Principle: Liability of one person for the tort of another who is subject to him in the exercise of his duty even if that other person is carrying out that duty in an improper way not expressly approved by the principal.' A, C, and D are unrelated contract-law principles, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: When a court evaluates whether a banker exercised due diligence in a lending decision, what standard does the manual say the test applies?
opts: A subjective standard, measuring what appeared reasonable to the particular banker.
An objective standard, asking whether a reasonable banker would have acted similarly.
A standard set entirely by the bank's own internal credit policy, ignoring industry norms.
A standard requiring proof that the banker intended to cause loss to the customer.
questionBank.ans: An objective standard, asking whether a reasonable banker would have acted similarly.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The test is objective. It is not a measure of what appears reasonable to the person doing an act but whether a 'reasonable banker' in that person's shoes would act in the same way.' A, C, and D misstate this test.

questionBank.q: An act or omission prohibited by the state, for which an offender is liable to a fine, imprisonment, or death, is the manual's definition of which of the following?
opts: A tort, a form of civil liability distinct from criminal liability.
A crime, an act or omission prohibited by the state and punishable as such.
A breach of warranty, a less serious term remediable by damages.
A nuisance, injury to a neighbour's enjoyment of his land.
questionBank.ans: A crime, an act or omission prohibited by the state and punishable as such.
questionBank.exp: Manual, 'Basic Criminal Law': 'A crime is an act or omission prohibited by the state and an offender is liable to be punished by a fine, imprisonment or death.' A, C, and D are other real legal concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Almost all crimes require proof of both 'an act' and a 'state of mind', except for a narrow category of offences. What is that exception called?
opts: Financial crimes, which always require proof of a heightened state of mind.
Strict liability crimes, which do not require proof of a state of mind.
Vicarious crimes, attributed to an employer regardless of the employer's state of mind.
Inchoate crimes, which require intent but never proof of any act.
questionBank.ans: Strict liability crimes, which do not require proof of a state of mind.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Almost all crimes (except strict liability crimes) consist of 'an act' and a 'state of mind'.' A, C, and D misstate or invent categories not found in this section.

questionBank.q: A financial crime, as the manual defines it, is one that relates to which of the following, attracting punishment under the law?
opts: Any breach of a banking contract's terms, regardless of money involved.
The use of money or other valuables, attracting punishment under the law.
Any tort committed by a bank official, regardless of money involved.
Any failure to observe due diligence, regardless of money involved.
questionBank.ans: The use of money or other valuables, attracting punishment under the law.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A financial crime is one that relates to the use of money or other valuables and it attracts punishment under the law.' A, C, and D misapply unrelated legal concepts from other sections.

questionBank.q: Beyond the Criminal Code Act, which piece of legislation does the manual identify as regulating banking practice and creating obligations relating to banking and lending?
opts: The Land Use Act, primarily governing ownership and transfer of land.
The Banks & Other Financial Institutions Act, regulating banking practice and lending.
The Companies and Allied Matters Act, primarily governing incorporation of companies.
The Bills of Exchange Act, primarily governing negotiable instruments.
questionBank.ans: The Banks & Other Financial Institutions Act, regulating banking practice and lending.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The Banks & Other Financial Institutions Act basically regulates the practice of banking and creates several obligations and offences relating to banking practice and lending.' A, C, and D are real statutes from elsewhere in the manual, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank employee dishonestly takes funds belonging to the bank without any pretence or deception involved. Which financial crime under the Criminal Code Act does this most directly describe?
opts: Forgery under section 465, since documents were involved.
Stealing under section 383, for dishonestly taking funds.
Counterfeiting Currency under the Counterfeit Currency Act.
Obtaining by false pretences under section 419, since credit was obtained.
questionBank.ans: Stealing under section 383, for dishonestly taking funds.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists 'Stealing (s. 383 Criminal Code Act)' among examples of financial crime. A, C, and D are the other listed financial crimes, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A person alters a genuine bank document, making a false document with intent to deceive, without necessarily using it yet to obtain anything. Which financial crime does this most directly describe?
opts: Stealing under section 383, for taking property without consent.
Forgery under section 465, for making a false document with intent to deceive.
Counterfeiting Currency under the Counterfeit Currency Act.
Obtaining by false pretences under section 419, for obtaining credit.
questionBank.ans: Forgery under section 465, for making a false document with intent to deceive.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists 'Forgery (s. 465 Criminal Code Act)' among examples of financial crime, distinct from stealing, false pretences, and counterfeiting, which are the other listed offences misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A person reproduces fake banknotes intending to pass them off as genuine currency. Which financial crime does this most directly describe?
opts: Obtaining by false pretences under section 419 of the Criminal Code Act.
Counterfeiting Currency under the Counterfeit Currency (Special Provisions) Act.
Forgery under section 465 of the Criminal Code Act.
Stealing under section 383 of the Criminal Code Act.
questionBank.ans: Counterfeiting Currency under the Counterfeit Currency (Special Provisions) Act.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists 'Counterfeiting Currency (s. 1, s. 5 Counterfeit Currency (Special Provisions) Act)' among examples of financial crime. A, C, and D are the other listed offences, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A person begins putting his intention to commit an offence into execution by an overt act, but does not complete the offence, and later chooses to desist. Under Section 4 of the Criminal Code Act, is he still liable?
opts: No, since voluntarily desisting before completion always removes liability.
Yes, he is deemed to have attempted the offence, and desistance is immaterial.
No, since an overt act without full completion cannot amount to attempt.
Yes, but only if the offence he intended was a strict liability crime.
questionBank.ans: Yes, he is deemed to have attempted the offence, and desistance is immaterial.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 4: where a person begins to put his intention into execution by an overt act but does not complete it, 'he is said to attempt to commit the offence,' and 'it is immaterial that he chose to desist.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Under Section 7 of the Criminal Code Act, a person who counsels, aids, or enables another to commit an offence, without personally doing the act, is treated as which of the following?
opts: An accessory after the fact, guilty only of assisting escape afterward.
A principal offender, deemed to have taken part and guilty of the offence.
A conspirator, guilty only where the offence in question is a felony.
Not liable at all, since only the person who physically commits the act is liable.
questionBank.ans: A principal offender, deemed to have taken part and guilty of the offence.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 7: 'Every person is deemed to have taken part in committing an offence and to be guilty of that offence, who actually does the act...or who counsels, aids or enables another person to commit the offence.' A, C, and D misapply the other rules from the same section.

questionBank.q: Under Section 519 of the Criminal Code Act, a person who receives or assists another, knowing that person to be guilty of an offence, in order to help him escape punishment, is guilty of which of the following?
opts: Conspiracy to commit a crime, guilty of a felony liable to imprisonment.
Accessory after the fact of a crime, for assisting the offender to escape.
Attempt to commit a crime, guilty despite not completing the offence.
An offence as a principal offender, treated identically to the primary actor.
questionBank.ans: Accessory after the fact of a crime, for assisting the offender to escape.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 519: 'Any person who receives or assists another, who to his knowledge is guilty of an offence in order to enable him escape punishment commits a crime' as an accessory after the fact. A, C, and D misapply the other rules from the same broader section.

questionBank.q: Under Section 516 of the Criminal Code Act, two or more persons who agree together to commit a felony, without necessarily completing it, are guilty of which of the following?
opts: Accessory after the fact, for assisting an offender escape punishment.
Conspiracy to commit a crime, guilty of a felony and liable to imprisonment.
Attempt to commit a crime, guilty despite desisting before completion.
Principal offenders, guilty only if each personally performed the prohibited act.
questionBank.ans: Conspiracy to commit a crime, guilty of a felony and liable to imprisonment.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 516: 'Any person who conspires with another to commit any felony...is guilty of a felony and liable to imprisonment.' A, C, and D misapply the other rules from the same section.

questionBank.q: A bank officer receives a freezing order against a customer's account. According to the manual, what is the most urgent consequence for the officer's handling of the account?
opts: The officer should defer action until the customer's lawyer formally objects.
The order operates immediately on service, and delay exposes the bank to liability.
The officer may wait until the next scheduled account review before acting.
The order only takes effect once the Legal Department separately confirms it.
questionBank.ans: The order operates immediately on service, and delay exposes the bank to liability.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'an Order to freeze an account is expected to operate immediately upon service and if the funds are moved by the customer after the service, then the bank is liable to pay what should have been paid by the customer to the beneficiary of the Order.' A, C, and D invent delays not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: What does the manual say a bank officer who receives any court process relating to a customer's account should do?
opts: Comply with the process personally without escalating it to any other department.
Ensure that the process is immediately referred to the Legal Department.
Ignore the process until the customer confirms its authenticity in writing.
Return the process to the court, requesting re-service on the customer directly.
questionBank.ans: Ensure that the process is immediately referred to the Legal Department.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'An officer of a bank who receives any court process must ensure that it is immediately referred to the Legal Department.' A, C, and D are not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: When a person dies having written a Will stating how his assets should be managed or distributed, what is he said to have died?
opts: Intestate, since a Will always overrides any statutory distribution.
Testate, since he has left a testamentary disposition governing his estate.
Insolvent, since a Will is only relevant where the estate cannot cover debts.
Incapacitated, since only a person of full capacity may leave a valid Will.
questionBank.ans: Testate, since he has left a testamentary disposition governing his estate.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'If a man had written a Will (testamentary disposition) stating how his estate should be managed or distributed, he is said to have died 'Testata'.' A, C, and D misstate this term.

questionBank.q: When a person dies without having left a Will governing the management or distribution of his estate, what is he said to have died?
opts: Testate, since absence of a Will is treated as an implied testamentary disposition.
Intestate, the term used where a person dies without having left a Will.
Insolvent, since dying without a Will is treated as an inability to pay debts.
Incapacitated, since only a Will can establish that a person had full capacity.
questionBank.ans: Intestate, the term used where a person dies without having left a Will.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'If otherwise, he died 'Intestate'.' A, C, and D misstate this term.

questionBank.q: Court approval for the administration of a deceased customer's estate is granted through Letters of Probate to persons named as Executors. In which circumstance does this specific document apply?
opts: Where the deceased died Intestate, since Probate is issued only without a Will.
Where the deceased died Testate, since Executors are named in a Will.
Where the deceased was a minor, since Probate exists solely to appoint a Guardian.
Where the deceased was mentally infirm at death, regardless of whether a Will existed.
questionBank.ans: Where the deceased died Testate, since Executors are named in a Will.
questionBank.exp: Manual: administration is subject to court approval 'through the issuance of 'Letters of Probate' to the persons named as Executors in a Will.' A, C, and D misapply this to the wrong circumstance.

questionBank.q: Court approval for the administration of a deceased customer's estate is granted through Letters of Administration. In which circumstance does this specific document apply?
opts: Upon a death testate, since Administration confirms Executors named in the Will.
Upon a death intestate, since there is no Will naming Executors to be confirmed.
Where the deceased was a minor, since Administration exists solely to appoint a Guardian.
Where the deceased was mentally infirm at death, regardless of whether a Will existed.
questionBank.ans: Upon a death intestate, since there is no Will naming Executors to be confirmed.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the issuance of 'Letters of Administration' follows 'a death intestate.' A, C, and D misapply this to the wrong circumstance.

questionBank.q: Once Letters of Probate or Letters of Administration have been issued, what power do the Executors or Administrators hold in relation to suits brought by third parties, including banks?
opts: They may only defend suits brought against the estate, never initiate any suit.
They are empowered to initiate and defend suits relating to the estate.
They must obtain a fresh court order before responding to any suit.
They hold no power over suits at all until the estate has been fully distributed.
questionBank.ans: They are empowered to initiate and defend suits relating to the estate.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'In either case, the Administrators or Executors are empowered to initiate and defend suits relating to the estate instituted by third parties including banks.' A, C, and D misstate this power.

questionBank.q: A customer loses his ability to comprehend issues and can no longer give reasoned instructions to his bank, but still holds a credit balance requiring management. What role is appointed to administer his affairs?
opts: An Executor, appointed under a Will the customer made before losing capacity.
A Guardian, appointed to administer the affairs of the mentally infirm.
A Trustee in Bankruptcy, appointed once the estate is declared insolvent.
An Attorney, appointed under a Power of Attorney signed after losing capacity.
questionBank.ans: A Guardian, appointed to administer the affairs of the mentally infirm.
questionBank.exp: Manual: for a mentally infirm customer, 'the implementation of this lies in the appointment of someone closely related to him, usually family, or a court-appointed person, as his 'Guardian' to administer his affairs.' A, C, and D invent or misapply roles not stated for this circumstance.

questionBank.q: A Guardian appointed to manage a minor's assets stands in what kind of relationship with the minor, and what limit applies to the Guardian's own benefit from the arrangement?
opts: An agency relationship, and the guardian may freely benefit without restriction.
A fiduciary relationship, and the guardian may not benefit unless specifically authorized.
A debtor/creditor relationship, and the guardian may benefit only after the minor turns 18.
A bailment relationship, and the guardian may never benefit under any circumstances.
questionBank.ans: A fiduciary relationship, and the guardian may not benefit unless specifically authorized.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The guardian is in a fiduciary relationship (trusteeship) with the minor and is liable for abuse of the minor's assets. A guardian may not benefit from the arrangement unless he is specifically authorized to do so.' A, C, and D misstate this relationship.

questionBank.q: Beyond having the contents of a document read and explained to them before a Magistrate, illiterate and blind persons are especially liable to be cheated in which area the manual highlights?
opts: Litigation generally, since illiterate persons may never appear before a court.
Contract, due to the deficiencies that make them liable to be cheated in that context.
Tort claims exclusively, since only tortious liability requires comprehension.
Criminal proceedings exclusively, since only criminal liability requires comprehension.
questionBank.ans: Contract, due to the deficiencies that make them liable to be cheated in that context.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'These categories of persons are also liable to be cheated, especially in Contract due to their deficiencies.' A, C, and D misstate or narrow this beyond what the material supports.

questionBank.q: A sworn statement in writing, made under oath or affirmation before an authorised Magistrate or Notary Public, and used for purposes such as age declaration or attestation to a marriage, is best described as which of the following?
opts: A Jurat, the closing endorsement on a document confirming it was read and explained.
An Affidavit, a sworn statement in writing verifying facts before an authorised officer.
A Deed of Guarantee & Indemnity, combining two forms of liability.
A Memorandum of Deposit, evidencing the deposit of title documents.
questionBank.ans: An Affidavit, a sworn statement in writing verifying facts before an authorised officer.
questionBank.exp: Manual, 'Nature and Use of Affidavits': a sworn statement in writing made under oath before an authorised magistrate or officer, used for age declaration, attestation to marriage, litigation and other official circumstances. A, C, and D are other real documents from elsewhere in the manual, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Section 3 of the Bills of Exchange Act defines a bill of exchange as an unconditional order in writing, signed by the person giving it, requiring the addressee to do which of the following?
opts: To repay a sum already advanced, together with interest accrued to date.
To pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time a sum certain in money.
To transfer title in a specified chattel to a named party within a reasonable time.
To hold a sum certain in money on trust for a named beneficiary until a future date.
questionBank.ans: To pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time a sum certain in money.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.3 Bills of Exchange Act: a bill of exchange is 'an unconditional order in writing...requiring the person to whom it is addressed to pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time, a sum certain in money to, or to the order of a specified person or to bearer.' A, C, and D misstate this definition.

questionBank.q: A bill of exchange is described in the manual as a non-interest-bearing written order used primarily in which context, binding one party to pay a fixed sum at a predetermined future date?
opts: Domestic retail banking, binding a bank to honour a standing instruction.
International trade, binding one party to pay a fixed sum at a future date.
Company law, binding a company to issue new shares at a future date.
Land transactions, binding a purchaser to complete payment upon registration.
questionBank.ans: International trade, binding one party to pay a fixed sum at a future date.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A bill of exchange is a non-interest-bearing written order used primarily in international trade that binds one party to pay a fixed sum of money to another party at a predetermined future date.' A, C, and D misapply this description.

questionBank.q: A financial instrument representing value, used in commercial transactions, and transferable by mere delivery or by endorsement plus delivery, is best described as which of the following?
opts: A Formal Contract, transferable only where reduced to writing and signed.
A negotiable instrument, transferable by mere delivery or by endorsement.
A fixed debenture, transferable only upon registration of a specific charge.
A letter of comfort, transferable only where the issuing party consents.
questionBank.ans: A negotiable instrument, transferable by mere delivery or by endorsement.
