questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A negotiable instrument is a financial instrument representing value which is used in commercial transactions and which can be transferred to another person by mere delivery or by endorsement plus delivery.' A, C, and D are unrelated concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed in the manual as an example of a negotiable instrument, alongside cheques, dividend warrants, and treasury bills?
opts: Deeds of Guarantee, listed among the manual's examples.
Promissory Notes, listed among the manual's examples.
Memoranda of Deposit, listed among the manual's examples.
Letters of Administration, listed among the manual's examples.
questionBank.ans: Promissory Notes, listed among the manual's examples.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Examples: Cheques, Dividend Warrants, Treasury Bills and Promissory Notes and bearer bonds.' A, C, and D are real documents from other sections, not listed among negotiable instruments.

questionBank.q: The legal term for the transfer of the entire rights in a negotiable instrument to a transferee for value, who acquires all the rights of the transferor, is which of the following?
opts: Perfection, the process of documenting and registering a security interest.
Negotiation, the transfer of the entire rights in a negotiable instrument.
Novation, the substitution of a new contract for an existing one.
Rescission, the termination of a contract for a fundamental breach.
questionBank.ans: Negotiation, the transfer of the entire rights in a negotiable instrument.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Negotiation is a legal term which means transfer of the entire rights in a negotiable instrument to a transferee for value who acquires all the rights of the transferor.' A, C, and D are unrelated concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Negotiation of a negotiable instrument is achieved through a valid instruction written on the back which, when signed, transfers the instrument's total value. What is this instruction called?
opts: A Jurat, the closing endorsement confirming a document's contents were read.
An endorsement, a valid instruction on the back transferring value.
A crossing, two transverse lines drawn across the face of the instrument.
An inchoate bill, an incompletely filled-out bill lacking certain details.
questionBank.ans: An endorsement, a valid instruction on the back transferring value.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Negotiation is achieved through an endorsement which is a valid instruction written on the back of a bill and which when signed transfers the total value of the bill to the endorsee.' A, C, and D are other real negotiable-instrument concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: By endorsing a negotiable instrument, an endorser is deemed to be giving the endorsee an undertaking about which of the following, according to the manual's list of endorser warranties?
opts: That the instrument will retain its market value until next presented.
That the instrument is genuine, its title is good, and no defect is known.
That the instrument has already cleared the banking system without dishonour.
That the instrument is a Formal Contract requiring no further formality.
questionBank.ans: That the instrument is genuine, its title is good, and no defect is known.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists the warranties of an endorser as: the instrument is genuine; he has a good/transferable title; and he is not aware of any defect at the time of endorsement. A, C, and D invent warranties not listed in the material.

questionBank.q: Among the parties to a negotiable instrument, which party is defined as the person who writes and signs the payment instruction on it?
opts: The Payee, the person named on the instrument and entitled to receive value.
The Drawer, the person who writes and signs the payment instruction.
The Drawee, the person to whom the payment instruction is addressed.
The Endorsee, the person in favour of whom a transfer instruction is made.
questionBank.ans: The Drawer, the person who writes and signs the payment instruction.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Drawer – Person who writes and signs the payment instruction on it.' A, C, and D are the other listed parties, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the parties to a negotiable instrument, which party is defined as the person to whom the payment instruction on the instrument is addressed?
opts: The Payee, the person named on the instrument and entitled to receive value.
The Drawee, the person to whom the payment instruction is addressed.
The Endorser, a payee who signs an instruction on the back of the instrument.
The Drawer, the person who writes and signs the payment instruction.
questionBank.ans: The Drawee, the person to whom the payment instruction is addressed.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Drawee – Person to whom the instruction is addressed.' A, C, and D are the other listed parties, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the parties to a negotiable instrument, which party is defined as the person named on the instrument who is entitled to receive value on it?
opts: The Drawee, the person to whom the payment instruction is addressed.
The Payee, the person named on the instrument and entitled to receive value.
The Endorsee, the person in favour of whom a transfer instruction is made.
The Drawer, the person who writes and signs the payment instruction.
questionBank.ans: The Payee, the person named on the instrument and entitled to receive value.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Payee – Person named on the instrument and is thus entitled to receive value on it.' A, C, and D are the other listed parties, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the parties to a negotiable instrument, which party is defined as a payee who signs an instruction on the back, transferring the value due to him to another named person?
opts: The Endorsee, the person in favour of whom a transfer instruction is made.
The Endorser, a payee who signs an instruction on the back transferring value.
The Drawee, the person to whom the payment instruction is addressed.
The Payee, the person named on the instrument and entitled to receive value.
questionBank.ans: The Endorser, a payee who signs an instruction on the back transferring value.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Endorser – A payee who signs an instruction on the back of the instrument through which he transfers the value due to him to be paid to another named person.' A, C, and D are the other listed parties, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the parties to a negotiable instrument, which party is defined as the person in favour of whom a transfer instruction on the instrument is made?
opts: The Endorser, a payee who signs an instruction on the back.
The Endorsee, the person in favour of whom the transfer instruction is made.
The Payee, the person named on the instrument and entitled to receive value.
The Drawer, the person who writes and signs the payment instruction.
questionBank.ans: The Endorsee, the person in favour of whom the transfer instruction is made.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Endorsee – Person in favour of whom the transfer instruction is made.' A, C, and D are the other listed parties, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A written instruction to pay, drawn on a bank and payable on demand, is best described as what specific type of bill of exchange?
opts: An inchoate bill, an incompletely filled-out bill with details left unfilled.
A cheque, a bill of exchange drawn on a bank and payable on demand.
A promissory note, an unconditional promise to pay a sum certain.
A dividend warrant, an instrument used to pay a shareholder's dividend.
questionBank.ans: A cheque, a bill of exchange drawn on a bank and payable on demand.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A cheque is a bill of exchange (written instruction to pay) drawn on a bank and payable on demand.' A, C, and D are other real instruments/concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bill on which the drawer has signed and left all other details unfilled is described in the manual by what specific term?
opts: A crossed bill, one on which two transverse lines have been drawn across its face.
An inchoate bill, an incompletely filled-out bill with details left unfilled.
A dishonoured bill, one that has been presented for payment and refused.
A special bill, one bearing the name of a bank stamped on its face.
questionBank.ans: An inchoate bill, an incompletely filled-out bill with details left unfilled.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'An incompletely filled-out bill is described as an inchoate bill e.g when the drawer signs and leaves all other details unfilled.' A, C, and D are other real cheque-related concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: When a cheque bears two transverse lines across its face, without any bank's name stamped on it, what type of crossing does the manual say this is?
opts: Special crossing, where the name of a bank is stamped on the face.
General crossing, marked by two transverse lines across the face.
An inchoate crossing, one left incomplete by the drawer at the time of issue.
A negotiated crossing, one that has already been endorsed and delivered.
questionBank.ans: General crossing, marked by two transverse lines across the face.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'General - Two transverse lines across the face of the cheque. Sometimes, phrases such as 'A/c payee only' or 'Not Negotiable' are written between the lines.' A, C, and D misapply or invent terms not in the material.

questionBank.q: When a cheque bears the name of a specific bank stamped on its face, rather than merely two transverse lines, what type of crossing does the manual say this is?
opts: General crossing, marked by two transverse lines across the face.
Special crossing, marked by the name of a bank stamped on the face.
An inchoate crossing, one left incomplete by the drawer at the time of issue.
A dishonoured crossing, one that has already been refused by the paying bank.
questionBank.ans: Special crossing, marked by the name of a bank stamped on the face.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Special - Name of a bank stamped on the face of the cheque.' A, C, and D misapply or invent terms not in the material.

questionBank.q: Once a cheque is crossed, what does the manual say about a bank's ability to pay cash on it?
opts: A banker may always pay cash on it, since crossing has no effect on cash payment.
A banker should not pay cash on it unless the cheque is opened by the drawer.
A banker must always dishonour it, since a crossed cheque can never be paid at all.
A banker may pay cash only if the payee personally endorses it in the banker's presence.
questionBank.ans: A banker should not pay cash on it unless the cheque is opened by the drawer.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'When a cheque is crossed, a banker should not pay cash on it unless the cheque is opened by the drawer.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: A bank pays out on a cheque that later turns out to have been forged. Under what condition does the manual say the paying bank will still enjoy protection from liability?
opts: Only if the amount involved falls below a statutory minimum threshold.
Only if it can prove it made the payment in good faith, without negligence, and in the ordinary course.
Automatically, since a paying bank is never liable for paying on a forged cheque.
Only if the customer whose signature was forged had reported the loss of his chequebook.
questionBank.ans: Only if it can prove it made the payment in good faith, without negligence, and in the ordinary course.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A paying bank must be careful not to pay on a forged cheque because it will not enjoy protection if it pays one except it can prove that he made the payment in good faith, without negligence and in the ordinary course of business.' A, C, and D misstate this condition.

questionBank.q: A clearing bank collects a cheque for a person who is not its true owner. What potential liability does the manual say the clearing bank may face as a result?
opts: Liability under the Dishonoured Cheques Act, since collecting for a non-owner is itself an offence.
Liability in conversion to the true owner of the cheque.
No liability at all, since a clearing bank's duty runs strictly to the presenting customer.
Liability solely to the Central Bank, rather than to the true owner.
questionBank.ans: Liability in conversion to the true owner of the cheque.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A clearing bank should collect or clear cheques only for the true owner of the cheque or it may be liable in conversion to the owner.' A, C, and D misstate this liability.

questionBank.q: When a bank takes on the risk of clearing third-party cheques for its customer, what does the manual say it should, at a minimum, obtain to protect itself?
opts: A Deed of Guarantee & Indemnity from the drawer of each third-party cheque.
An Indemnity from the customer for whom the third-party cheques are being cleared.
A Letter of Comfort from the customer's own bank, confirming the cheques are genuine.
A perfected legal mortgage over an asset of equivalent value to the cheques.
questionBank.ans: An Indemnity from the customer for whom the third-party cheques are being cleared.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'When a bank takes the risk of clearing 3rd party cheques for its customer, it should at a minimum protect itself by obtaining an Indemnity from such customer.' A, C, and D invent or misapply protections not stated for this situation.

questionBank.q: Under the Dishonoured Cheques (Offences) Act, issuing a cheque that is later dishonoured for insufficient funds, after being used to obtain credit, is treated as which of the following?
opts: A civil matter only, resolved exclusively through a private claim for damages.
An offence, since it is an offence under the Act to issue dud cheques.
A regulatory breach sanctioned only by the CBN, without criminal consequence.
A matter left entirely to the discretion of the paying bank to report or ignore.
questionBank.ans: An offence, since it is an offence under the Act to issue dud cheques.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Under the Dishonoured Cheques (Offences) Act...it is an offence to issue dud cheques.' A, C, and D understate or misstate this classification.

questionBank.q: Under Section 1 of the Dishonoured Cheques (Offences) Act, within what period after the date of a cheque must it be presented and dishonoured for insufficient funds for the offence to apply?
opts: Not later than six months after the date of the cheque.
Not later than three months after the date of the cheque.
Not later than thirty days after the date of the cheque.
Not later than twelve months after the date of the cheque.
questionBank.ans: Not later than three months after the date of the cheque.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 1: the offence applies where a cheque 'presented for payment not later than three months after the date of the cheque, is dishonoured' for lack of sufficient funds. A, C, and D misstate this period.

questionBank.q: Under Section 1 of the Dishonoured Cheques (Offences) Act, what is the prescribed term of imprisonment on conviction for an individual who commits the offence of issuing a dud cheque?
opts: One year imprisonment.
Two years imprisonment.
Five years imprisonment.
Six months imprisonment.
questionBank.ans: Two years imprisonment.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 1: on conviction, an offender 'shall be sentenced to 2 years imprisonment (and if a company, to over N5000 fine).' A, C, and D misstate this term.

questionBank.q: Under the CBN circular cited in the manual, what must a bank do with unused cheque books already issued to a customer identified as a serial issuer of dud cheques?
opts: Convert the customer's account to a savings account with no cheque privileges.
Recall or cancel all unused cheque books issued to that customer.
Retain the cheque books but flag each cheque individually before payment.
Transfer the customer's account to another bank within the same group.
questionBank.ans: Recall or cancel all unused cheque books issued to that customer.
questionBank.exp: Manual, CBN circular: banks must 'Recall/cancel all unused cheque books issued to serial issuers of dud cheques.' A, C, and D are not among the directed activities.

questionBank.q: Under the same CBN circular, for how long must a serial issuer of dud cheques be barred from use of the clearing system?
opts: Two years.
Five years.
Ten years.
One year.
questionBank.ans: Five years.
questionBank.exp: Manual: banks must 'Bar the affected customers from use of the clearing system for a period of five (5) years.' A, C, and D misstate this period.

questionBank.q: Under the same CBN circular, banks must forward the names of dud cheque offenders to the Credit Bureaux and CRMS for five years. What happens if an offender is again found wanting after the name is removed?
opts: The offender receives only a formal written warning, with no further listing.
The offender's name is permanently reinstated in the databases.
The offender's name is listed for a further five-year period before reinstatement.
The offender's account is automatically closed by every bank in Nigeria.
questionBank.ans: The offender's name is permanently reinstated in the databases.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'if the offender is found wanting after the name is removed, such an offender shall be permanently reinstated in the data base of both the three (3) Credit Bureaux and the CRMS.' A, C, and D misstate this consequence.

questionBank.q: Under the same CBN circular, what must occur before any institution may remove a serial dud cheque issuer's name from the Credit Bureaux and CRMS?
opts: The affected customer's own written request to the reporting bank.
The prior written approval of the CBN.
A court order specifically directing the deletion of the record.
The mere expiry of the initial five-year listing period.
questionBank.ans: The prior written approval of the CBN.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'No institution shall, EXCEPT with the prior written approval of the CBN, remove such a person's name from the three Credit Bureaux and the Credit Risk Management System (CRMS).' A, C, and D misstate this requirement.

questionBank.q: Under the same CBN circular, for how long must serial issuers of dud cheques be barred from accessing credit facilities from the banking system?
opts: Two years.
Five years.
Ten years.
One year.
questionBank.ans: Five years.
questionBank.exp: Manual: banks must 'Bar the serial issuers of dud cheques from accessing credit facilities from the banking system for a period of five (5) years.' A, C, and D misstate this period.

questionBank.q: A financial institution fails to report a serial dud cheque issuer as required. Under which law does the manual say it becomes liable to be penalized?
opts: The Land Use Act, since non-compliant institutions forfeit land held as security.
The Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act, whose provisions govern this penalty.
The Companies and Allied Matters Act, since non-compliance is a winding-up ground.
The Bills of Exchange Act, since non-compliance is treated as dishonour of the instrument.
questionBank.ans: The Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act, whose provisions govern this penalty.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A financial institution that fails to report a serial dud cheque issuer...is liable to be penalized in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act.' A, C, and D misapply unrelated statutes.

questionBank.q: Beyond the financial institution itself, which specific officers does the manual say are also liable to sanctions for a bank's failure to report a serial dud cheque issuer?
opts: Only the Chief Executive Officer, since the CEO alone bears personal responsibility.
The CEO, CFO, Chief Compliance Officer, and Chief Risk Officer.
Only branch-level tellers who personally processed the dishonoured cheques.
Only the bank's external auditors, since they certify compliance annually.
questionBank.ans: The CEO, CFO, Chief Compliance Officer, and Chief Risk Officer.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Chief Financial Officer (CFO), Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) and Chief Risk Officer (CRO) shall also be liable to sanctions under the same law.' A, C, and D misstate or narrow this list of officers.

questionBank.q: Regulations and Guidelines issued by the CBN Governor in exercise of his statutory powers have what legal status in relation to banks, according to the manual?
opts: They constitute mere internal advice, binding on the CBN but not enforceable against banks.
They constitute law and are binding on banks once issued.
They constitute persuasive guidance only, effective once ratified by the National Assembly.
They constitute a code of ethics enforceable solely through professional bodies, not by CBN itself.
questionBank.ans: They constitute law and are binding on banks once issued.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the CBN Governor 'has issued several Regulations and Guidelines which constitute law and through which it regulates banking practice.' A, C, and D understate this binding legal status.

questionBank.q: Under Section 57 of BOFIA, the CBN Governor enacted the Regulation on the Scope of Banking Activities & Ancillary Matters, No. 3 of 2010. What did this Regulation do to the scope of 'banking business'?
opts: It expanded the scope to include all forms of insurance underwriting.
It contracted the scope and repealed the Universal Banking Guidelines.
It left the scope entirely unchanged from the prior Universal Banking Guidelines.
It transferred the power to define banking business from the CBN Governor to the National Assembly.
questionBank.ans: It contracted the scope and repealed the Universal Banking Guidelines.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the Regulation 'contracted the scope of 'banking business'' and, in Section 2, 'repealed the Universal Banking Guidelines then in force.' A, C, and D misstate this effect.

questionBank.q: Under Section 3 of the Regulation on the Scope of Banking Activities, 'Banking Business' is defined to include receiving deposits on current, savings or similar accounts, and which other activity?
opts: Underwriting insurance for corporate policyholders.
Paying or collecting cheques, and provision of finance.
Managing pension assets for registered administrators.
Issuing shares to the public without a prospectus.
questionBank.ans: Paying or collecting cheques, and provision of finance.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Banking Business' means 'the business of receiving deposits...paying or collecting cheques, drawn by or paid in by customers; provision of finance or such other business as the Governor may...designate as banking business.' A, C, and D are not part of this definition.

questionBank.q: Under Section 4(1) of the Regulation, which of the following is listed among the only types of banks permitted to carry on banking business in Nigeria?
opts: Investment banks, listed as a distinct permitted category.
Specialised banks, including non-interest, microfinance, development and mortgage banks.
Offshore banks, permitted to carry on business without a CBN licence.
Cooperative banks, permitted to carry on business without CBN supervision.
questionBank.ans: Specialised banks, including non-interest, microfinance, development and mortgage banks.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 4(1): permitted bank types are limited to Commercial banks, Merchant banks, and Specialised banks, 'which include non-interest banks, microfinance banks, development banks and mortgage banks.' A, C, and D are not listed categories.

questionBank.q: Under Section 5(1) of the Regulation, what are banks compelled to do in relation to any Related Enterprise, such as a subsidiary or associate they control?
opts: Consolidate its accounts fully into the bank's own audited financial statements.
Divest from the Related Enterprise.
Convert the Related Enterprise into a wholly owned subsidiary within 12 months.
Transfer supervision of the Related Enterprise entirely to the NDIC.
questionBank.ans: Divest from the Related Enterprise.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 5(1): 'Compels banks to divest from any Related Enterprise i.e. subsidiary or associate controlled by the bank.' A, C, and D are not stated consequences.

questionBank.q: Under Section 5(2) of the Regulation, beyond restricting real estate acquisition to purposes of the bank's own banking business, what else are banks barred from doing?
opts: Opening more than five branches in any single state within a calendar year.
Giving loans or gifts for any political purpose.
Accepting deposits from customers resident outside Nigeria.
Extending credit facilities to any registered non-governmental organization.
questionBank.ans: Giving loans or gifts for any political purpose.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 5(2): banks 'may not acquire real estate except for purposes of their banking business and may not give loans or gifts for any political purpose.' A, C, and D are not stated restrictions.

questionBank.q: The requirement that banks verify a customer's identity before opening or operating an account is rooted in which specific statutory provision, according to the manual?
opts: Section 18 of the Companies and Allied Matters Act, 2019.
Section 3 of the Money Laundering (Prohibition) Act, 2011.
Section 3 of the Bills of Exchange Act.
Section 57 of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act.
questionBank.ans: Section 3 of the Money Laundering (Prohibition) Act, 2011.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'KYC principles require that banks know their customers, therefore, we must verify their identity before opening or operating accounts for them. [Section 3, Money Laundering (Prohibition) Act, 2011].' A, C, and D are real statutory provisions from elsewhere, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the manual's established categories of bank customers, alongside Individuals, Sole Proprietors, and Partnerships?
opts: Government Parastatals, listed as a distinct customer category.
Unincorporated Associations, listed among the established categories.
Diplomatic Missions, listed as a distinct customer category.
Non-Resident Nigerians, listed as a distinct customer category.
questionBank.ans: Unincorporated Associations, listed among the established categories.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Established categories of customers include Individuals, Sole Proprietors, Partnerships, Incorporated Companies, unincorporated Associations and Trusts.' A, C, and D are not among the listed categories.

questionBank.q: A sole proprietor who carries on business under a name other than his own actual name is required to do what, according to the manual?
opts: Register with the Corporate Affairs Commission.
Obtain a special banking licence from the CBN before opening any account.
Convert the business into a private company limited by shares within one year.
Register the business name with the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation.
questionBank.ans: Register with the Corporate Affairs Commission.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a sole proprietor 'is required to be registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission if business is carried on in a name other than the actual names of the proprietor.' B, C, and D are not stated requirements.

questionBank.q: Because a sole proprietorship has no separate legal existence from its owner, what does the manual say about a credit facility granted to the business?
opts: It is treated as a facility to the Corporate Affairs Commission.
It is treated as a facility to the sole proprietor personally.
It is treated as a facility to any future incorporated entity the business may become.
It is treated as unsecured by default, regardless of any security actually taken.
questionBank.ans: It is treated as a facility to the sole proprietor personally.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a sole proprietor 'has no separate legal existence distinct from his business. A credit facility to his business is a facility to him in person.' A, C, and D are not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: Alongside a certificate of registration, what other specific document must a registered sole proprietorship submit to the bank when opening an account, according to the manual?
opts: CAC 7, the form detailing particulars of a company's directors.
Form II, a certified copy of the application form submitted to the CAC for registration.
CAC 2, the statement of a company's share capital.
A Deed of Guarantee & Indemnity executed by the proprietor's next of kin.
questionBank.ans: Form II, a certified copy of the application form submitted to the CAC for registration.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a registered sole proprietor must submit 'a certificate of registration...to the bank alongside Form II which is a certified copy of the application form submitted to the CAC for registration.' A, C, and D are documents used for other customer types, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Under Section 19 of CAMA as cited in the manual, partnership membership is generally limited to 20 persons, except for which professions or bodies?
opts: Doctors, engineers and religious organizations.
Lawyers, accountants and co-operative societies.
Architects, surveyors and trade unions.
Bankers, insurers and pension fund administrators.
questionBank.ans: Lawyers, accountants and co-operative societies.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.19 CAMA: partnership 'membership limited to 20 (except for lawyers, accountants & co-operative societies).' A, C, and D invent categories not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: In the absence of a partnership deed providing otherwise, what does the applicable Partnership Law say happens to a partnership upon the death of a partner?
opts: It ordinarily dissolves the partnership.
It converts the partnership into a Limited Liability Partnership.
It has no effect on the partnership's existence.
It transfers the partner's share to the CAC in trust.
questionBank.ans: It ordinarily dissolves the partnership.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'the death of a partner ordinarily dissolves a partnership unless they have a deed that provides otherwise.' B, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Because a partnership is not a legal person, what is the manual's stated consequence for its ability to sue or be sued in its own name?
opts: It can always sue or be sued in the partnership name, regardless of incorporation.
It cannot sue or be sued in the partnership name unless incorporated as a Limited Liability Partnership under CAMA.
It can sue but never be sued in the partnership name, since liability rests solely with individual partners.
It can be sued but never sue in the partnership name, since it lacks standing to initiate litigation.
questionBank.ans: It cannot sue or be sued in the partnership name unless incorporated as a Limited Liability Partnership under CAMA.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A partnership is not a legal person and so it cannot sue or be sued in the partnership name unless it is incorporated as a Limited Liability Partnership under Part C of CAMA (Sec. 746).' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: What does the manual say about the liability of every general partner for the debts and obligations of the partnership business incurred while that person was a partner?
opts: It is limited strictly to the amount that partner personally invested.
It is joint and several for all such debts and obligations.
It is deferred entirely until the partnership is formally dissolved by court order.
It is guaranteed exclusively by the partnership's registered trade name.
questionBank.ans: It is joint and several for all such debts and obligations.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'liability of each general partner is joint and several for all the debts and obligations of the business incurred while that person was a partner.' A, C, and D misstate this rule, with A instead describing a Limited Partner's liability.

questionBank.q: Unlike a general partner, a Limited Partner's liability for the partnership's debts and obligations is restricted to what, according to the manual?
opts: Half the amount invested, the balance guaranteed by others.
The amount he has invested in the business.
His full personal assets, identical to a general partner.
Nothing at all, since Limited Partners bear no liability.
questionBank.ans: The amount he has invested in the business.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Liability of a Limited Partner is however restricted to the loss of the amount he has invested in the business.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Under Section 18 of CAMA as cited in the manual, how many persons are ordinarily required to form and incorporate a company, and what exception applies?
opts: Two or more persons ordinarily, but one person may incorporate a private company.
Five or more persons ordinarily, with no exception for any company type.
Two or more persons ordinarily, with no exception permitting a single-person company.
One person ordinarily, with a minimum of two required only for public companies.
questionBank.ans: Two or more persons ordinarily, but one person may incorporate a private company.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.18 CAMA: 'any two or more persons may form and incorporate a company...one person may form and incorporate a private company.' B, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: What legal characteristic allows an incorporated company to own property and sue or be sued in its own name, distinct from its shareholders?
opts: Its Memorandum of Association, which alone confers legal personality.
Its perpetual legal existence, distinct from the individuals that comprise it.
Its registration with the Corporate Affairs Commission as a business name.
Its appointment of a minimum of two directors under Section 271 of CAMA.
questionBank.ans: Its perpetual legal existence, distinct from the individuals that comprise it.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A company has perpetual legal existence and is distinct from the individuals that comprise it...It can own property, sue and be sued in its corporate name.' A, C, and D misapply other real requirements from the same section.

questionBank.q: Under Section 283 of CAMA as cited in the manual, which of the following persons is barred from serving as a company director?
opts: A person who previously directed an unrelated company.
A bankrupt.
A person holding shares in more than one listed company.
A non-Nigerian citizen of sound mind and unconvicted.
questionBank.ans: A bankrupt.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 283: 'a minor, lunatic or insane, a corporation, bankrupt or convict cannot be directors.' A, C, and D are not stated disqualifications.

questionBank.q: Under Section 21 of CAMA (2019) as cited in the manual, which of the following is listed as one of the different types of companies the Act creates?
opts: Companies limited by turnover, based on revenue.
Companies limited by guarantee.
Companies limited by workforce, based on headcount.
Companies limited by tenure, based on company age.
questionBank.ans: Companies limited by guarantee.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.21 CAMA: creates 'Unlimited liability companies, Companies limited by Guarantee, Companies limited by shares.' A, C, and D invent categories not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: A private company limited by shares must state certain restrictions in its Memorandum & Articles of Association. Which of the following is one of them, according to the manual?
opts: A restriction limiting its membership to 50 persons, excluding staff and ex-staff.
A restriction limiting its authorized share capital to exactly N100,000 for its entire existence.
A restriction requiring at least five directors to be appointed at incorporation.
A restriction barring it from ever converting to a public company under any circumstance.
questionBank.ans: A restriction limiting its membership to 50 persons, excluding staff and ex-staff.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a private company must restrict 'Membership, to 50 persons. [Excluding staff and ex-staff].' B, C, and D misstate the stated restrictions.

questionBank.q: What is the minimum authorized share capital the manual states is required for a private company limited by shares, as distinct from a public company?
questionBank.exp: Manual: a private company limited by shares 'is incorporated with a minimum authorized share capital of N100,000.' A, C, and D misstate this figure or apply the public-company figure instead.

questionBank.q: What is the minimum authorized share capital the manual states is permitted for a public company, as distinct from a private company?
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Minimum authorized share capital permitted is N2,000,000' for a public company. A, C, and D misstate this figure or apply the private-company figure instead.

questionBank.q: Upon insolvency of a company limited by shares, to what extent is a member personally liable for the company's obligations, according to the manual?
opts: Fully liable, to the same extent as a general partner.
Only to the value of shares owned in the company.
Not liable at all, even to the extent of any unpaid amount on shares.
Liable only if the member is also a director at the time of insolvency.
questionBank.ans: Only to the value of shares owned in the company.
questionBank.exp: Manual: companies limited by shares enjoy limited liability, so 'upon insolvency, the liability of their members is limited to the value of shares owned in the company. Members are thus not personally liable for any obligations of the company.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is stated in the manual to be contained in a company's Memorandum of Association?
opts: The company's borrowing powers and the procedure for its winding up.
The company's name and its objects, covering the powers and nature of its business.
The company's rules on shareholding classes and restrictions on share transfer.
The company's rules on the appointment of directors and secretaries.
questionBank.ans: The company's name and its objects, covering the powers and nature of its business.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the Memorandum of Association states 'Name of the company & its Objects (Powers and nature of business)' among other things. A, C, and D are contents of the Articles of Association, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is stated in the manual to be contained in a company's Articles of Association, as distinct from its Memorandum?
opts: The nature of the company, i.e. whether it is private or public.
The company's borrowing powers and accounts.
The subscription clause executed by the subscribers.
Whether the company's registered office is situate in Nigeria.
questionBank.ans: The company's borrowing powers and accounts.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the Articles of Association govern 'Borrowing powers and accounts' among other internal matters. A, C, and D are contents of the Memorandum of Association, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: If a company's directors authorize the company to engage in a business activity not listed in its Memorandum of Association, what does CAMA hold the directors personally liable for, according to the manual?
opts: Only obligations exceeding N2,000,000 arising from that unauthorized activity.
Any loss or obligations created by that unauthorized activity.
Nothing at all, since the company itself bears sole liability for any ultra vires act.
Only obligations arising from unauthorized activity involving real estate transactions.
questionBank.ans: Any loss or obligations created by that unauthorized activity.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'CAMA holds directors of a company personally liable for any loss or obligations created when the directors have authorized the company to engage in a business activity not listed in its Memorandum of Association.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Under Section 271 of CAMA as cited in the manual, what is the minimum number of directors every company must have, and what must occur if the number falls below it?
opts: A minimum of five, and the company must be wound up if the number falls below.
A minimum of two, and a new director must be appointed if the number falls below.
A minimum of one, and no further appointment is ever required regardless of vacancies.
A minimum of three, and the CBN must approve any replacement director appointed.
questionBank.ans: A minimum of two, and a new director must be appointed if the number falls below.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 271: 'Every company shall have at least two directors and must appoint a new one if the number falls below that statutory minimum.' A, C, and D misstate this requirement.

questionBank.q: Under Section 274 of CAMA as cited in the manual, who has the power to appoint a new director to fill a casual vacancy arising from death, resignation, retirement or removal, and subject to what?
opts: The Board of directors, subject to the approval of the shareholders.
The company's external auditors, subject to CBN approval where the company is a bank.
The subscribers of the Memorandum of Association, without any further approval.
The Corporate Affairs Commission, subject to a formal application by the remaining directors.
questionBank.ans: The Board of directors, subject to the approval of the shareholders.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 274: 'The Board of directors shall have power to appoint new directors to fill any casual vacancy...subject to the approval of the shareholders.' B, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Under Section 305(3) of CAMA as cited in the manual, in whose interests must a director act at all times, and to what standard?
opts: The shareholder who nominated him, over the company's interests.
The company as a whole, to the standard of a diligent director.
The company's creditors exclusively, ahead of shareholders.
The CBN's supervisory objectives, ahead of the company's own.
questionBank.ans: The company as a whole, to the standard of a diligent director.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 305(3): a director must act 'in what he believes to be the best interests of the company as a whole...in such manner as a faithful, diligent, careful and ordinarily skillful director would act.' A, C, and D misstate this standard.

questionBank.q: Compliance with which specific code, effective April 3, 2006, is mandatory for all banks according to the manual's discussion of Company Directors?
opts: The Nigerian Code of Corporate Governance for Public Companies.
The CBN Code of Corporate Governance for Banks in Nigeria.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's Code of Best Practice.
The Financial Reporting Council's Code of Accounting Standards.
questionBank.ans: The CBN Code of Corporate Governance for Banks in Nigeria.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Compliance with the CBN Code of Corporate Governance for Banks in Nigeria effective April 3, 2006 is mandatory for all banks.' A, C, and D are not the code named in this section.

questionBank.q: Under the revised (2022) tenure rules the manual cites, for what maximum period will an Executive Director, Deputy Managing Director or Managing Director/CEO ordinarily hold their position?
opts: A maximum period of 5 years.
A maximum period of 10 years.
A maximum period of 15 years.
A maximum period of 8 years.
questionBank.ans: A maximum period of 10 years.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Every Executive Director (ED), Deputy Managing Director (DMD) and Managing Director/CEO (MD/CEO) will hold their positions...for a maximum period of 10 years.' A, C, and D misstate this figure.

questionBank.q: Under the revised tenure rules, if a DMD becomes MD/CEO of a bank before the end of his tenure, what is his maximum cumulative tenure, according to the manual?
opts: A maximum tenure of 10 years, identical to the ordinary rule.
A maximum tenure of 12 years.
A maximum tenure of 20 years, since the two roles are counted separately.
A maximum tenure of 8 years, shorter than the ordinary rule.
questionBank.ans: A maximum tenure of 12 years.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Where a DMD becomes MD/CEO of a bank or another bank before the end of his tenure, he/she will serve for a maximum tenure of 12 years.' A, C, and D misstate this figure.

questionBank.q: Under the revised tenure rules, into how many terms is a Non-Executive Director's (excluding Independent Directors) maximum cumulative tenure of 12 years divided, according to the manual?
opts: 2 terms of 6 years each.
3 terms of 4 years each.
4 terms of 3 years each.
6 terms of 2 years each.
questionBank.ans: 3 terms of 4 years each.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'For Non-Executive directors (NED), (except Independent Directors) their cumulative tenure shall not exceed 12 years divided into 3 terms of 4 years each.' A, C, and D misstate this structure.

questionBank.q: Under the revised tenure rules, an ED, DMD or MD who exits the Board of a bank before or at the end of their tenure must observe what before becoming eligible for appointment as a Non-Executive Director of any other bank?
opts: A 'cooling off' period of 5 years.
A 'cooling off' period of 1 year.
No cooling-off period at all, since immediate appointment elsewhere is permitted.
A 'cooling off' period of 6 months.
questionBank.ans: A 'cooling off' period of 1 year.
questionBank.exp: Manual: such a director 'shall serve a 'cooling off' period of 1 year before being eligible for appointment as NED to the Board of any other bank.' A, C, and D misstate this period.

questionBank.q: Under the tenure rules the manual cites, what is the maximum period an external auditor may serve a bank before the firm must wait a further period before reappointment?
opts: A maximum of five years, followed by a further five-year wait.
A maximum of ten years, followed by a further ten-year wait.
A maximum of three years, followed by a further three-year wait.
A maximum of ten years, with immediate reappointment permitted.
questionBank.ans: A maximum of ten years, followed by a further ten-year wait.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A maximum of ten (10) years and firm shall not be reappointed in the bank until after a period of another 10 years.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Unincorporated Associations, such as religious bodies, charities, clubs and trade unions, are described by the manual as lacking which legal characteristic?
opts: They are not juristic persons.
They may not open any bank account under Nigerian law.
They dissolve automatically on any founding member's death.
They may not appoint a Board of Trustees at all.
questionBank.ans: They are not juristic persons.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'These include religious bodies, charities, clubs, societies and trade unions and they are not juristic persons.' B, C, and D are not stated consequences.

questionBank.q: Once registered, who does the manual say exercises all the legal powers of an Unincorporated Association and can sue or be sued on its behalf?
opts: The association's largest individual donor, acting in a fiduciary capacity.
A Board of Trustees, also called Incorporated Trustees when incorporated.
The Corporate Affairs Commission, acting as statutory administrator of the association.
Any individual member who volunteers to represent the association in litigation.
questionBank.ans: A Board of Trustees, also called Incorporated Trustees when incorporated.
questionBank.exp: Manual: an Unincorporated Association is 'usually administered by a Board of Trustees (also called Incorporated trustees when incorporated) which exercises all the legal powers of and can sue or be sued on behalf of the association as soon as it is registered.' A, C, and D are not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: Beyond a completed account opening package and certificates of registration, what other document does the manual say the bank should obtain from an Unincorporated Association, alongside identification of the Trustees?
opts: A Deed of Guarantee & Indemnity executed by every member of the association.
The Constitution and Minutes of the meeting where the trustees were appointed.
A Certificate of Occupancy over any land the association owns or occupies.
A resolution of the Corporate Affairs Commission approving the association's registration.
questionBank.ans: The Constitution and Minutes of the meeting where the trustees were appointed.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the bank should obtain 'copies of their certificates of registration, Constitution and Minutes of the meeting where the trustees were appointed and identification papers of the Trustees.' A, C, and D invent documents not stated for this customer type.

questionBank.q: For a Joint Account operated by two individuals, what does the manual say a bank must receive before it can operate the account, absent contrary authority?
opts: A court order confirming the relationship between the two account holders.
A written mandate signed by both account holders.
Individual mandates signed separately, with no need for both to sign a single document.
A joint indemnity signed by both account holders' next of kin.
questionBank.ans: A written mandate signed by both account holders.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A bank must receive a written mandate signed by both and in the absence of contrary authority, the banker should only honor transaction instruments signed by both.' A, C, and D misstate this requirement.

questionBank.q: On the death of one holder of a Joint Account, and absent a contrary instruction in the mandate, what does the manual say happens to the balance on the account?
opts: The account is frozen permanently until the deceased's estate is fully distributed.
The survivorship principle applies, and the survivor becomes wholly entitled to the balance.
The balance is split automatically between the survivor and the deceased's next of kin.
The bank must transfer the entire balance to the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation.
questionBank.ans: The survivorship principle applies, and the survivor becomes wholly entitled to the balance.
questionBank.exp: Manual: on death of one joint account holder, 'in the absence of a contrary instruction in the mandate, the survivorship principle applies such that the survivor becomes wholly entitled to the balance on the account.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: For a Trust Account, the manual describes the 'trustee' as holding what, and for whose use?
opts: Only a power of attorney over the account, for the trustee's own benefit.
The legal right to money in the account, for the use of a 'beneficiary'.
Equitable title only, with legal title vested permanently in the bank itself.
No enforceable right at all, since a Trust Account is merely an informal arrangement.
questionBank.ans: The legal right to money in the account, for the use of a 'beneficiary'.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a Trust Account is 'operated by one person for the benefit of someone else such that the 'trustee' holds the legal right to money in an account for the use of a 'beneficiary'.' A, C, and D misstate this arrangement.

questionBank.q: What does the manual say a bank must avoid doing in relation to a Trust Account, while also not preventing the trustee from performing his duties under the trust?
opts: Disclosing the existence of the trust to any regulatory authority, including the CBN.
Knowingly being part of a breach of trust.
Permitting the trustee to make any withdrawal at all from the account.
Allowing the beneficiary to receive statements of account directly from the bank.
questionBank.ans: Knowingly being part of a breach of trust.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A bank must not knowingly be part of a breach of trust but it must also not prevent the trustee from performing his duties under the trust.' A, C, and D are not stated obligations.

questionBank.q: Absent express permission under the Trust's terms, what does the manual say about a trustee's power to borrow or invest trust funds in the name of the trust?
opts: Trustees always have that power, since it is inherent in the office of trustee.
Trustees generally do not have that power unless the Trust terms permit it.
Trustees have that power only after obtaining the bank's written consent, regardless of the Trust terms.
Trustees have that power only where the beneficiary is of full age and mental capacity.
questionBank.ans: Trustees generally do not have that power unless the Trust terms permit it.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Trustees generally do not have power to borrow or invest trust funds in the name of the trust unless the Trust terms permit.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Which two individual customer types does the manual identify as sharing the common feature that the underlying arrangement continues to be governed by a written mandate or trust terms rather than the general banker/customer duties alone?
opts: Sole Proprietorships and Partnerships, both governed by CAMA's default rules.
Joint Accounts and Trust Accounts, each governed by its own mandate or trust terms.
Unincorporated Associations and Incorporated Companies, both governed by a single Constitution.
Minors and Illiterates, both governed exclusively by the Jurat process before a Magistrate.
questionBank.ans: Joint Accounts and Trust Accounts, each governed by its own mandate or trust terms.
questionBank.exp: Manual discusses Joint Accounts (governed by a written mandate and the survivorship principle) and Trust Accounts (governed by the Trust's terms) as distinct customer arrangements with their own governing documents. A, C, and D misapply unrelated customer types.

questionBank.q: Loans extended by a bank are described in the manual, for balance-sheet purposes, by what specific term?
opts: Contingent liabilities, since they depend on future events.
Risk assets, since they constitute part of the bank's assets.
Deferred receivables, since they represent future cash inflows.
Trust property, since they are held for the benefit of depositors.
questionBank.ans: Risk assets, since they constitute part of the bank's assets.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Loans constitute part of the assets of a bank. They are referred to as 'risk assets'.' A, C, and D are not the term used in the material.

questionBank.q: According to the manual's discussion of general lending principles, what should a prudent banker lend against, rather than security alone?
opts: The customer's personal reputation within the local community.
A sound credit proposal submitted by the customer, in accordance with the bank's credit policy.
The average lending rate declared by competing banks in the same market.
The customer's projected future income, without regard to current credit policy.
questionBank.ans: A sound credit proposal submitted by the customer, in accordance with the bank's credit policy.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A prudent banker will not lend against security but against a sound credit proposal submitted to it by the customer and in accordance with the credit policy of his bank.' A, C, and D are not the stated principle.

questionBank.q: To safeguard the bank's position in lending decisions, which two departments does the manual say work closely together?
opts: The Marketing Department and the Human Resources Department.
The Legal Department and the Risk Management Department.
The Treasury Department and the Information Technology Department.
The Compliance Department and the Corporate Communications Department.
questionBank.ans: The Legal Department and the Risk Management Department.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'To safeguard the bank's position the Legal Department works closely with the Risk Management Department of the bank.' A, C, and D are not the departments named.

questionBank.q: Beyond the commercial need to protect funds from loss, what other reason does the manual give for banks taking security when lending?
opts: Taking security is required solely by internal bank policy.
Bankers are required by law to take security, under BOFIA.
Taking security is required only where the CBN specifically directs it.
Taking security is required only for facilities exceeding N2,000,000.
questionBank.ans: Bankers are required by law to take security, under BOFIA.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Banks lend other people's money thus they need to protect the funds from loss by taking security. Bankers are also required by law to take security. (BOFIA).' A, C, and D misstate or narrow this requirement.

questionBank.q: In the banking context, the manual describes 'security' as a resource given by a debtor to his bank for what specific purpose?
opts: To satisfy a statutory registration requirement, independent of the debt itself.
To assure repayment of his debt, relieving the bank's anxiety of possible financial loss.
To provide the bank with an alternative source of income unrelated to the facility granted.
To transfer full ownership of the debtor's business to the bank for the facility's duration.
questionBank.ans: To assure repayment of his debt, relieving the bank's anxiety of possible financial loss.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Security in the banking context, is a resource given by a debtor to his bank in order to assure the repayment of his debt thus relieving the bank's anxiety of possible financial loss.' A, C, and D misstate this purpose.

questionBank.q: The five-step process of preparing legal documents, execution, processing, stamping and registration of a security asset is collectively described in the manual by what term?
opts: Negotiation, the transfer of rights in an instrument to a transferee for value.
Perfection, full documentation preserving the bank's priority over other claimants.
Ratification, the process by which a minor confirms a contract upon reaching majority.
Consideration, the value given by a debtor in exchange for the facility granted.
questionBank.ans: Perfection, full documentation preserving the bank's priority over other claimants.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Perfection means full documentation of the security asset so as to preserve the bank's priority over any other claimant. Perfection entails: 1) Preparation...2) Execution 3) Processing...4) Stamping 5) Registration.' A, C, and D are unrelated concepts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the five steps of perfection the manual lists, which step specifically involves obtaining the Governor's consent to a land transaction?
opts: Execution, since signing must occur before processing.
Processing, which includes obtaining Governor's consent.
Stamping, since consent is part of the stamping process.
Registration, since consent is obtained at the Lands Registry.
questionBank.ans: Processing, which includes obtaining Governor's consent.
questionBank.exp: Manual: perfection's third step is 'Processing (e.g. Governor's consent to land transactions).' A, C, and D are the other listed steps, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Beyond the civil consequence of losing priority over other claimants, what does the manual say an unperfected security constitutes, where security is required by BOFIA?
opts: A tort of conversion actionable by any third-party claimant.
An offence under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act.
A breach of the Money Laundering (Prohibition) Act, 2011.
A ground for automatic revocation of the bank's operating licence.
questionBank.ans: An offence under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'An unperfected security fails and that constitutes an offence under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) where security is required.' A, C, and D misapply unrelated statutes.

questionBank.q: Among the qualities of a good security asset the manual lists, which quality requires that the asset be identifiable and available, with an assured, undisputed and unencumbered title?
opts: The quality requiring the asset to be readily realizable.
The quality requiring the asset to be identifiable and available, with clear title.
The quality requiring the asset's value to exceed the value of the facility granted.
The quality requiring the asset to have been perfected before the facility is disbursed.
questionBank.ans: The quality requiring the asset to be identifiable and available, with clear title.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a good security asset 'must be identifiable and available i.e. an assured, undisputed and unencumbered title.' A, C, and D are the other listed qualities, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the qualities of a good security asset the manual lists, which quality specifically concerns how easily the asset can be converted into cash if the bank needs to enforce it?
opts: The quality requiring the asset to have an ascertainable value exceeding the facility.
The quality requiring the asset to be readily realizable.
The quality requiring the asset to be identifiable and available with unencumbered title.
The quality requiring the asset to have been perfected before the facility is disbursed.
questionBank.ans: The quality requiring the asset to be readily realizable.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a good security asset 'must be readily realizable.' A, C, and D are the other listed qualities, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Under Section 6 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what must a bank obtain before opening or closing any branch, whether within or outside Nigeria?
opts: A resolution of its shareholders at an AGM.
CBN written approval.
A Certificate of Occupancy for the branch premises.
Approval from the NDIC only.
questionBank.ans: CBN written approval.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 6: 'CBN written approval to be obtained before opening and closing any branch within or outside Nigeria.' A, C, and D are not the stated requirement.

questionBank.q: Under Section 7 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, whose approval is required before a bank may undergo a merger, reconstruction or acquisition?
opts: The Securities and Exchange Commission's approval only.
The CBN Governor's approval.
The Federal High Court's approval only.
The Corporate Affairs Commission's approval only.
questionBank.ans: The CBN Governor's approval.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 7: 'Merger, reconstruction or acquisition only with CBN Governor's approval.' A, C, and D are not the stated approving authority.

questionBank.q: Under Section 8 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what must a foreign bank obtain before it may operate in Nigeria?
opts: A resolution of the Senate approving its market entry.
A CBN licence.
A reciprocal licence agreement with its home country.
Registration as a public company under CAMA.
questionBank.ans: A CBN licence.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 8: 'No foreign bank may operate in Nigeria without CBN licence.' A, C, and D are not the stated requirement.

questionBank.q: Under Section 9 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what is the CBN empowered to prescribe in relation to banks, with sanctions for non-compliance?
opts: The maximum number of branches a bank may operate nationwide.
The minimum paid-up share capital of banks.
The specific software systems banks must use for core operations.
The maximum tenure of a bank's external auditors.
questionBank.ans: The minimum paid-up share capital of banks.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 9: 'CBN may prescribe minimum paid-up share capital of banks and banks must comply or face sanctions.' A, C, and D are not the stated power.

questionBank.q: Under Section 13 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what may the CBN prescribe, failing which a bank may be barred from certain strategic banking activities?
opts: A maximum ratio of foreign currency deposits to total deposits.
A minimum capital ratio unimpaired by losses.
A minimum number of branches to be opened in rural areas.
A maximum interest rate chargeable on unsecured personal loans.
questionBank.ans: A minimum capital ratio unimpaired by losses.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 13: 'CBN may prescribe minimum capital ratio (unimpaired by losses) to be maintained by banks, failing which they may be barred from certain strategic banking activities.' A, C, and D are not the stated power.

questionBank.q: Under Sections 15 and 16 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, from what may a bank only declare a dividend?
opts: Its gross revenue for the financial year, before any deduction for tax or expenses.
Its net profit after provision for tax, expenses and losses including contingent losses.
Its total shareholders' fund, regardless of the year's actual trading performance.
Its reserve funds exclusively, without regard to the year's net profit or loss.
questionBank.ans: Its net profit after provision for tax, expenses and losses including contingent losses.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Sections 15 & 16: banks 'may only declare dividend from their net profit after provision for tax, expenses and losses including contingent losses.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Under Section 17 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what must a director, manager or officer of a bank do regarding any interest they have in a credit facility?
opts: Transfer the facility to a family member instead.
Disclose it.
Resign their position immediately, regardless of size.
Obtain a court order confirming arm's-length terms.
questionBank.ans: Disclose it.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 17: 'Directors, Managers or officers of a bank must disclose any interest they have in a credit facility.' A, C, and D are not the stated obligation.

questionBank.q: Under Section 18 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what is a bank barred from doing in relation to a person previously convicted of fraud, dishonesty or professional misconduct?
opts: Extending credit even after a prior facility is repaid.
Re-employing that person.
Disclosing the conviction without a court order.
Reporting the conviction to the CBN's CRMS.
questionBank.ans: Re-employing that person.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 18: 'a bank cannot re-employ any person who has been convicted by a court for any offence involving fraud or dishonesty or professional misconduct.' A, C, and D are not the stated bar.

questionBank.q: Under Section 19(1)(a) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what is the maximum credit facility a bank may grant to any person without the CBN's prior written approval, expressed as a percentage of shareholders' fund?
opts: 10% of the bank's shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses.
20% of the bank's shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses.
5% of the bank's shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses.
50% of the bank's shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses.
questionBank.ans: 20% of the bank's shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 19(1)(a): a bank shall not, without CBN's prior written approval, 'grant any credit facility to any person in excess of 20% of its shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses.' A, C, and D misstate this figure.

questionBank.q: Under Section 19(3)(a) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what maximum unsecured credit facility may a bank grant to any of its directors without the CBN's written approval?
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 19(3)(a): forbids a bank from 'granting a credit facility in excess of N1,000,000 to any of its directors without security except with CBN's written approval.' A, C, and D misstate this figure.

questionBank.q: Under Section 19(3)(c) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what does a bank need before it may grant forbearance on credit to any of its directors?
opts: A Board resolution excluding the director in question.
CBN approval.
Unanimous written consent of all shareholders.
A court order authorizing the forbearance.
questionBank.ans: CBN approval.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 19(3)(c): the section 'precludes a bank from giving forbearance on credit to any of its directors without CBN approval.' A, C, and D are not the stated requirement.

questionBank.q: Under Section 19(8)(d) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what does a bank require before purchasing, selling, disposing, acquiring or leasing any real estate for whatever purpose?
opts: A Certificate of Occupancy in the bank's own name.
CBN written approval.
Approval of the Federal Ministry of Lands.
A resolution at the bank's next scheduled AGM.
questionBank.ans: CBN written approval.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 19(8)(d): 'requires a bank to have CBN written approval before purchasing, selling, disposing, acquiring or leasing any real estate for whatever purpose.' A, C, and D are not the stated requirement.

questionBank.q: Under Section 22 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what is every bank required to display at its offices?
opts: Its most recent audited financial statements in full.
Its lending and deposit interest rates.
The names and photographs of its current directors.
Its CBN operating licence number and date of issue only.
questionBank.ans: Its lending and deposit interest rates.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 22: 'requires every bank to display at its offices its lending and deposit interest rates.' A, C, and D are not the stated requirement.

questionBank.q: Under Section 23 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what is the consequence of a bank's failure to keep proper books of account with respect to all its transactions?
opts: A formal CBN warning only, with no further sanction.
It is a crime.
Automatic suspension of dividend rights for one year.
A requirement to engage an additional auditor.
questionBank.ans: It is a crime.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 23: 'Every bank shall cause to be kept proper books of account with respect to all the transactions of the bank and failure to do so is a crime.' A, C, and D understate this consequence.

questionBank.q: Under Section 33 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, the Governor may order a special examination of a bank's books and affairs where he is satisfied of certain conditions. Which of the following is one of them?
opts: That the bank's most recent AGM was not attended by a quorum.
That the bank has insufficient assets to cover its liabilities to the public.
That the bank has changed its registered office address without prior notice.
That the bank has appointed a new external auditor within the last twelve months.
questionBank.ans: That the bank has insufficient assets to cover its liabilities to the public.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 33 lists grounds including where 'the bank has 'insufficient' assets to cover its liabilities to the public.' A, C, and D are not among the listed grounds.

questionBank.q: Under Section 33 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, besides the Governor's own initiative, who else may apply for a special examination of a bank's books and affairs?
opts: Any member of the public with no direct relationship to the bank.
A depositor or creditor of the bank.
A competing bank seeking commercial intelligence.
A journalist investigating the bank's financial condition for publication.
questionBank.ans: A depositor or creditor of the bank.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 33 lists an application 'by - a director or shareholder of the bank; or a depositor or creditor of the bank.' A, C, and D are not among the listed applicants.

questionBank.q: Under Section 34 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, in exercising his powers over a Failing Bank, what may the Governor do to the composition of the bank's Board, and how does the bank's own constitution affect this?
opts: Appoint directors only; removal needs a court order.
Appoint or remove directors, unaffected by the Memo & Articles.
Remove directors only; appointment needs shareholder approval.
Neither, since Section 34 only restricts forex activities.
questionBank.ans: Appoint or remove directors, unaffected by the Memo & Articles.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 34: the Governor 'may also appoint or remove directors and the composition of the new Board shall not be affected by any limitations contained in the bank's Memo & Articles.' A, C, and D misstate this power.

questionBank.q: Under Section 47(1) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what is required before any person may be appointed as Director or chief executive of a bank?
opts: Five years' banking experience, certified by the Board.
CBN's prior approval.
Registration as a chartered accountant or banker.
A shareholders' resolution passed by simple majority.
questionBank.ans: CBN's prior approval.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 47(1): 'No person may be appointed as Director or chief executive of a bank without CBN's prior approval.' A, C, and D are not the stated requirement.

questionBank.q: Under Section 46 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, directors and employees of banks are prohibited from receiving what, for rendering any banking service, for themselves or their relations?
opts: Only cash payments; non-cash gifts are expressly permitted.
Commissions, gifts, employment, service, gratuity, money, property or any other thing of value.
Only gifts exceeding N1,000,000 in value; smaller gifts are permitted.
Only gifts from existing customers; gifts from prospective customers are permitted.
questionBank.ans: Commissions, gifts, employment, service, gratuity, money, property or any other thing of value.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 46: directors and employees are prohibited 'from receiving commissions gift, employment, service, gratuity, money, property or thing of value for themselves or their relations from any person for rendering any banking service.' A, C, and D invent exceptions not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: Under Section 47(2)(a) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, which of the following persons may not be appointed or remain a director, secretary or officer of a bank?
opts: A person who has previously worked for a competing bank within the last five years.
A person convicted for dishonesty or serious misconduct in relation to his duties.
A person who holds a minority shareholding in a rival financial institution.
A person who has not completed a CBN-approved leadership training programme.
questionBank.ans: A person convicted for dishonesty or serious misconduct in relation to his duties.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 47(2)(a): bars a person 'who is of unsound mind, bankrupt, convict for dishonesty or serious misconduct in relation to his duties.' A, C, and D are not stated disqualifications.

questionBank.q: Under Section 47(2)(f) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, a professionally qualified person is also barred from serving as a bank director where he is disqualified or suspended from practicing his profession by whom?
opts: A resolution of the professional body's annual general meeting only.
The order of any competent authority made in respect of him personally.
A newspaper publication naming him in connection with professional misconduct.
An internal disciplinary panel of the bank employing him at the time.
questionBank.ans: The order of any competent authority made in respect of him personally.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 47(2)(f): applies where a professionally qualified person 'is disqualified or suspended...from practicing his profession in Nigeria by the order of any competent authority made in respect of him personally.' A, C, and D misstate this source.

questionBank.q: What is the primary purpose of the Failed Banks (Recovery of Debts) and Financial Malpractices in Banks Act, 2004, as stated in the manual?
opts: To provide for the voluntary winding-up of solvent banks seeking to exit the market.
To provide for recovery of debts owed to failed banks and punishment of financial malpractices.
To provide for the licensing of new commercial banks entering the Nigerian market.
To provide a compensation scheme for depositors of banks that have since been fully recapitalized.
questionBank.ans: To provide for recovery of debts owed to failed banks and punishment of financial malpractices.
questionBank.exp: Manual: this Act is 'generally an Act to provide for recovery of debts owed to failed banks and punishment of persons found guilty of financial malpractices in Banks and Other Financial Institutions.' A, C, and D misstate this purpose.

questionBank.q: Under Section 12 of the Failed Banks Act as cited in the manual, if the debtor on an irrecoverable loan is found to be non-existent, fake, fictitious or otherwise unidentifiable, whom does the court hold liable for the outstanding loan and interest?
opts: The CBN Governor personally, for having licensed the failed bank.
The directors, shareholders, partners, managers, officers and other employees connected with granting the loan.
The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation, as insurer of the failed bank's deposits.
The failed bank's external auditors, regardless of any connection to the loan's approval.
questionBank.ans: The directors, shareholders, partners, managers, officers and other employees connected with granting the loan.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 12: in such circumstances, 'the Court shall hold liable, for the outstanding loan and interest thereon, the directors, shareholders, partners...managers officers and other employees of the failed bank who...were found to have been connected in any way with the granting of the loan.' A, C, and D misapply liability to the wrong parties.

questionBank.q: Under Section 12(2) of the Failed Banks Act as cited in the manual, what exception may relieve an officer of the liability described in Section 12(1)?
opts: Where the officer resigned from the bank before the loan became irrecoverable.
Where the court is satisfied that the debt was incurred without the consent of such officer.
Where the officer's total remuneration from the bank was below a prescribed statutory threshold.
Where the officer can show that a more senior colleague also approved the same loan.
questionBank.ans: Where the court is satisfied that the debt was incurred without the consent of such officer.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 12(2): liability applies '...unless the Court is satisfied that the debt was incurred without the consent of such officer.' A, C, and D are not the stated exception.

questionBank.q: Under Section 13 of the Failed Banks Act as cited in the manual, what does the Act say about the application of the Laws of Limitation to the liability provisions in Section 12?
opts: They apply in full, barring claims after six years.
They shall not apply to those provisions.
They apply only where the officer has died or is insolvent.
They apply only to claims against external auditors.
questionBank.ans: They shall not apply to those provisions.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 13: 'Laws of Limitations shall not apply to the provisions above.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Under Section 15(1) of the Failed Banks Act as cited in the manual, which of the following is listed as conduct that makes a director, manager, officer or employee of a bank guilty of an offence?
opts: Granting a loan strictly in accordance with the bank's own credit policy.
Granting a loan without perfecting, through his negligence, a security or collateral obtained.
Granting a loan to a customer who has since fully repaid the facility ahead of schedule.
Granting a loan after obtaining two independent credit bureau reports on the borrower.
questionBank.ans: Granting a loan without perfecting, through his negligence, a security or collateral obtained.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 15(1)(a)(iii) lists conduct including granting a facility 'without perfecting through his negligence or otherwise a security or collateral obtained.' A, C, and D describe compliant conduct, not an offence.

questionBank.q: Under Section 16 of the Failed Banks Act as cited in the manual, what penalty applies to a person found guilty of an offence under Section 15, and is a fine available as an alternative?
