opts: A fine only, with imprisonment reserved for repeat offenders.
Imprisonment, without an option of fine.
Imprisonment, with an option of fine at the convicted person's election.
A formal reprimand only, recorded in the CBN's CRMS.
questionBank.ans: Imprisonment, without an option of fine.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 16: an offender under Section 15 'is guilty of an offence under the Act and liable to imprisonment without an option of fine.' A, C, and D misstate this penalty.

questionBank.q: Under the Failed Banks Act as cited in the manual, does an officer's explanation that he was merely obeying the instruction of a superior officer necessarily terminate his personal liability for an irregular loan?
opts: Yes, such an explanation always fully terminates personal liability.
No, liability is personal and such an explanation will not necessarily terminate it.
Yes, but only where the superior officer who gave the instruction has since left the bank.
No, but only where the value of the facility granted exceeded N5,000,000.
questionBank.ans: No, liability is personal and such an explanation will not necessarily terminate it.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Note that liability is personal and an explanation that the officer was obeying the instruction of a superior officer will not necessarily terminate personal liability.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: Under the Failed Banks Act as cited in the manual, does the value of the facility granted by an officer affect whether Section 15 liability applies to him?
opts: Yes, liability applies only where the facility granted exceeded N1,000,000.
No, the value of the facility granted is immaterial.
Yes, liability applies only where the facility exceeded 20% of the bank's shareholders' fund.
No, but only where the facility was granted to a director rather than an ordinary customer.
questionBank.ans: No, the value of the facility granted is immaterial.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The value of the facility granted by such officer is also immaterial.' A, C, and D invent thresholds not stated in this section.

questionBank.q: Under Section 7(1)(b) of the EFCC Act as cited in the manual, the Commission has power to investigate the properties of a person under what circumstance?
opts: Where he has been resident outside Nigeria for more than six consecutive months.
Where his lifestyle and extent of properties are not justified by his source of income.
Where he has changed his primary bank account more than twice within a single year.
Where he holds a significant shareholding, as defined by the Prudential Guidelines, in a bank.
questionBank.ans: Where his lifestyle and extent of properties are not justified by his source of income.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 7(1)(b): the Commission may investigate 'the properties of any person if it appears to the Commission that the person's life style and extent of the properties are not justified by his source of income.' A, C, and D are not the stated trigger.

questionBank.q: Under Section 7(2) of the EFCC Act as cited in the manual, the Commission is the coordinating agency for enforcement of several laws. Which of the following is one of them?
opts: The Land Use Act, 1978.
The Advance Fee Fraud and Other Related Offences Act, 1995.
The Companies and Allied Matters Act, 2019.
The Bills of Exchange Act.
questionBank.ans: The Advance Fee Fraud and Other Related Offences Act, 1995.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 7(2) lists 'the Advance Fee Fraud and Other Related Offences Act 1995' among the laws the Commission coordinates enforcement of, alongside the Money Laundering Act, the Failed Banks Act, and BOFIA. A, C, and D are not among the listed laws.

questionBank.q: Under 3.2(a) of the Prudential Guidelines as cited in the manual, what percentage of a bank's shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses may total outstanding exposure to a single obligor or group of related borrowers not exceed?
questionBank.exp: Manual, 3.2(a): 'The total outstanding exposure by a bank to any single person or a group of related borrowers shall not at any point in time exceed 20% of the bank's shareholders fund unimpaired by losses.' A, C, and D misstate this figure.

questionBank.q: Under 3.2(c) of the Prudential Guidelines as cited in the manual, total outstanding exposure by a bank to all tiers of government and their agencies shall not exceed what percentage of the bank's total credit portfolio?
questionBank.exp: Manual, 3.2(c): 'The total outstanding exposure...by a bank to all tiers of government and their agencies shall not at any point in time exceed 10% of the total credit portfolio.' A, C, and D misstate this figure.

questionBank.q: Under 3.4(a) of the Prudential Guidelines as cited in the manual, a significant shareholding is defined as a holding of at least what percentage of a bank's equity, individually or in aggregate?
questionBank.exp: Manual, 3.4(a): 'A significant shareholding is defined as a holding of at least 5% (individually or in aggregate) of a bank's equity.' A, C, and D misstate this figure.

questionBank.q: Under the Land Use Act as cited in the manual, all land within a state (except land vested in the Federal Government or its agencies) is vested in whom, to be held in trust for the people?
opts: The Local Government Chairman of the area.
The Governor of the state.
The Minister of Lands, Housing and Urban Development.
The Corporate Affairs Commission, as land custodian.
questionBank.ans: The Governor of the state.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the Act's essence is 'to vest all land comprised in the territory of each state...solely in the governor of the state, who would hold such land in trust for the people.' A, C, and D misstate this vesting.

questionBank.q: The manual divides security broadly into two classes based on tangibility. Which class includes Guarantee and Indemnity as intangible examples?
opts: Real security, since they provide direct rights over assets.
Personal security, since they are intangible and depend on a person's promise.
Registered security, since they must be registered at the CAC.
Perfected security, since they require full documentation to be valid.
questionBank.ans: Personal security, since they are intangible and depend on a person's promise.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Security may be Personal (Intangible such as Guarantee or Indemnity) or Real (Tangible) and this determines the mode of realization.' A, C, and D are not the classification used for this example.

questionBank.q: Among the further divisions of Real Security the manual lists, which category involves the bank obtaining ownership rights over a tangible asset without taking possession of it?
opts: Charges & Non-possessory liens, giving neither ownership nor possession.
Mortgage Securities, giving ownership rights without possession.
Pledges or Possessory liens, giving possession without ownership.
Negative pledges, giving only a contractual promise not to grant security.
questionBank.ans: Mortgage Securities, giving ownership rights without possession.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Mortgage Securities whereby the bank obtains ownership rights over tangible security assets without possession.' A, C, and D are other real classifications or documents, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the further divisions of Real Security the manual lists, which category involves the bank taking physical possession of the asset without acquiring ownership over it?
opts: Mortgage Securities, giving ownership without possession.
Pledges or Possessory liens, taking possession without ownership.
Charges & Non-possessory liens, giving neither ownership nor possession.
Fixed debentures, giving a specific charge over a specified asset.
questionBank.ans: Pledges or Possessory liens, taking possession without ownership.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Pledges or Possessory liens whereby the bank takes physical possession of the security asset without ownership.' A, C, and D are other real classifications, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the further divisions of Real Security the manual lists, which category gives the bank neither ownership nor possession rights over the asset?
opts: Mortgage Securities, giving ownership without possession.
Charges & Non-possessory liens, giving neither ownership nor possession.
Pledges or Possessory liens, taking possession without ownership.
Floating debentures, hovering over assets until crystallization.
questionBank.ans: Charges & Non-possessory liens, giving neither ownership nor possession.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Charges & Non-possessory liens whereby the bank neither obtains ownership or possession rights over the asset.' A, C, and D are other real classifications, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: According to the manual, what is the essential difference in the rights a lender obtains from taking real security compared to personal security?
opts: Real security gives only a right to sue on default, while personal security gives direct rights.
Real security gives direct rights over the pledged asset, while personal security only gives a right to sue.
Both give identical direct rights over the underlying asset, differing only in documentation.
Neither gives any enforceable right until a court has entered judgment against the debtor.
questionBank.ans: Real security gives direct rights over the pledged asset, while personal security only gives a right to sue.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'taking real security gives the lender direct rights over the pledged asset while personal security only gives the lender a right to sue for the default on a Guarantee or Suretyship.' A, C, and D misstate this distinction.

questionBank.q: A Legal Mortgage is created by what specific transaction, according to the manual, subject to re-conveyance once the debt is repaid?
opts: A mere deposit of the original title document with the bank.
A complete transfer of an interest in land to the bank.
A registration of a caveat against the title at the Lands Registry.
A notarized letter confirming the customer's intent to offer land as security.
questionBank.ans: A complete transfer of an interest in land to the bank.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A legal mortgage is created by a complete transfer of an interest in land to the bank on the condition that it will be re-conveyed to the mortgagor when the debt owed is fully repaid.' A, C, and D misstate this creation method.

questionBank.q: An Equitable Mortgage is created, according to the manual, through what kind of step, without much formality?
opts: A complete transfer of the entire legal interest in the land to the bank.
Any step demonstrating both parties' intention to appropriate the land as security for the loan.
A formal deed executed before a High Court judge and registered the same day.
A resolution of the Corporate Affairs Commission approving the arrangement.
questionBank.ans: Any step demonstrating both parties' intention to appropriate the land as security for the loan.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'An equitable mortgage is created without much formality through any step which in concrete terms demonstrates the intention of both the bank and the customer to appropriate the land as security for the loan.' A, C, and D misstate this creation method.

questionBank.q: Which of the following does the manual give as an example of how an equitable mortgage may be created?
opts: Registration of a statutory right of occupancy at the Corporate Affairs Commission.
Deposit of the original title document with the bank, with or without a Memorandum of Deposit.
Execution of a Deed of Guarantee & Indemnity over the land in question.
Issuance of a Certificate of Occupancy directly in the bank's own name.
questionBank.ans: Deposit of the original title document with the bank, with or without a Memorandum of Deposit.
questionBank.exp: Manual gives as an example: 'Deposit of the original title document to the bank with or without a Memorandum of Deposit, provided it is clear that the deposit is made as security for the loan.' A, C, and D are not the stated example.

questionBank.q: What key practical advantage does a legal mortgage give the bank over an equitable mortgage, according to the manual?
opts: A legal mortgage gives the bank a right against the property itself, allowing sale without suing or a court order.
A legal mortgage merely gives the bank a right to sue the mortgagor, identical to an equitable mortgage.
A legal mortgage requires the bank to obtain a court order before it may even register its interest.
A legal mortgage gives the bank no priority whatsoever over any subsequently created equitable mortgage.
questionBank.ans: A legal mortgage gives the bank a right against the property itself, allowing sale without suing or a court order.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A legal mortgage gives the bank a right against the property itself, thus the bank can sell the property without having to sue or obtain a court Order. On the other hand, an equitable mortgage only gives the bank a right to sue the mortgagor.' B, C, and D misstate this distinction.

questionBank.q: What does the manual say happens to an existing equitable mortgage's priority if a legal mortgage over the same property is subsequently created?
opts: The existing equitable mortgage always retains priority over any later legal mortgage.
The existing equitable mortgage can be overtaken by the subsequently created legal mortgage.
Both mortgages automatically rank equally, sharing any recovery in proportion to their value.
The subsequently created legal mortgage is void for conflicting with the existing equitable mortgage.
questionBank.ans: The existing equitable mortgage can be overtaken by the subsequently created legal mortgage.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A legal mortgage takes priority over any other interest but an existing equitable mortgage can be overtaken by a subsequently created legal mortgage.' A, C, and D misstate this priority rule.

questionBank.q: A Debenture, as described in the manual, is a document issued by what kind of entity, acknowledging its indebtedness?
opts: A sole proprietor under a registered trade name.
An incorporated company.
An unincorporated association with a Board of Trustees.
A partnership registered as a Limited Liability Partnership.
questionBank.ans: An incorporated company.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'This is a document issued by an incorporated company acknowledging its indebtedness and usually it constitutes a charge over the assets of the debtor company.' A, C, and D are other customer types, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Which type of debenture does the manual describe as a specific charge over a specified company asset?
opts: A Floating Debenture, which hovers over floating assets.
A Fixed Debenture, which gives a specific charge over a specified asset.
A Mortgage Debenture, which includes a company's land.
An equitable debenture, which is created without formality.
questionBank.ans: A Fixed Debenture, which gives a specific charge over a specified asset.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Fixed Debenture – a specific charge over a specified company asset.' A, C, and D are other real or invented terms, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Which type of debenture does the manual describe as hovering over a company's floating assets, only affixing to existing products at the point of default?
opts: A Fixed Debenture, giving a specific charge over a specified asset.
A Floating Debenture, hovering over assets until crystallization.
A Mortgage Debenture, including a company's land.
An equitable debenture, created without much formality.
questionBank.ans: A Floating Debenture, hovering over assets until crystallization.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Floating Debenture - does not affix to any specific asset but hovers over the company's floating assets...The charge affixes unto the existing products only at the point of default.' A, C, and D are other real or invented terms, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Where a debenture's assets covered include a company's land, what does the manual say this specific arrangement is described as?
opts: A Fixed Debenture, since land is a specified asset.
A Mortgage Debenture, where assets include a company's land.
A Floating Debenture, since land is a floating asset.
A Legal Mortgage, since it transfers ownership of land.
questionBank.ans: A Mortgage Debenture, where assets include a company's land.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Where the assets covered by a debenture includes a company's land, it is described as a Mortgage Debenture.' A, C, and D are other real terms, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: What is the key distinction the manual draws between a mortgage and a mere charge, in terms of ownership of the secured property?
opts: A mortgage gives only limited rights over the property, while a charge transfers full ownership.
A mortgage transfers ownership subject to redemption, while a charge gives only limited rights.
Both a mortgage and a charge transfer full, unconditional ownership of the property to the lender.
Neither a mortgage nor a charge affects ownership; both merely register an interest for priority.
questionBank.ans: A mortgage transfers ownership subject to redemption, while a charge gives only limited rights.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'While a mortgage transfers ownership of the property to a lender subject to a right of redemption, a charge only gives the chargee (lender) limited rights over the property.' A, C, and D misstate this distinction.

questionBank.q: According to the manual's definition, a bank's right of set-off allows it to seize a borrower's account balance in the same bank to apply toward the borrower's loan in arrears, with what specific exception?
opts: Except a foreign currency account, always excluded by law.
Except a sub-account balance.
Except a trust account in the borrower's own right.
Except a joint account, always excluded regardless of mandate.
questionBank.ans: Except a sub-account balance.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Right of Set-off is a bank's legal right to seize a borrower's any account balance (except a sub-account balance) in the same bank to apply it toward the borrower's any loan in arrears, or in anticipation of a default.' A, C, and D are not the stated exception.

questionBank.q: Unlike a right of set-off, how does the manual describe a 'lien'?
opts: A right to seize any account balance across all of a debtor's accounts.
A right of retention, exercised by a creditor in possession of a debtor's property.
A right to compel a third party to forward contract proceeds directly to the creditor.
A right to have a court formally divest a debtor of his equity of redemption.
questionBank.ans: A right of retention, exercised by a creditor in possession of a debtor's property.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Unlike a right of set-off, a 'lien' is a right of retention. It is exercised by the creditor in possession of a debtor's property when he retains the property and makes its release conditional on receiving payment of the debt.' A, C, and D misapply other concepts.

questionBank.q: Under what specific circumstance does the manual say a lien can be exercised over a debtor's property?
opts: At any time, regardless of how the property came into the creditor's possession.
Only if the property falls into the creditor's hands in the normal course of business.
Only after the creditor has obtained a court order authorizing its exercise.
Only where the debtor has given prior written notice consenting to the lien.
questionBank.ans: Only if the property falls into the creditor's hands in the normal course of business.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a lien 'can only be exercised if the property of the debtor falls into the creditor's hands in the normal course of business.' A, C, and D misstate this condition.

questionBank.q: If a creditor exercises his right of sale under a lien, what must he do with any surplus remaining after deducting his debt from the sale proceeds?
opts: Retain it as a charge for exercising the lien.
Refund it to the debtor.
Remit it to the Central Bank as an unclaimed balance.
Apply it to any other unrelated debt owed by the debtor.
questionBank.ans: Refund it to the debtor.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'If the creditor exercises his right of sale, then he must obtain fair market price and refund any surplus to the debtor after deducting his debt.' A, C, and D misstate this obligation.

questionBank.q: Does the manual require a bank to give the customer prior notice before exercising the right of set-off or lien?
opts: Yes, prior notice of at least 30 days is required in every case.
No, prior notice is not necessary, though its exercise may be excluded by contract.
Yes, but only where the customer's account has been dormant for more than one year.
No, and its exercise can never be excluded or restricted by any contract term.
questionBank.ans: No, prior notice is not necessary, though its exercise may be excluded by contract.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Prior notice to the customer is not necessary for the exercise of the right but its exercise may be excluded by contract.' A, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: According to the manual, can the right of set-off be exercised across a customer's accounts that are held in different rights, such as a trust account the banker is aware of?
opts: No, the right cannot be exercised where accounts are held in different rights.
Yes, the right may always be exercised regardless of the rights in which accounts are held.
Yes, but only where the trust account in question has a credit balance exceeding the debt.
No, but only where the banker was unaware that one account was a trust account.
questionBank.ans: No, the right cannot be exercised where accounts are held in different rights.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The right cannot be exercised if accounts are held in different rights e.g. a trust account of which a banker is aware.' B, C, and D misstate this rule.

questionBank.q: What does the manual say about whether accounts maintained in foreign currency may be combined for the purposes of set-off, and what does it recommend to the bank as a result?
opts: It has been conclusively determined that such accounts may always be combined.
It has not been judicially determined, so the bank should obtain a contract reserving that right.
It has been conclusively determined that such accounts may never be combined.
It is governed exclusively by CBN foreign exchange regulations, with no room for contractual variation.
questionBank.ans: It has not been judicially determined, so the bank should obtain a contract reserving that right.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'it has not been judicially determined whether accounts maintained in foreign currency may be combined so it is safer for the bank to obtain a contract reserving such right.' A, C, and D misstate this position.

questionBank.q: A Guarantee, as described in the manual, is an indirect personal security given by an individual promising to be liable for what, and under what condition?
opts: Any loss the bank suffers, howsoever arising, regardless of any default.
The debt of another person (the principal debtor), if that other person defaults.
The full value of a mortgaged property, if the mortgagor fails to maintain adequate insurance.
The debts of the bank itself, if the bank becomes insolvent before the facility is repaid.
questionBank.ans: The debt of another person (the principal debtor), if that other person defaults.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a Guarantee is 'an indirect personal security given by an individual (Guarantor) promising to be liable for the debt of another person (principal debtor), if that other person defaults.' A, C, and D misstate this arrangement or describe an indemnity instead.

questionBank.q: According to the manual, how may a Guarantee be expressed by the parties, beyond being payable strictly on demand?
opts: Subject to ratification by the principal debtor after he attains full capacity.
Subject to a pre-agreed condition, as a conditional guarantee.
Subject to registration at the Corporate Affairs Commission within 90 days.
Subject only to the guarantor's own discretion as to when, if ever, to pay.
questionBank.ans: Subject to a pre-agreed condition, as a conditional guarantee.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A Guarantee may be expressed by the parties as payable on demand (demand guarantee) or subject to a pre-agreed condition (conditional guarantee).' A, C, and D are not stated alternatives.

questionBank.q: According to the manual, what does the value of a guarantee or indemnity chiefly depend on?
opts: The market value of the principal debtor's own assets, regardless of the guarantor's means.
The guarantor's ability and willingness to pay, so his integrity and net worth are key considerations.
The length of the guarantor's prior banking relationship with the lending institution.
Whether the guarantor is a natural person rather than an incorporated company.
questionBank.ans: The guarantor's ability and willingness to pay, so his integrity and net worth are key considerations.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The value of a guarantee or indemnity depends on the guarantor's ability and willingness to pay, so his integrity and net worth are key considerations.' A, C, and D are not the stated basis.

questionBank.q: An Indemnity, as described in the manual, is a personal security whereby a person undertakes what kind of liability for another's obligation?
opts: A secondary liability that only crystallizes upon the other person's default.
A direct personal liability for an obligation of another which results in a loss.
A liability limited strictly to the value of any real property the indemnifier owns.
A liability that automatically transfers to the indemnifier's estate only upon his death.
questionBank.ans: A direct personal liability for an obligation of another which results in a loss.
questionBank.exp: Manual: an Indemnity is 'a personal security whereby a person undertakes a Direct personal liability for an obligation of another which results in a loss.' A, C, and D misstate this arrangement or describe a guarantee instead.

questionBank.q: A 'Counter-Indemnity', as described in the manual, allows an indemnifier to do what, once he has paid part of a claim he guaranteed?
opts: Automatically transfer his remaining liability to a co-indemnifier without consent.
Seek reimbursement from the primary obligor upon that obligor's default.
Rescind the original indemnity retroactively, as if it had never been given.
Recover the full amount paid directly from the bank that received the claim.
questionBank.ans: Seek reimbursement from the primary obligor upon that obligor's default.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A 'Counter-Indemnity' allows an indemnifier to seek reimbursement from the primary obligor in the event that he has to pay any part of a claim he guaranteed in a primary contract upon the default of that primary obligor.' A, C, and D misstate this arrangement.

questionBank.q: According to the manual, what is the essential wording-based difference between a Guarantee and an Indemnity in terms of what triggers liability?
opts: A guarantee is triggered by any loss howsoever arising; an indemnity is triggered by default.
A guarantee is triggered by the principal debtor's default; an indemnity is triggered by a loss howsoever arising.
Both are triggered identically by the principal debtor's default, differing only in remedy.
Neither is triggered by default or loss; both require an independent court finding of liability first.
questionBank.ans: A guarantee is triggered by the principal debtor's default; an indemnity is triggered by a loss howsoever arising.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'While liability under a guarantee is triggered by the default of the principal debtor, an indemnity is triggered by a loss howsoever arising on the part of the creditor.' A, C, and D misstate this distinction.

questionBank.q: Lending against a portfolio of shares as security is described in the manual by what other term?
opts: Domiciliation of receivables, where contract proceeds are forwarded to the lender.
Margin lending, lending against a portfolio of shares as security.
Negative pledge lending, where the borrower promises not to grant security.
Debenture lending, where a company issues a charge over its assets.
questionBank.ans: Margin lending, lending against a portfolio of shares as security.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Another term for this is margin lending i.e lending against a portfolio of shares as security.' A, C, and D are other real terms from elsewhere, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Before lending against shares as security, what must the bank first confirm, according to the manual, beyond simply verifying the signature of the owner?
opts: That the shares trade only on the Nigerian Exchange.
Ownership of the shares.
That the borrower has no facility with any other bank.
That the shares were acquired over twelve months ago.
questionBank.ans: Ownership of the shares.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The Bank would firstly confirm ownership of shares and verify the signature of the owner on the share certificates or documents.' A, C, and D are not stated requirements.

questionBank.q: Where shares taken as security are listed on the CSCS, what does the manual say happens to those shares at the instance of the parties?
opts: The shares are automatically transferred into the bank's own trading account.
A lien is placed on the shares by the CSCS.
The shares are delisted from the CSCS for the duration of the facility.
A floating debenture is automatically created over the shares.
questionBank.ans: A lien is placed on the shares by the CSCS.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Where shares are listed on CSCS, a lien is placed on the shares by the CSCS at the instance of the parties.' A, C, and D are not stated consequences.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed in the manual as an advantage of using shares as security?
opts: Their value never fluctuates once pledged to the bank.
Value is readily ascertainable.
Banks may lend on their own shares without prior approval.
There is no cap on shareholder numbers, regardless of company type.
questionBank.ans: Value is readily ascertainable.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists among the advantages: 'Value is readily ascertainable.' A, C, and D misstate the manual's own listed disadvantages of shares as security.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed in the manual as a disadvantage of using shares as security?
opts: Fluctuating value.
Their value is fixed permanently once pledged.
Realization on default is always simplified regardless of company type.
There is no restriction on transferring private company shares.
questionBank.ans: Fluctuating value.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists among the disadvantages: 'Fluctuating value.' B, C, and D misstate the manual's own listed advantages of shares as security.

questionBank.q: Under BOFIA, what restriction does the manual note applies specifically to a bank lending on the security of its own shares?
opts: Banks may freely lend on the security of their own shares without any restriction.
Banks cannot lend on the security of their own shares without CBN's prior approval.
Banks may lend on the security of their own shares only to existing shareholders.
Banks may lend on the security of their own shares only up to N100,000 per borrower.
questionBank.ans: Banks cannot lend on the security of their own shares without CBN's prior approval.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists among the disadvantages of shares as security: 'Restriction in BOFIA that banks cannot lend on the security of their own shares without CBN's prior approval.' A, C, and D misstate this restriction.

questionBank.q: An Equipment Lease, as described in the manual, is a contract between a lessor and lessee for the hire of a specific asset required by the lessee but financed by whom?
opts: The lessee's own holding company, as lease guarantor.
The bank.
A third-party insurer, acting as underwriter of the lease.
The CAC, as statutory financier of last resort.
questionBank.ans: The bank.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'An equipment lease is a contract between a lessor (bank) and lessee for the hire of a specific asset required by the lessee (Borrower) but financed by the bank.' A, C, and D are not the stated financier.

questionBank.q: In an Operating Lease, as described in the manual, who bears the economic risks such as maintenance and insurance of the leased asset?
opts: The lessee, since the asset's cost fully amortizes in the term.
The lessor.
A third-party insurer, jointly nominated by both parties.
Neither party; the manufacturer bears such risk under warranty.
questionBank.ans: The lessor.
questionBank.exp: Manual: in an Operating Lease, 'the lessor bears all the economic risks such as maintenance and insurance,' and the cost of the asset 'is not fully amortized during the period of such lease.' A, C, and D misstate this allocation of risk.

questionBank.q: In a Finance Lease, as described in the manual, who assumes all economic risks of ownership of the leased asset?
opts: The lessor, since the lessee's payments cannot amortize the outlay.
The lessee (Borrower).
A third-party insurer jointly nominated by lessor and lessee.
Neither party, since ownership never transfers under this lease.
questionBank.ans: The lessee (Borrower).
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The lessee (Borrower) in a Finance lease assumes all economic risks of ownership.' A, C, and D misstate this allocation of risk.

questionBank.q: Because the bank retains ownership of a leased asset as security until full repayment, whereupon ownership transfers to the lessee, what does the manual say this arrangement has the same structure as?
opts: A Deed of Guarantee & Indemnity.
A Hire Purchase contract.
A Negative Pledge clause.
A Letter of Comfort.
questionBank.ans: A Hire Purchase contract.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The bank retains ownership of the asset as its security until full repayment whereupon it transfers ownership to the lessee. Consequently, the arrangement has the same structure as a Hire Purchase contract.' A, C, and D are unrelated documents, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A Letter of Comfort, also known as a Letter of Intent, is described in the manual as an assurance about a debt that falls short of what?
opts: A Simple Contract, since a Letter of Comfort is itself Formal.
A legal guarantee.
An indemnity, since it creates only primary liability.
A negative pledge, since it restricts further borrowing.
questionBank.ans: A legal guarantee.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A letter of comfort is an assurance about a debt, short of a legal guarantee, given to a bank by a third party.' A, C, and D misstate or misapply this description.

questionBank.q: Where a holding company issues a Letter of Comfort in favour of its subsidiary, and the subsidiary later defaults, what does the manual say about the lender's remedy?
opts: The lender may sue the parent company directly and successfully enforce the Letter of Comfort as a guarantee.
The parent company cannot be sued successfully; the remedy lies in a suit against the borrowing subsidiary.
The lender has no remedy at all, since a Letter of Comfort extinguishes the underlying debt.
The lender must sue both the parent and subsidiary jointly, or the suit will fail entirely.
questionBank.ans: The parent company cannot be sued successfully; the remedy lies in a suit against the borrowing subsidiary.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'When issued by a holding company in favour of its subsidiary, the parent company cannot be sued successfully by a lender upon default. The remedy lies in a suit against the borrowing subsidiary.' A, C, and D misstate this position.

questionBank.q: Hypothecation, in the general sense described in the manual, is simply a charge on specific goods, usually arising in what kind of situation?
opts: Where the goods' acquisition is funded by a lender.
Where the goods have already been sold to a third party by the debtor.
Where the goods are held in a bonded warehouse pending customs clearance.
Where the goods form part of a company's floating assets under a debenture.
questionBank.ans: Where the goods' acquisition is funded by a lender.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'This is simply a charge on specific goods (usually when their acquisition is funded by a lender).' B, C, and D are not the stated situation.

questionBank.q: Which species of hypothecation does the manual describe as being contracted when the debtor delivers the goods to the creditor, subject to redelivery upon repayment?
opts: Hypothecation (properly so called), contracted without delivery.
Pledge, contracted with delivery to the creditor.
A floating charge, affixing to assets at the point of default.
A negative pledge, giving only a contractual promise not to grant security.
questionBank.ans: Pledge, contracted with delivery to the creditor.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Pledge is that species of hypothecation which is contracted when the debtor delivers to the creditor, the things (goods) hypothecated subject to redelivery upon repayment of a loan.' A, C, and D are other real or invented terms, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: According to the manual, what is the obvious distinction between a Pledge and Hypothecation (properly so called)?
opts: Whether the goods are movable or immovable in nature.
Who has physical control of the goods.
Whether the lender is a bank or a non-bank financial institution.
Whether the underlying facility exceeds N1,000,000 in value.
questionBank.ans: Who has physical control of the goods.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The obvious distinction here is about who has physical control of the goods.' A, C, and D are not the stated distinction.

questionBank.q: A Bond, as described in the manual, is basically an undertaking to answer for an obligation arising out of what?
opts: The bank's own failure to disburse an approved credit facility on time.
The default of another in a contractual relationship.
A shortfall in the value of a mortgaged asset compared to the facility granted.
The insolvency of the bond issuer's own holding company.
questionBank.ans: The default of another in a contractual relationship.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A Bond is basically an undertaking to answer for an obligation arising out of the default of another in a contractual relationship. It is therefore a kind of Guarantee.' A, C, and D misstate this description.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is given in the manual as an example of the different forms a Bond may come in?
opts: Performance Bond.
Floating Bond.
Domiciliation Bond.
Negative Pledge Bond.
questionBank.ans: Performance Bond.
questionBank.exp: Manual: bonds 'come in different forms including Advance Payment Bond, Tender or Bid Bond, Performance Bond etc.' B, C, and D are not real forms listed in the material.

questionBank.q: When issuing a bond, what does the manual say it is in the bank's interest to ensure regarding the extent of its own obligation?
opts: That its obligation extends automatically to cover any future contracts the beneficiary may enter.
That the basis of its obligation is clearly stipulated and limited to a specific sum.
That its obligation is left open-ended, to preserve maximum flexibility for the bond holder.
That its obligation is contingent solely on the bond holder's own creditworthiness.
questionBank.ans: That the basis of its obligation is clearly stipulated and limited to a specific sum.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'It is in the bank's interest to ensure that the basis of its obligation under the bond is clearly stipulated and its obligation limited to a specific sum.' A, C, and D misstate this interest.

questionBank.q: An Endowment insurance policy, as described in the manual, provides for the sum assured to be payable at what point?
opts: Only at death, whenever it occurs, with no earlier payment possible.
At an agreed date or at death, whichever comes earlier.
Only once the assured reaches the statutory retirement age of 65.
Only upon the surrender of the policy by the assured during his lifetime.
questionBank.ans: At an agreed date or at death, whichever comes earlier.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'An endowment policy usually provides for the sum assured to be payable at an agreed date or at death whichever comes earlier.' A, C, and D misstate this feature.

questionBank.q: A Whole Life insurance policy, as described in the manual, provides for the sum assured to be payable when?
opts: At an agreed date during the assured's lifetime, or at death, whichever comes earlier.
On the death of the assured, whenever it occurs.
Only once the policy has been in force for a minimum of ten years.
Only if the assured survives to the end of the policy's stated term.
questionBank.ans: On the death of the assured, whenever it occurs.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A whole life policy provides for the sum assured to be payable on the death of the assured whenever it occurs.' A, C, and D misstate this feature, with A instead describing an endowment policy.

questionBank.q: What term does the manual use for the current value an assurance policy must have to be acceptable as security?
opts: Surrender value.
Facility value.
Ascertainable value.
Ad valorem value.
questionBank.ans: Surrender value.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Assurance policies must have a current value to be acceptable as security. That present value is known as the 'surrender value'.' B, C, and D are not the term used in the material.

questionBank.q: Under which of the following circumstances does the manual say a life policy taken as security may become unrealizable?
opts: Where the policyholder changes his bank between taking out the policy and its maturity.
Where the assured commits suicide or made a false declaration in his proposal form.
Where the premiums paid exceed the policy's stated surrender value at any point.
Where the policy has been in force for longer than ten consecutive years.
questionBank.ans: Where the assured commits suicide or made a false declaration in his proposal form.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'a policy may be unrealizable if assured commits suicide or has made a false declaration in his proposal form.' A, C, and D are not stated grounds.

questionBank.q: Beyond the insurance company being viable and the policy still being in force and assignable, what must the bank ensure is noted on an insurance policy taken as security?
opts: That the policyholder's employer has co-signed the policy as a guarantor.
That the bank is noted thereon as loss payee or beneficiary.
That the policy has been independently reappraised within the preceding 90 days.
That the policy expressly excludes any claim arising from suicide, regardless of timing.
questionBank.ans: That the bank is noted thereon as loss payee or beneficiary.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'the bank must be noted thereon as loss payee or beneficiary.' A, C, and D are not stated requirements.

questionBank.q: A negative pledge clause is described in the manual as a negative covenant stating that a corporation will not do what, if doing so would give lenders less security?
opts: Declare any dividend to its shareholders in a given financial year.
Pledge any of its assets.
Increase its authorized share capital beyond the statutory minimum.
Appoint any new director without the existing lender's prior consent.
questionBank.ans: Pledge any of its assets.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A negative pledge clause is a negative covenant in an indenture stating that a corporation will not pledge any of its assets if doing so gives the lenders less security.' A, C, and D are not the stated covenant.

questionBank.q: Because a negative pledge clause is generally not registrable, what practical risk does the manual identify for the unsecured lender relying on it?
opts: The clause automatically expires after 90 days regardless of intent.
The borrower can create such an interest, since a later lender gets no notice even after a title search.
The clause binds only the borrower's real property, not movables.
The clause binds only the original lender, not its successors.
questionBank.ans: The borrower can create such an interest, since a later lender gets no notice even after a title search.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Since this document is generally not registrable, the borrower can, de facto create such an interest because a subsequent lender will not have notice of the interest even if it had conducted a title search.' A, C, and D are not stated consequences.

questionBank.q: If a borrower breaches a negative pledge clause by granting security to another lender, what does the manual say is the only remedy available to the bank protected by that clause?
opts: To immediately seize the asset pledged to the other lender.
To sue.
To petition for winding-up, regardless of solvency.
To convert its facility automatically into a legal mortgage.
questionBank.ans: To sue.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'If this undertaking is breached, the only remedy of the bank is to sue.' A, C, and D are not stated remedies.

questionBank.q: According to the manual, all bank advances fall into which two broad classes?
opts: Secured or unsecured facilities only, with no other classification.
Loans or overdrafts.
Personal or corporate facilities only, with no other classification.
Perfected or unperfected facilities only, with no other classification.
questionBank.ans: Loans or overdrafts.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'All bank advances fall into two broad classes i.e. loans or overdrafts.' A, C, and D are not the classification used in this section.

questionBank.q: What must a bank deliver to a debtor before any form of enforcement of a security may commence, according to the manual?
opts: A winding-up petition, whether the debtor is a company or individual.
A formal demand.
A bankruptcy notice, whether or not any act of bankruptcy occurred.
A Global Standing Instruction petition to the CBN.
questionBank.ans: A formal demand.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'All forms of enforcement may only commence after a formal demand has been delivered to the debtor. This establishes 'default' if the debtor does not pay after the demand.' A, C, and D are separate remedies, not the stated precondition.

questionBank.q: Once a bank has sued a defaulting debtor and obtained judgment, what does the manual say the bank becomes, and what may it then do?
opts: A secured creditor automatically, regardless of whether security was taken.
A judgment creditor, who can enforce judgment by levying execution or obtaining a Garnishee Order.
A preferential creditor automatically, ranking ahead of all other creditors in any insolvency.
A receiver of the debtor's estate, with power to manage the debtor's business directly.
questionBank.ans: A judgment creditor, who can enforce judgment by levying execution or obtaining a Garnishee Order.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'If after suing the debtor, the bank is successful and obtains judgment, it becomes a judgment creditor and can enforce judgment through: 1. Levying execution...or 2. Obtaining a Garnishee Order.' A, C, and D misstate this status.

questionBank.q: Where a bank has perfected its security, what does the manual say is generally the better recovery option, with what further step still available afterward?
opts: Immediately petitioning for the debtor's winding-up, without attempting to sell the asset first.
Selling the pledged asset, and suing for any balance still outstanding thereafter.
Waiting for the debtor's voluntary repayment, without taking any active recovery step.
Reporting the debtor to the CBN's CRMS as the sole recovery step.
questionBank.ans: Selling the pledged asset, and suing for any balance still outstanding thereafter.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Where a bank has perfected its security, selling the asset pledged is a better option and if thereafter there is still an outstanding, it can sue for the balance.' A, C, and D are not the stated approach.

questionBank.q: According to the manual's notes on enforcement, what does the ease of recovering from a loan default directly depend on?
opts: The number of years the customer has maintained an account with the bank.
The legal standing of the bank.
The debtor's personal relationship with the branch manager who approved the facility.
The size of the bank's total loan portfolio relative to its competitors.
questionBank.ans: The legal standing of the bank.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'The chances of recovering from loan default is directly dependent on the legal standing of the bank.' A, C, and D are not the stated factor.

questionBank.q: According to the manual's notes on enforcement, why must securities be perfected in order to ease recovery?
opts: Because perfection automatically extends the limitation period for any recovery action indefinitely.
Because perfection gives the bank direct rights over the security asset.
Because perfection converts a personal security into a real security by operation of law.
Because perfection is a precondition for a bank to obtain a Global Standing Instruction.
questionBank.ans: Because perfection gives the bank direct rights over the security asset.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Securities must be perfected to ease recovery as this gives direct rights over the security asset.' A, C, and D are not the stated reason.

questionBank.q: Among the remedies of a mortgagee or debenture holder the manual lists, which remedy involves the mortgagee using the property for its own benefit, with that use quantified in monetary terms and offset against the debt?
opts: Sale of the security asset, effected by an auctioneer.
Entry into possession, for the mortgagee's own use offset against the debt.
Foreclosure, a court order divesting the mortgagor of its equity of redemption.
Receivership, one of the extreme measures of recovery.
questionBank.ans: Entry into possession, for the mortgagee's own use offset against the debt.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Entry into possession of the property for his own use or use of another at his option. Such use is quantified in monetary terms and offset against the debt.' A, C, and D are other listed remedies, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the remedies of a mortgagee or debenture holder the manual lists, which remedy is usually effected through an auctioneer appointed by the bank?
opts: Entry into possession, for the mortgagee's own use offset against the debt.
Sale of the security asset, usually effected by an auctioneer appointed by the bank.
Foreclosure, a court order divesting the mortgagor of its equity of redemption.
Receivership, one of the extreme measures of recovery.
questionBank.ans: Sale of the security asset, usually effected by an auctioneer appointed by the bank.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Sale of the security asset and application of the proceeds of sale in satisfaction of the debt. The sale is usually effected by an auctioneer appointed by the bank.' A, C, and D are other listed remedies, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the remedies of a mortgagee or debenture holder the manual lists, which remedy is a court order formally divesting the mortgagor of its equity of redemption, entitling the mortgagee to sell?
opts: Entry into possession, for the mortgagee's own use offset against the debt.
Sale of the security asset, usually effected by an auctioneer.
Foreclosure, a court order divesting the mortgagor of its equity of redemption.
Receivership, one of the extreme measures of recovery.
questionBank.ans: Foreclosure, a court order divesting the mortgagor of its equity of redemption.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Foreclosure – an order of the court formally divesting the mortgagor of its equity of redemption thus entitling the mortgagee to sell.' A, B, and D are other listed remedies, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Among the remedies of a mortgagee or debenture holder the manual lists, which remedy does the manual describe as one of the extreme measures of recovery open to a creditor/mortgagee?
opts: Entry into possession, for the mortgagee's own use offset against the debt.
Sale of the security asset, usually effected by an auctioneer.
Foreclosure, a court order divesting the mortgagor of its equity of redemption.
Receivership, one of the extreme measures of recovery.
questionBank.ans: Receivership, one of the extreme measures of recovery.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Receivership – This is one of the extreme measures of recovery which is open to a creditor/mortgagee.' A, B, and C are other listed remedies, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Where a Receiver is appointed by creditors rather than by the Court, within how many days must notice of the appointment be filed with the CAC, according to the manual?
opts: 7 days, the period for a court appointment.
14 days, the period for a creditor appointment.
21 days, the period for neglect under Section 572.
30 days, the period for satisfying a bankruptcy notice.
questionBank.ans: 14 days, the period for a creditor appointment.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Notice of appointment of a Receiver must be advertised in two national newspapers and filed with the CAC within 14 days if appointed by creditors and within 7 days if appointed by Court.' A, C, and D misstate this period.

questionBank.q: Where a Receiver is appointed by the Court rather than by creditors, within how many days must notice of the appointment be filed with the CAC, according to the manual?
opts: 14 days, the period for a creditor appointment.
7 days, the period for a court appointment.
21 days, the period for neglect under Section 572.
30 days, the period for satisfying a bankruptcy notice.
questionBank.ans: 7 days, the period for a court appointment.
questionBank.exp: Manual: notice must be filed with the CAC 'within 14 days if appointed by creditors and within 7 days if appointed by Court.' A, C, and D misstate this period for a court appointment.

questionBank.q: Under Section 572 of CAMA as cited in the manual, above what sum must a creditor's unpaid statutory demand be, for a company's failure to pay within the stated period to support a winding-up petition?
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 572: a company is deemed unable to pay its debts where 'a creditor...to whom the company is indebted in a sum exceeding N200,000, then due, has served on the company...a demand...and the company has for (21 days) three weeks thereafter neglected to pay.' A, C, and D misstate this figure.

questionBank.q: Under Section 572 of CAMA as cited in the manual, for how long must a company neglect to pay, secure, or compound a qualifying statutory demand before it is deemed unable to pay its debts on that ground?
opts: 14 days (two weeks).
21 days (three weeks).
30 days (one month).
7 days (one week).
questionBank.ans: 21 days (three weeks).
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 572(a): the company must have 'for (21 days) three weeks thereafter neglected to pay the sum or to secure or compound for it to the reasonable satisfaction of the creditor.' A, C, and D misstate this period.

questionBank.q: Under Section 572 of CAMA as cited in the manual, besides an unpaid statutory demand, which of the following is also listed as a ground on which a company is deemed unable to pay its debts?
opts: The company's shares have not traded for six months.
Execution on a judgment in the creditor's favour is returned unsatisfied.
The company missed its AGM for two consecutive years.
The auditor resigned without a replacement within 30 days.
questionBank.ans: Execution on a judgment in the creditor's favour is returned unsatisfied.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 572(b): a company is also deemed unable to pay its debts where 'execution or other process issued on a judgment, act or order of any Court in favour of a creditor of the company is returned unsatisfied in whole or in part.' A, C, and D are not stated grounds.

questionBank.q: Once a Petition for winding-up is presented against a company, what does the manual say immediately happens to the company's assets, employees and Board?
opts: The assets are transferred to the petitioning creditor pending the court's final determination.
The assets are frozen, and all employees and the Board of the company stand dismissed.
The employees and Board continue in office, but the assets are frozen pending the hearing.
The assets and employees are unaffected, but the Board is immediately replaced by a court-appointed panel.
questionBank.ans: The assets are frozen, and all employees and the Board of the company stand dismissed.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'As soon as a Petition for winding-up is presented, the company debtor's assets are frozen in place and all employees and the Board of the company stand dismissed.' A, C, and D misstate this consequence.

questionBank.q: In a company winding-up, which category of creditor does the manual say is listed first in priority, ahead of government claims and owed wages?
opts: Government claims, listed second in priority.
Liquidation expenses, listed first in priority.
Owed wages and salaries, listed third in priority.
Ordinary unsecured trade creditors, listed last in priority.
questionBank.ans: Liquidation expenses, listed first in priority.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Priority creditors are listed in the CAMA starting with liquidation expenses, then government, owed wages and salaries follow, then others.' A, C, and D are ranked after liquidation expenses in this priority order.

questionBank.q: Unlike a company, which can be wound up, what does the manual say happens to a natural person who cannot pay his debts?
opts: He can be wound up in exactly the same manner as a company, under CAMA.
He can only be declared bankrupt, not wound-up.
He is placed under a Guardian's administration, identical to a mentally infirm customer.
He is automatically disqualified from banking with any institution for life.
questionBank.ans: He can only be declared bankrupt, not wound-up.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Natural persons can only be declared bankrupt not wound-up.' A, C, and D misstate this distinction.

questionBank.q: Besides being disqualified from holding certain elective and public offices, what does the manual say a bankrupt is barred from doing in relation to companies?
opts: Serving on the Board of any company.
Owning shares in any private company limited by shares.
Opening a savings account with any licensed bank in Nigeria.
Acting as an employee of any company, in any capacity whatsoever.
questionBank.ans: Serving on the Board of any company.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a bankrupt 'also cannot serve on the Board of any company,' though he is not barred from practising a regulated profession 'as an employee.' B, C, and D misstate this bar.

questionBank.q: Under Section 1 of the Bankruptcy Act as cited in the manual, if a creditor has obtained a final judgment and served a bankruptcy notice, within how many days must the debtor comply or satisfy the court of a valid set-off, to avoid committing an act of bankruptcy?
opts: 7 days, the period for a court-appointed receiver.
14 days, the period for compliance with a bankruptcy notice.
21 days, the period for neglect under Section 572.
30 days, the period for satisfying a judgment.
questionBank.ans: 14 days, the period for compliance with a bankruptcy notice.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 1(a)(ii): the debtor commits an act of bankruptcy if he 'does not, within 14 days after service of the notice, comply with the requirements of the notice or satisfy the court that he has a counter-claim, set off or cross demand.' A, C, and D misstate this period.

questionBank.q: Under Section 1 of the Bankruptcy Act as cited in the manual, a debtor also commits an act of bankruptcy if execution has been levied against him and the goods have been sold or held by the bailiff for how long?
opts: 14 days, the period for compliance with a bankruptcy notice.
21 days, the period for goods held by the bailiff.
30 days, the period for satisfying a judgment.
7 days, the period for a court-appointed receiver.
questionBank.ans: 21 days, the period for goods held by the bailiff.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 1(b): an act of bankruptcy occurs 'if execution against him has been levied, and the goods have either been sold or held by the bailiff for 21 days.' A, C, and D misstate this period.

questionBank.q: Under Section 1 of the Bankruptcy Act as cited in the manual, besides a creditor's bankruptcy notice or a levied execution, what other act by the debtor himself constitutes an act of bankruptcy?
opts: Failing to attend a single scheduled meeting with any one of his creditors.
Filing a declaration of his inability to pay his debts, or presenting a bankruptcy petition against himself.
Transferring any asset to a family member, regardless of the asset's value.
Changing his primary bank account without notifying his existing creditors.
questionBank.ans: Filing a declaration of his inability to pay his debts, or presenting a bankruptcy petition against himself.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 1(c): an act of bankruptcy occurs 'if he files in the court a declaration of his inability to pay his debts or presents a bankruptcy petition against himself.' A, C, and D are not the stated act.

questionBank.q: The manual describes 'fraudulent preference' in bankruptcy as the transfer of property by a debtor to his creditors for what purpose?
opts: To repay the creditor with the highest outstanding balance ahead of all other creditors, in good faith.
To conceal assets, destroy, withhold or falsify documents in an effort to defeat bankruptcy proceedings.
To settle a debt that is not yet due, at the creditor's own voluntary request.
To satisfy a court-ordered garnishee order issued against the debtor's account.
questionBank.ans: To conceal assets, destroy, withhold or falsify documents in an effort to defeat bankruptcy proceedings.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Fraudulent preference in bankruptcy can be explained as the transfer of property by a debtor to his creditors in order to conceal assets, destroy, withhold or falsify documents in an effort to defeat bankruptcy proceedings.' A, C, and D misstate this concept.

questionBank.q: Among the bankruptcy procedure stages the manual lists leading up to adjudication, which stage involves the debtor's finances being examined in public?
opts: Preparation of statement of affairs, where the debtor lists his assets.
Public examination of the debtor, where his finances are examined in public.
Meeting of the creditors, where creditors vote on the debtor's proposal.
Receiving order, where the court makes an interim order.
questionBank.ans: Public examination of the debtor, where his finances are examined in public.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists 'Public examination of the debtor' as one of the seven stages of the bankruptcy procedure. A, C, and D are the other listed stages, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Under Section 126 of the Bankruptcy Act as cited in the manual, a bankrupt is disqualified from being elected to which of the following?
opts: The board of trustees of a purely private, unregistered family trust.
Any legislative house of the National or State Assembly.
Membership of any registered trade union, regardless of his profession.
Any position within a company where he is not also a shareholder.
questionBank.ans: Any legislative house of the National or State Assembly.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.126: a bankrupt is disqualified from 'Being elected into any legislative house of the National or State Assembly.' A, C, and D are not among the listed disqualifications.

questionBank.q: Under Section 126 of the Bankruptcy Act as cited in the manual, a bankrupt is disqualified from participating or engaging in any regulated profession, except in what capacity?
opts: As a sole proprietor operating under his own trade name.
As an employee.
As a director of an incorporated company practising that profession.
As a partner in a partnership practising that profession.
questionBank.ans: As an employee.
questionBank.exp: Manual, S.126(v): a bankrupt is disqualified from 'Participating or engaging in any regulated profession except as an employee.' A, C, and D are not the stated exception.

questionBank.q: The Global Standing Instruction (GSI) clause, directed by the CBN in August 2019, requires banks to include a clause in credit offer letters signed by borrowers before disbursement. What does this clause enable banks to do?
opts: Access a defaulter's funds in other banks, through the CBN, to repay debts owed on utilized facilities.
Automatically convert any unsecured facility into a legal mortgage over the borrower's known assets.
Directly debit a defaulter's employer's payroll account without any further authorization.
Report a defaulter to the three private Credit Bureaux without first issuing a demand notice.
questionBank.ans: Access a defaulter's funds in other banks, through the CBN, to repay debts owed on utilized facilities.
questionBank.exp: Manual: by virtue of the GSI clause, 'banks will have access to funds of defaulters in other banks to repay debts owed on utilized facilities through CBN,' using the CBN to track and instruct other banks via the borrower's BVN. B, C, and D misstate this mechanism.

questionBank.q: By signing the GSI undertaking, what does the manual say a borrower waives, and what does he agree to do for his other banks?
opts: He waives his right to dispute the underlying facility amount in any future court proceeding.
He waives his right to confidentiality and indemnifies his other banks for that purpose.
He waives his right to receive any further statement of account from his other banks.
He waives his right to open any new account with any other bank for the facility's duration.
questionBank.ans: He waives his right to confidentiality and indemnifies his other banks for that purpose.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'By virtue of the undertaking, borrowers also waive their right to confidentiality and indemnify their other banks for that purpose.' A, C, and D are not stated consequences.

questionBank.q: Among the manual's tips to reduce recovery stress, what does it recommend regarding a business that revolves around one key individual, where the business risks failing if he dies?
opts: Insist the individual personally guarantees the facility.
Consider a Keyman Insurance policy.
Decline the facility outright regardless of the credit proposal's strength.
Require him to transfer his business shares as security.
questionBank.ans: Consider a Keyman Insurance policy.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Where business revolves around one person and there is a risk of business failure if he dies, consider a Keyman Insurance policy.' A, C, and D are not the stated recommendation.

questionBank.q: Among the manual's tips to reduce recovery stress, what does it recommend a bank obtain before treating a loan to a company as duly authorized?
opts: A personal guarantee from every director, regardless of size.
A Board resolution.
A letter of comfort from a parent company, if one exists.
A certified valuation of every balance-sheet asset.
questionBank.ans: A Board resolution.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Ensure that loans to companies are authorized by their board by obtaining a Board resolution.' A, C, and D are not the stated recommendation.

questionBank.q: Setting aside the misrepresentation of his age, which principle most directly governs whether Ikemefuna can be held personally liable on the loan used to buy the power bike, watch, and sunglasses?
opts: Quantum meruit, since part-performance of the loan disbursement entitles the bank to pro-rated repayment.
Contractual capacity, since a loan for non-necessary luxury items is generally unenforceable against a minor.
Privity of contract, since only Ikemefuna and the bank are parties and no third party may enforce the loan.
Beneficial contract of service, since the loan funded acquisitions comparable to a contract of employment.
questionBank.ans: Contractual capacity, since a loan for non-necessary luxury items is generally unenforceable against a minor.
questionBank.exp: Manual, 'Contractual Capacity/Personality': minors are non-persons in law except for contracts for necessaries of life and beneficial contracts of service, in which they are liable as adults. A power bike, watch, and sunglasses are not necessaries, so the loan is generally unenforceable against Ikemefuna personally. A, C, and D are real contract-law concepts from the same section but misapplied here.
questionBank.case: Ikemefuna, a 16-year-old secondary school student, had operated a savings account at your bank for over three years before reaching that age. Recently, he visited a branch to open a current account and apply for a personal loan. To support the application, he presented an authentic driver's licence — genuinely issued by the licensing authority — showing his date of birth as making him 23 years old, though he is in fact 16. Relying on this document, the branch opened the current account and approved a loan facility. With the funds, Ikemefuna purchased a Yamaha power bike, a Rolex wristwatch, and a pair of Giorgio Armani sunglasses. To reassure the bank of repayment, he introduced a guarantor — his friend's uncle, Mr. Eze — who signed the bank's standard deed of guarantee undertaking to repay the facility if Ikemefuna defaulted. Ikemefuna has since defaulted on the loan repayments entirely, and the bank is now considering its options for recovering the outstanding debt from him, from Mr. Eze, or from both.

questionBank.q: What formality does the law impose specifically on Mr. Eze's deed of guarantee, distinguishing it from most other contracts Ikemefuna could have entered into?
opts: The guarantee is a Simple Contract, so it may be made in any form without any documentary requirement.
The guarantee is a Formal Contract, so the law requires it to be in writing to be enforceable.
The guarantee is a Formal Contract, so it requires the Governor's consent before it takes effect.
The guarantee is a Simple Contract, so it must be stamped and registered at the Lands Registry to be valid.
questionBank.ans: The guarantee is a Formal Contract, so the law requires it to be in writing to be enforceable.
questionBank.exp: Manual, 'Essentials of a Contract – Compliance with formality': Formal/Specialty Contracts, which include contracts of Guarantee, must be in writing. C confuses this with the Governor's consent required for land transactions under the Land Use Act; A and D misclassify the guarantee as a Simple Contract.

opts: The bank may foreclose Mr. Eze's equity of redemption, since foreclosure follows automatically from any default.
The bank may sue Mr. Eze directly, since every lender has a right to sue upon default.
The bank may apply for Mr. Eze's receivership, since receivership is available against any individual guarantor.
The bank may enter into possession of Mr. Eze's property, since entry into possession applies to all guarantee arrangements.
questionBank.ans: The bank may sue Mr. Eze directly, since every lender has a right to sue upon default.

opts: The Contractual Capacity doctrine, which requires banks to confirm a customer's age before honouring any cheque.
KYC principles under the Money Laundering (Prohibition) Act, which require banks to verify identity before opening accounts.
The Duty of Confidentiality, which requires banks to verify identity before disclosing account details.
The Right of Lien, which requires banks to verify identity before retaining property in the ordinary course.

questionBank.q: What specifically triggers Mr. Eze's obligation to pay under the deed of guarantee he signed?
opts: Mr. Eze's obligation is triggered by any loss suffered by the bank, whether or not Ikemefuna has defaulted.
Mr. Eze's obligation is triggered by Ikemefuna's default on repayment of the loan facility.
Mr. Eze's obligation is triggered automatically the moment the deed of guarantee is signed and dated.
Mr. Eze's obligation is triggered only if Ikemefuna dies before completing repayment of the facility.

opts: File a winding-up petition against Mr. Eze under the Companies and Allied Matters Act.
Issue a demand notice to Mr. Eze requiring payment following Ikemefuna's default.
Apply to the court for a receivership order over Mr. Eze's personal assets.
Obtain a bankruptcy notice against Mr. Eze under the Bankruptcy Act, 2004.

questionBank.q: If Mr. Eze also happens to maintain a personal savings account at your bank, can the bank simply net off his savings balance against Ikemefuna's defaulted loan using its right of set-off?
opts: Yes, since the right of set-off applies to any account at the same bank, regardless of ownership.
No, since the right of set-off applies only to a debtor's own accounts held in the same right.
Yes, since the right of lien lets the bank retain any property lawfully in its possession.

opts: Yes, since consideration must be adequate and the loan amount matched the value of items purchased.
Yes, since consideration need only be sufficient, and the loan disbursement and repayment promise satisfy that test.
No, since the agreement lacked an intention to create legal relations, which courts never presume in lending transactions.

Counterfeiting currency under the Counterfeit Currency Act, since he used a fraudulent instrument to obtain funds.
Accessory after the fact under section 519 of the Criminal Code Act, since he assisted another offender escape punishment.
