The drawer is liable on the altered amount, since the alteration was made after the cheque was issued.
questionBank.ans: The drawer remains liable on the original terms of the cheque, and the alteration is void.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a material alteration to a negotiable instrument without the drawer's consent renders the instrument void as to the drawer, who remains liable only on the original terms. B overstates the consequence (the drawer is not completely discharged); C and D misstate the rule.

questionBank.q: A customer has a crossed cheque that he wishes to negotiate to a third party. What is required for the negotiation to be effective, according to the manual?
opts: The cheque must be opened by the drawer before it can be negotiated.
The cheque must be endorsed by the payee and delivered to the third party.
The cheque must be presented to the paying bank for conversion before negotiation.
The cheque must be stamped ad valorem before it can be endorsed.
questionBank.ans: The cheque must be endorsed by the payee and delivered to the third party.
questionBank.exp: Manual: negotiation is achieved 'through an endorsement which is a valid instruction written on the back of a bill and which when signed transfers the total value of the bill to the endorsee.' A misapplies the crossing opening rule; C and D are not stated requirements.

questionBank.q: Upon the death of a partner in a partnership that operates without a partnership deed, what happens to the partnership's bank account and the surviving partners' authority to operate it?
opts: The partnership automatically dissolves, and the surviving partners must close the account immediately.
The partnership automatically dissolves, and the surviving partners should inform the bank of the dissolution.
The partnership continues unchanged, since the death of a partner has no effect without a court order.
The partnership continues, but only the deceased partner's next of kin may operate the account.
questionBank.ans: The partnership automatically dissolves, and the surviving partners should inform the bank of the dissolution.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'the death of a partner ordinarily dissolves a partnership unless they have a deed that provides otherwise.' The surviving partners should inform the bank so the account can be properly handled. A overstates the immediate closure requirement; C and D misstate the effect of dissolution.

questionBank.q: Under Section 19(1)(b) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what restriction applies to a bank granting an advance against the security of its own shares?
opts: Banks may freely grant advances against their own shares without any restriction.
Banks cannot grant advances against their own shares without CBN's prior written approval.
Banks may grant advances against their own shares only to existing shareholders.
Banks may grant advances against their own shares only up to N100,000 per borrower.
questionBank.ans: Banks cannot grant advances against their own shares without CBN's prior written approval.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 19(1)(b): prohibits a bank from granting 'any advance against the security of its own shares or any unsecured advances...unless authorized by the bank's rules and adequate security taken where the rules state that security is to be taken.' A, C, and D misstate this restriction.

questionBank.q: Under Section 29(4) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what obligation does every bank have in relation to examiners appointed by the CBN?
opts: Banks must produce all books, accounts, documents and information which the examiners may require.
Banks must produce only the documents specifically listed in the bank's constitution.
Banks must produce documents only after obtaining the customer's written consent.
Banks must produce documents only once the examiner has obtained a court order.
questionBank.ans: Banks must produce all books, accounts, documents and information which the examiners may require.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 29(4): 'provides that every bank shall produce to the examiners at such times as the examiners may specify, all books, accounts, documents and information which they may require.' B, C, and D invent restrictions not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: Under Section 46 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what is the consequence for a director or employee who receives a prohibited commission, gift or gratuity for rendering any banking service?
opts: Only the recipient is liable to a fine, with no other consequence.
The recipient is liable to a fine, imprisonment, or both, plus forfeiture of the gain to the Federal Government.
The recipient must return the gain to the bank, but faces no criminal liability.
The recipient is liable only if the value of the gift exceeds N1,000,000.
questionBank.ans: The recipient is liable to a fine, imprisonment, or both, plus forfeiture of the gain to the Federal Government.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 46: directors and employees are prohibited from receiving such items, and the 'Penalty for breaches include fines, imprisonment or both plus forfeiture of the gain to the Federal Government.' A, C, and D misstate or narrow this consequence.

questionBank.q: Under the Land Use Act as cited in the manual, what is required before a holder of a statutory right of occupancy may alienate his right by assignment, mortgage, transfer of possession, sublease or otherwise?
opts: Only registration of the transaction at the Corporate Affairs Commission.
The prior consent of the Governor.
Only payment of the prescribed stamp duty.
A resolution of the Local Government Council.
questionBank.ans: The prior consent of the Governor.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 22: 'A holder of a statutory right of Occupancy cannot alienate his right by assignment, mortgage, transfer of possession, sublease or otherwise howsoever without the prior consent of the Governor.' A, C, and D are not the stated requirement.

questionBank.q: Under the Land Use Act as cited in the manual, for what purpose may the Governor revoke a right of occupancy, and what compensation is payable?
opts: For any reason at the Governor's absolute discretion, with no compensation payable.
For overriding public interest, with compensation for the value of unexhausted improvements.
Only for non-payment of ground rent, with compensation for the full market value.
For any breach of the terms of the right, with compensation for the value of the land only.
questionBank.ans: For overriding public interest, with compensation for the value of unexhausted improvements.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 28: 'It shall be lawful for the Governor to revoke a right of Occupancy for overriding public interest.' Section 29 provides that revocation attracts 'compensation for the value at the date of revocation of their unexhausted improvements.' A, C, and D misstate the grounds or compensation.

questionBank.q: A company issues a debenture creating a floating charge over all its present and future assets. When does the charge crystallize and affix to specific assets?
opts: Immediately upon execution of the debenture document.
At the point of default by the company on the secured debt.
Only when the company voluntarily winds up its operations.
Only when a court order specifically directs the charge to crystallize.
questionBank.ans: At the point of default by the company on the secured debt.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a floating charge 'hovers over the company's floating assets...The charge affixes unto the existing products only at the point of default.' A, C, and D misstate this crystallization trigger.

questionBank.q: A bank takes a charge over a company's assets and registers it at the Corporate Affairs Commission. What is the effect of registration on the bank's priority over other creditors?
opts: Registration gives the bank priority only over unsecured creditors.
Registration preserves the bank's priority over other claimants who register later.
Registration gives the bank priority over all other creditors regardless of when they registered.
Registration has no effect on priority, which is determined solely by the date of the underlying contract.
questionBank.ans: Registration preserves the bank's priority over other claimants who register later.
questionBank.exp: Manual: perfection through registration 'preserves the bank's priority over any other claimant.' Registration does not necessarily defeat earlier registered charges, but it does preserve priority against later registrants. A, C, and D misstate the effect of registration.

questionBank.q: A bank accepts a life insurance policy as security for a loan. What is the critical factor in determining the current value of the policy as security?
opts: The face value of the policy, which is the sum assured.
The surrender value, which represents the policy's current worth.
The total premiums paid to date, without regard to the surrender value.
The policy's maturity value, regardless of when it matures.
questionBank.ans: The surrender value, which represents the policy's current worth.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Assurance policies must have a current value to be acceptable as security. That present value is known as the 'surrender value'.' A, C, and D are not the term used or misstate the relevant value.

questionBank.q: A bank has obtained a judgment against a defaulting debtor who owns a house and operates a business. Which enforcement route would the manual describe as involving the seizure and sale of the debtor's property to satisfy the judgment?
opts: Garnishee Order, which attaches money owed to the debtor by a third party.
Levying execution on personal or real property belonging to the debtor.
Foreclosure, which divests the mortgagor of its equity of redemption.
Receivership, which appoints a receiver to manage the debtor's property.
questionBank.ans: Levying execution on personal or real property belonging to the debtor.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a judgment creditor can enforce judgment through 'Levying execution on personal or real property belonging to the debtor.' A is a separate remedy (attaching money owed by a third party); C and D are mortgagee/debenture holder remedies, not judgment creditor enforcement against property generally.

questionBank.q: A bank has a perfected security over a defaulting debtor's property, but the debtor's business is still operating and has ongoing contracts. Which remedy might the bank use to protect its interest without necessarily selling the property immediately?
opts: Sale of the security asset, since that is always the preferred remedy.
Appointment of a Receiver to manage the debtor's property pending realization.
Foreclosure, to divest the debtor of its equity of redemption immediately.
Winding-up, to ensure all creditors are treated equally.
questionBank.ans: Appointment of a Receiver to manage the debtor's property pending realization.
questionBank.exp: Manual: Receivership is 'one of the extreme measures of recovery which is open to a creditor/mortgagee,' and a receiver can manage the debtor's property. Sale is a different remedy; foreclosure is a court order; winding-up applies to companies.

questionBank.q: Under the Global Standing Instruction (GSI) clause, what must the borrower have signed before the bank can access his funds in other banks through the CBN?
opts: A Deed of Guarantee & Indemnity from the borrower's next of kin.
An undertaking in the credit offer letter agreeing to the GSI mechanism.
A Letter of Comfort from the borrower's holding company.
A resolution of the borrower's board of directors authorizing the GSI.
questionBank.ans: An undertaking in the credit offer letter agreeing to the GSI mechanism.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the GSI requires 'a clause in all their credit offer letters to be signed by all borrowers before disbursement of credit to them.' A, C, and D are not the stated requirement.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT listed in the manual as one of the qualifications or disqualifications for appointment as a director of a bank under BOFIA Section 47(2)?
opts: Being of unsound mind.
Being bankrupt.
Being convicted for dishonesty or serious misconduct.
Being a non-Nigerian citizen without a valid work permit.
questionBank.ans: Being a non-Nigerian citizen without a valid work permit.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 47(2)(a): disqualifications include 'of unsound mind, bankrupt, convict for dishonesty or serious misconduct.' Non-Nigerian citizenship without a work permit is not listed as a disqualification. A, B, and C are real disqualifications, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: A bank customer wishes to withdraw from his account using a cheque drawn on the account. The cheque is not signed by the customer in the manner specified in the bank's records. What is the bank's obligation?
opts: The bank must honour the cheque if the customer's identity can be verified.
The bank must dishonour the cheque, since it must only honour drawings by the customer in proper form.
The bank must refer the cheque to a court for determination of validity.
The bank must pay the cheque but note the irregular signature for future reference.
questionBank.ans: The bank must dishonour the cheque, since it must only honour drawings by the customer in proper form.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the bank must honour drawings on demand 'provided his instruction is made in proper form.' A, C, and D are not consistent with the proper form requirement.

questionBank.q: A bank receives notice that one of its customers has become bankrupt. Under the manual's termination grounds, what is the effect on the customer's banking contract?
opts: The contract is automatically terminated on notice of the customer's bankruptcy.
The contract is suspended only, pending the outcome of the bankruptcy proceedings.
The contract continues unchanged, since bankruptcy only affects the customer's assets.
The contract automatically converts into a trust account for the benefit of the customer's creditors.
questionBank.ans: The contract is automatically terminated on notice of the customer's bankruptcy.
questionBank.exp: Manual lists 'Insolvency of an individual or company' as a ground for termination of the banking contract. A correctly identifies automatic termination; B, C, and D are not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: A customer claims that a bank employee made a false statement about his credit history to a credit bureau, damaging his reputation. Which tort does this most closely resemble?
opts: Defamation, a statement injuring reputation and exposing to contempt.
Negligence, an omission to do what a reasonable person would do.
Conversion, an unjustifiable interference with a person's chattel.
Nuisance, injury to a neighbour's enjoyment of his land.
questionBank.ans: Defamation, a statement injuring reputation and exposing to contempt.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'Defamation: A statement which injures the reputation of the person to whom it refers and which exposes him to hatred, contempt, ridicule, fear, dislike or disesteem.' B, C, and D are other listed torts, misapplied here.

questionBank.q: Under Section 516 of the Criminal Code Act as cited in the manual, what is the mens rea requirement for the offence of conspiracy to commit a felony?
opts: An actual agreement between two or more persons to commit a felony.
An overt act in furtherance of the felony by at least one of the conspirators.
Completion of the felony by at least one of the conspirators.
A written agreement signed by all conspirators.
questionBank.ans: An actual agreement between two or more persons to commit a felony.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 516: 'Any person who conspires with another to commit any felony...is guilty of a felony.' The essence is the agreement itself; overt act is not required for this offence as it would be for attempt. B, C, and D misstate the requirement.

questionBank.q: A bank officer receives a garnishee order against a customer's account. According to the manual, what is the officer's immediate obligation?
opts: To refer the order to the Legal Department immediately.
To freeze the account immediately upon receipt of the order.
To notify the customer before taking any action on the order.
To wait for a court hearing before complying with the order.
questionBank.ans: To refer the order to the Legal Department immediately.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'An officer of a bank who receives any court process must ensure that it is immediately referred to the Legal Department.' B is a consequence of an order but not the officer's immediate step; C and D are not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: A bank pays a cheque that is later discovered to have been altered by the payee after it was issued. Does the paying bank have protection if it paid in good faith, without negligence, and in the ordinary course?
opts: Yes, the bank has full protection if it paid in good faith, without negligence, and in the ordinary course.
No, the bank is strictly liable for any alteration to a cheque, regardless of good faith.
Yes, but only if the alteration was of a minor nature, such as a date correction.
No, since the bank must verify the drawer's signature on every payment.
questionBank.ans: Yes, the bank has full protection if it paid in good faith, without negligence, and in the ordinary course.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a paying bank has protection if it 'made the payment in good faith, without negligence and in the ordinary course of business.' B, C, and D misstate this protection.

questionBank.q: A company's Articles of Association contain a provision requiring the bank's consent before the company can borrow above a certain amount. What is the effect of a director borrowing beyond this limit without consent?
opts: The director is personally liable for the excess borrowing under the ultra vires principle.
The company is bound by the borrowing, since the directors have ostensible authority.
The borrowing is void and the bank has no recourse against the company or the director.
The borrowing is valid only if the bank had actual knowledge of the Articles' restriction.
questionBank.ans: The director is personally liable for the excess borrowing under the ultra vires principle.
questionBank.exp: Manual: directors are personally liable for losses or obligations from unauthorized activities not listed in the Memorandum. The Articles' borrowing limit similarly constrains authority. B, C, and D misstate the liability.

questionBank.q: A bank opens an account for an Unincorporated Association and obtains its Constitution and Minutes of the meeting appointing the Trustees. What is the legal effect of these documents on the bank's dealings with the association?
opts: They are irrelevant, since the bank's relationship is solely with the association's members.
They bind the bank to deal only with the Trustees as they are named and appointed in the documents.
They are advisory only, and the bank may deal with any member of the association.
They are required only if the association is incorporated as a company limited by guarantee.
questionBank.ans: They bind the bank to deal only with the Trustees as they are named and appointed in the documents.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the Constitution and Minutes of the meeting where trustees were appointed are required to identify who has authority to operate the account. A, C, and D misstate the effect.

questionBank.q: Under Section 33 of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what is the bank's obligation regarding the cost of a special examination ordered by the CBN Governor?
opts: The cost is borne by the CBN, since it orders the examination.
The cost is borne by the bank, since the examination is conducted at the bank's expense.
The cost is shared equally between the bank and the CBN.
The cost is borne by the bank's shareholders, not the bank itself.
questionBank.ans: The cost is borne by the bank, since the examination is conducted at the bank's expense.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 33: the Governor may appoint persons to conduct special examination 'under conditions of confidentiality, of the books and affairs of the bank (At the bank's expense).' A, C, and D misstate this cost allocation.

questionBank.q: Under Section 47(3) of BOFIA as cited in the manual, what restriction applies to a person related to non-performing credit in relation to directorship in any bank?
opts: Such a person is prevented from being considered as a director in any bank.
Such a person is prevented only from being a director in the bank that granted the non-performing credit.
Such a person may become a director if the non-performing credit is fully written off.
Such a person may become a director if they resign from the borrowing company first.
questionBank.ans: Such a person is prevented from being considered as a director in any bank.
questionBank.exp: Manual, Section 47(3): 'prevents a person related to non-performing credit from being considered as a director in any bank.' B, C, and D narrow or misstate this restriction.

questionBank.q: A bank takes a pledge of goods as security for a loan. What is the bank's obligation regarding the goods while they are in its possession?
opts: The bank may use the goods in its own business operations.
The bank must store the goods and return them on repayment.
The bank may sell the goods immediately to recover the loan.
The bank has no obligation, since the goods are security for the debt.
questionBank.ans: The bank must store the goods and return them on repayment.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a pledge is 'contracted when the debtor delivers to the creditor, the things (goods) hypothecated subject to re-delivery upon repayment of a loan.' A, C, and D are inconsistent with this obligation.

questionBank.q: A bank issues a Performance Bond on behalf of a contractor. The contractor defaults, and the bond holder demands payment from the bank. What must the bank do to ensure it can recover the amount paid from the contractor?
opts: The bank must obtain a counter-indemnity from the contractor before issuing the bond.
The bank must immediately sue the bond holder for an injunction to stop payment.
The bank must refuse payment and defend the claim in court.
The bank must rely on the contractor's goodwill to repay the amount voluntarily.
questionBank.ans: The bank must obtain a counter-indemnity from the contractor before issuing the bond.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A Counter-Indemnity allows an indemnifier to seek reimbursement from the primary obligor in the event that he has to pay any part of a claim.' B, C, and D are not the stated approach.

questionBank.q: A bank has a perfected security over a defaulting debtor's property and wishes to sell it without a court order. Which type of security does the bank hold to enable this?
opts: An equitable mortgage, since it only gives a right to sue.
A legal mortgage, since it gives a right against the property itself.
A floating charge, since it hovers over assets until default.
A personal guarantee, since it gives direct rights over property.
questionBank.ans: A legal mortgage, since it gives a right against the property itself.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'A legal mortgage gives the bank a right against the property itself, thus the bank can sell the property without having to sue or obtain a court Order.' A, C, and D do not give this right.

questionBank.q: A bank's debtor is a natural person who has committed an act of bankruptcy by failing to comply with a bankruptcy notice within 14 days. What is the next procedural step under the Bankruptcy Act?
opts: The debtor's estate is automatically placed under administration.
A bankruptcy petition may be presented against the debtor.
The debtor is immediately adjudicated bankrupt without further hearing.
The debtor's assets are automatically frozen for 21 days.
questionBank.ans: A bankruptcy petition may be presented against the debtor.
questionBank.exp: Manual: the bankruptcy procedure includes 'Presentation of petition' after the occurrence of the act of bankruptcy. A, C, and D are not the immediate next step.

questionBank.q: A bank obtains a Garnishee Order against a third party who owes money to the bank's debtor. What does this order require the third party to do?
opts: Pay the money owed to the debtor directly to the bank.
Freeze the money until the court determines the debtor's liability.
Transfer the money to the debtor's account for the bank to access.
Hold the money in a separate trust account pending the court's final order.
questionBank.ans: Pay the money owed to the debtor directly to the bank.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a garnishee order is one of the ways a judgment creditor can enforce judgment. A correctly states the effect; B, C, and D misstate the operation of the order.

questionBank.q: A minor obtains a loan by falsely representing his age as 18. The bank discovers the truth after the minor defaults. What is the bank's best course of action?
opts: Sue the minor for the full amount, since he misrepresented his age.
Sue the minor only for the value of necessaries purchased with the loan.
Pursue the guarantor, if any, for the full amount of the loan.
Write off the loan, since the minor's contract is void and the guarantor's guarantee is also void.
questionBank.ans: Pursue the guarantor, if any, for the full amount of the loan.
questionBank.exp: Manual: minors are non-persons except for necessaries and beneficial contracts of service; however, a guarantee given by an adult is enforceable against the guarantor. A is ineffective against the minor; B only covers necessaries; D misstates the guarantee's validity.

questionBank.q: A bank lends money to a company whose directors have not obtained a Board resolution authorizing the borrowing. The company defaults. Which of the following best states the bank's position?
opts: The bank has no recourse against the company or the directors, since the borrowing was unauthorized.
The bank may pursue the company if it can show the directors had ostensible authority.
The bank may pursue the directors personally for authorizing the unauthorized borrowing.
The bank must first obtain a court order confirming the validity of the borrowing.
questionBank.ans: The bank may pursue the directors personally for authorizing the unauthorized borrowing.
questionBank.exp: Manual: directors are personally liable for loss or obligations created when they authorize activities not listed in the Memorandum. The absence of a Board resolution also supports personal liability of the directors who authorized it. B, A, and D misstate the position.

questionBank.q: A bank takes a floating charge over a company's assets. The company defaults. What assets does the charge cover at the point of default?
opts: Only the assets the company had on the date the charge was created.
Only the assets the company had on the date the charge crystallized.
All assets the company had on the date of default, including those acquired after the charge was created.
Only the assets specifically listed in the debenture document.
questionBank.ans: All assets the company had on the date of default, including those acquired after the charge was created.
questionBank.exp: Manual: a floating charge hovers over the company's floating assets and affixes to existing products at the point of default. A, B, and D misstate this coverage.

questionBank.q: A bank sells a debtor's pledged goods without giving the debtor notice of the sale and without obtaining a fair market price. What is the bank's obligation to the debtor if there is a surplus?
opts: The bank must retain the surplus as a charge for exercising its right of sale.
The bank must refund the surplus to the debtor after deducting the debt.
The bank must remit the surplus to the court for the debtor to claim.
The bank has no obligation, since the debtor defaulted on the loan.
questionBank.ans: The bank must refund the surplus to the debtor after deducting the debt.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'If the creditor exercises his right of sale, then he must obtain fair market price and refund any surplus to the debtor after deducting his debt.' A, C, and D misstate this obligation.

questionBank.q: A bank lends money to a partnership with three general partners. One of the partners dies. The partnership deed is silent on the death of a partner. What is the effect on the partnership's liability to the bank?
opts: The partnership automatically dissolves, and the debt is immediately due and payable.
The partnership dissolves, but the surviving partners remain jointly and severally liable for the debt.
The partnership continues unchanged, since the debt is to the partnership, not the individual partners.
The debt is extinguished, since the partnership cannot continue without all three partners.
questionBank.ans: The partnership dissolves, but the surviving partners remain jointly and severally liable for the debt.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'the death of a partner ordinarily dissolves a partnership unless they have a deed that provides otherwise.' The surviving partners remain liable for the debts of the partnership. A overstates immediate due and payable; C ignores the dissolution; D extinguishes the debt incorrectly.

questionBank.q: A bank takes a charge over a company's land but fails to register the charge with the Corporate Affairs Commission within the statutory period. What is the consequence under CAMA?
opts: The charge is void against the company's liquidator and any other creditor.
The charge is void, but the bank may claim as an unsecured creditor.
The charge is valid against the company but not against third parties.
The charge is fully valid, since registration is optional under CAMA.
questionBank.ans: The charge is void against the company's liquidator and any other creditor.
questionBank.exp: Manual: 'any charge on property of an incorporated company not registered with the CAC within 90 days is null and void under CAMA.' The charge is void against the liquidator and creditors. B, C, and D misstate this consequence.

questionBank.q: A bank's customer dies intestate, and Letters of Administration are issued appointing an Administrator. The Administrator continues to operate the customer's bank account without the bank's knowledge of the death. What is the bank's liability if the Administrator misappropriates the funds?
opts: The bank has no liability, since it was unaware of the death.
The bank is liable for allowing the account to be operated after the death.
The bank is liable only if it had actual notice of the death.
The bank's liability is limited to the amount misappropriated by the Administrator.
questionBank.ans: The bank is liable for allowing the account to be operated after the death.
questionBank.exp: Manual: on notice of death, the mandate is terminated. The bank is liable for allowing the account to be operated after the death. A, C, and D misstate this liability.

questionBank.q: Zenith Textiles was never a customer of the bank but received payment through the account Uche approved. Can the bank owe Zenith a duty of care despite the absence of any contract between them?
opts: No, since duty of care can only arise from an existing contract.
Yes, since duty of care can arise without any contractual relationship.
No, since duty of care requires the parties to share a bank account.
Yes, but only once a court formally certifies the relationship.
questionBank.ans: Yes, since duty of care can arise without any contractual relationship.
questionBank.exp: Tort liability does not depend on a contractual relationship; Zenith may qualify as a 'neighbour' if closely and directly affected and reasonably within the bank's contemplation. Option A wrongly imports a contract-only view of duty of care that the law of tort does not require.
questionBank.case: Meridian Textiles: A bank's relationship officer, Uche, receives an internal fraud circular flagging a pattern of forged export documents linked to a customer's account. Without escalating or verifying, Uche personally approves an unusually large cross-border remittance for that customer, following his standard practice of trusting long-term clients. The remittance funds a fraud that causes loss to Zenith Textiles Ltd, a foreign supplier who had shipped goods on the strength of the payment appearing to clear. Zenith later discovers the payment was part of a fraudulent scheme and seeks to hold the bank liable, even though Zenith was never the bank's customer. Uche's manager argues Uche followed his own personal sense of what a careful officer would do and should not be judged by any stricter external standard, and further argues the bank cannot be liable since Uche deviated from the bank's own fraud-escalation policy when he approved the remittance without escalating it.

questionBank.q: Uche's manager argues that Uche should be judged only by his own personal sense of what a careful officer would do. Is that the correct test for negligence?
opts: Yes, since due diligence is always measured by personal judgment alone.
No, the test asks what a reasonable banker in his position would do.
Yes, since bank policy alone determines whether conduct was careless.
No, the test asks what the customer expected him to do.
questionBank.ans: No, the test asks what a reasonable banker in his position would do.
questionBank.exp: The test for a banker's negligence is objective - not what appeared reasonable to the person acting, but whether a reasonable banker in that person's shoes would have acted the same way. Option A wrongly substitutes personal judgment for this objective standard.
questionBank.case: Meridian Textiles: A bank's relationship officer, Uche, receives an internal fraud circular flagging a pattern of forged export documents linked to a customer's account. Without escalating or verifying, Uche personally approves an unusually large cross-border remittance for that customer, following his standard practice of trusting long-term clients. The remittance funds a fraud that causes loss to Zenith Textiles Ltd, a foreign supplier who had shipped goods on the strength of the payment appearing to clear. Zenith later discovers the payment was part of a fraudulent scheme and seeks to hold the bank liable, even though Zenith was never the bank's customer. Uche's manager argues Uche followed his own personal sense of what a careful officer would do and should not be judged by any stricter external standard, and further argues the bank cannot be liable since Uche deviated from the bank's own fraud-escalation policy when he approved the remittance without escalating it.

questionBank.q: Uche did not intend for any customer's fraud to succeed, and argues he cannot be liable since he never intended harm. Does the absence of intent shield him from liability in tort?
opts: Yes, since tortious liability always requires proof of deliberate intent to harm.
No, liability is established once a reasonable person could have foreseen the harm.
Yes, since only criminal law punishes conduct absent an intent to harm.
No, but only where the loss suffered exceeds a fixed monetary amount.
questionBank.ans: No, liability is established once a reasonable person could have foreseen the harm.
questionBank.exp: Liability in tort is established once a reasonable person could have foreseen the injury, regardless of whether the actor intended it. Option A wrongly imports a criminal-law-style intent requirement into ordinary negligence.

Only the partner who contributed the largest share of capital to the firm.

questionBank.q: While waiting for the Governor's consent to a full legal mortgage, the bank accepts the deposit of Delta's original title document along with a signed Memorandum of Deposit as interim security. What kind of security interest has the bank obtained at this stage?
opts: A legal mortgage, since the original title document has been physically handed over.
An equitable mortgage, created through the deposit of title documents as security.
A fixed debenture, since the deposit relates to a specific identified asset.
A pledge, since possession of the title document has passed to the bank.
questionBank.ans: An equitable mortgage, created through the deposit of title documents as security.
questionBank.exp: An equitable mortgage can be created without much formality through steps such as depositing the original title document with a Memorandum of Deposit, once it is clear the deposit is made as security. Option A wrongly treats mere deposit as equivalent to a completed legal mortgage requiring full transfer of interest and Governor's consent.
questionBank.case: Delta Aggregates: Delta Aggregates Ltd approaches a bank for a N50,000,000 facility, offering its factory land as security. While waiting for the Governor's consent needed for a full legal mortgage, the bank accepts a deposit of the original title document as interim security, along with a signed Memorandum of Deposit confirming the deposit is made as security for the loan. Before the legal mortgage documentation is completed, Delta separately grants an interest in the same land to another creditor without telling the bank. Delta's facility letter also contains a clause promising it will not pledge its assets to another lender without the bank's consent, but this clause was never registered anywhere.

questionBank.q: At this interim stage, with only the deposit-based mortgage in place, can the bank sell the factory land immediately if Delta defaults, without suing or obtaining a court order?
opts: Yes, since any mortgage over land automatically confers an immediate right of sale.
No, an equitable mortgage only gives the bank a right to sue the mortgagor.
Yes, but only if the Memorandum of Deposit is separately notarized.
No, but only because the facility amount exceeds the bank's internal lending limit.
questionBank.ans: No, an equitable mortgage only gives the bank a right to sue the mortgagor.
questionBank.exp: Unlike a legal mortgage, which gives a right against the property itself, an equitable mortgage only gives the bank a right to sue the mortgagor; it cannot sell without suing or a court order. Option A wrongly generalizes the stronger legal-mortgage right to all mortgages.

The bank's subsequently created legal mortgage can overtake the earlier equitable interest.
Both interests automatically rank equally and share in any eventual recovery.
The earlier dealing is void from the outset for lack of registration.
questionBank.ans: The bank's subsequently created legal mortgage can overtake the earlier equitable interest.
questionBank.exp: A legal mortgage takes priority over other interests, and an existing equitable mortgage can be overtaken by a subsequently created legal mortgage. Option D overstates the consequence, since the material does not say the earlier dealing is void outright, only that it can be overtaken.

No, since the clause is generally not registrable and a later lender gets no notice.
Yes, but only where the later lender specifically searches for negative covenants.
No, but only because Delta itself failed to disclose the clause voluntarily.

questionBank.exp: A negative pledge clause is generally not registrable, so a subsequent lender will have no notice of it even after conducting a title search. Option D misattributes the real cause, non-registrability, to Delta's own disclosure conduct instead.

questionBank.q: Delta goes on to grant security over the same assets to another creditor, breaching its negative pledge undertaking to the bank. What is the bank's remedy for this breach?
opts: To immediately seize the assets pledged to the other creditor without any court process.
To sue, since suing is the only remedy available for breach of this undertaking.
To automatically invalidate the security granted to the other creditor.
To petition for Delta's winding-up as the sole available response to any breach.
questionBank.ans: To sue, since suing is the only remedy available for breach of this undertaking.
questionBank.exp: Where a negative pledge undertaking is breached, the only remedy available to the protected bank is to sue; the clause gives no proprietary right to seize or invalidate the other creditor's security. questionBank.q: Solaris owes the bank N350,000, undisputed and due. The bank serves a written demand at Solaris's registered office, and three weeks pass with no payment, security, or compromise offered. Is Solaris deemed unable to pay its debts for winding-up purposes?
opts: No, since the statutory threshold for this ground is set well above N350,000.
Yes, since the debt exceeds N200,000 and remains unpaid three weeks after demand.
No, since three weeks falls short of the statutory notice period required.
Yes, but only once the bank has also obtained a court judgment against Solaris.
questionBank.ans: Yes, since the debt exceeds N200,000 and remains unpaid three weeks after demand.
questionBank.exp: A company is deemed unable to pay its debts where a creditor owed a sum exceeding N200,000 has served a demand and the company has neglected for three weeks to pay, secure, or compound it; Solaris's facts satisfy this. Option D wrongly adds a judgment requirement that is not part of this particular ground.
questionBank.case: Solaris Agro: Solaris Agro Ltd owes a bank N350,000, undisputed and due. The bank serves a written demand on Solaris at its registered office, and three weeks pass with no payment, security, or compromise offered. Separately, the bank has already obtained a court judgment against a different debtor, Mr. Tunde, for a personal loan. The bank also holds a floating debenture over Solaris's assets under a separate, larger facility, and is considering appointing a Receiver as debenture holder rather than immediately petitioning to wind up Solaris. The bank also wants to use the Global Standing Instruction mechanism against Mr. Tunde's accounts at other banks.

questionBank.q: Having already obtained judgment against Mr. Tunde, what are the bank's available methods to actually enforce that judgment and recover the sum owed?
opts: Filing a fresh winding-up petition against Mr. Tunde in his personal capacity.
Levying execution on his property, or obtaining a Garnishee Order.
Automatically converting the judgment into a perfected legal mortgage over his assets.
Requesting the CBN to revoke Mr. Tunde's personal bank verification number.
questionBank.ans: Levying execution on his property, or obtaining a Garnishee Order.
questionBank.exp: A judgment creditor can enforce judgment by levying execution on the debtor's property, or by obtaining a Garnishee Order against a third party holding the debtor's funds. Option A wrongly applies winding-up, a company-specific process, to an individual debtor.

questionBank.q: As debenture holder, the bank decides to appoint a Receiver over Solaris's assets rather than petition for winding-up. Within how many days must notice of this appointment be filed with the CAC, given that creditors rather than the court are making the appointment?
opts: Within 7 days, the period that applies to a court-ordered appointment.
Within 14 days, the period that applies to a creditor-made appointment.
Within 21 days, matching the statutory demand period for winding-up.
Within 30 days, matching a bankruptcy notice period.
questionBank.ans: Within 14 days, the period that applies to a creditor-made appointment.
questionBank.exp: Notice of a Receiver's appointment must be filed with the CAC within 14 days where the appointment is made by creditors, as opposed to 7 days for a court-made appointment. Options C and D borrow unrelated timeframes from the winding-up demand period and bankruptcy procedures respectively.

questionBank.q: Suppose the bank instead proceeds to present a winding-up petition against Solaris. What is the immediate effect on Solaris's Board and assets as soon as the petition is presented?
opts: Nothing changes until the court formally grants the winding-up order at hearing.
Solaris's assets are frozen and its employees and Board stand dismissed immediately.
Only Solaris's bank accounts are frozen, while the Board continues to function.
The Board is suspended, but the company's assets remain freely transferable.
questionBank.ans: Solaris's assets are frozen and its employees and Board stand dismissed immediately.
questionBank.exp: As soon as a winding-up petition is presented, the company's assets are frozen and all employees and the Board stand dismissed, well before any final hearing. Options C and D each wrongly preserve part of the company's operations that are in fact affected immediately.

questionBank.q: The bank wants to use the Global Standing Instruction mechanism to recover from Mr. Tunde's accounts at other banks, but Mr. Tunde never signed any GSI undertaking in his original credit offer letter. Can the bank still invoke the mechanism against him?
opts: Yes, since the GSI mechanism applies automatically to every bank customer nationwide.
No, the mechanism depends on the borrower having signed the GSI undertaking beforehand.
Yes, but only if the CBN separately approves an exception for this specific case.
No, but only because Mr. Tunde's facility was personal rather than corporate.

opts: Nothing changes until a court specifically orders the account frozen.
The mandate is terminated, since notice of a customer's death is a recognized ground.
The mandate continues unchanged until the executor formally objects.
The mandate converts automatically into a joint account with her next of kin.
questionBank.ans: The mandate is terminated, since notice of a customer's death is a recognized ground.
questionBank.exp: Notice of the death of a customer is one of the recognized grounds for termination of the banking contract or mandate. Option A wrongly requires a separate court order before any effect arises.

Letters of Probate, issued to the persons named as Executors in a Will.
A Guardian's appointment, issued to administer the affairs of a mentally infirm person.
A Jurat, endorsed by a Magistrate confirming the Will was read and explained to her.
questionBank.ans: Letters of Probate, issued to the persons named as Executors in a Will.
questionBank.exp: Since Mrs. Adigwe died testate, having left a Will naming Executors, the appropriate court approval is Letters of Probate. Option A wrongly applies the intestate procedure to a case where a valid Will exists.

Yes, Executors are empowered to initiate and defend suits relating to the estate.
